A pleasant judgment, that that proud one, the hammerer of the humble, unknowing, forges everlasting crowns for those same ones, by attacking all, and by succumbing to all. For everywhere and always the Lord will judge the peoples, and will save the sons of the poor, and will humble the false accuser. Everywhere, and always, he will defend his own, he will drive off those who harm, and he will take the rod of sinners away from above the lot of the just, so that the just may not stretch out their hands to iniquity (Ps. 125:3); and there will be a time at last when he will altogether break the bow, and shatter the arms, and burn the shields with fire. You, wretch, set a seat for yourself in the north, a region cloudy and cold; and behold, the needy are raised from the dust, and the poor from the dung, that they may sit with princes, and hold the throne of glory, and you may grieve that this is fulfilled: 'The poor and the needy shall praise your name' (Ps. 74:21).
17.7: Thanks to you, father of orphans and judge of wards: the curdled mountain has grown warm upon us, the fat mountain, the heavens have dropped at the face of the God of Sinai, the oil has been poured out, the name has been enlarged, which the wicked one envied us, and us to it; enlarged, I say, even to the hearts and mouths of little ones, and in the mouth of infants and of nursing children praise is perfected. But the sinner will see and be angry; and as the wrath is implacable, so the flame is inextinguishable, which is already prepared for him and for his angels. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this. How do you love me, my God, my love? how do you love me, remembering me everywhere, everywhere jealous for the salvation of the needy and the poor, not only against proud men, but also against the sublime angels? In heaven and on earth you judge, O Lord, those who harm me, you fight down those who attack me; everywhere you come to help, everywhere you stand by, everywhere you are at my right hand, O Lord, lest I be moved. These things I will sing to the Lord in my life, I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am. These are his virtues, these the wonders which he has done. This is the first and greatest judgment, which the virgin Mary, knowing the secrets, opened to me: 'He has put down,' she says, 'the mighty from their seat, and exalted the humble.' 'The hungry he has filled with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty' (Luke 1:52, 53). But the second is like this, which you have already heard, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind (John 9:39). In these two judgments let the poor man console himself, and say: 'I have remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and I have been comforted' (Ps. 119:52).
17.8: But let us return to ourselves, and let us search out our ways; and that we may be able to do this in truth, let us call upon the Spirit of truth, and call him back from the height to which he had led us, so that he may go before us even to ourselves, since without him we can do nothing. Nor is it to be feared that he disdains to come down to us, who rather is indignant if we attempt even a very little without him. For he is not one who goes and does not return, but he leads us and leads us back from glory to glory, as the Spirit of the Lord, sometimes catching us up to himself in his light, sometimes tempering himself, and enlightening our darkness, so that whether above us or with us, we may always walk in the light, always as sons of light. We have passed through the shadows of the allegories; we have come to searching out the moral senses. Faith has been built up, let life be instructed; the understanding has been exercised, let action be prescribed. For a good understanding is for all who do it (Ps. 111:10), if, however, both action and understanding are directed to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed unto ages. Amen.

18.1: 'Your name is oil poured out' (Song 1:2). What certain thing does the Holy Spirit show us in ourselves on the occasion of this chapter? Surely, what occurs for the time being, the experience of a certain twofold operation of his; of one, indeed, by which he first strengthens us within with virtues unto salvation; but of the other, by which he also adorns us without with gifts unto gain. Those we receive for ourselves, these for our own people. For example, faith, hope, and charity are given to us for our own sake; for without these we cannot be saved. But the word of knowledge or of wisdom, the grace of healing, prophecy, and the like, which we can lack even with the wholeness of our own salvation, are given, without doubt, to be spent for the salvation of our neighbors. And these operations of the Holy Spirit, which we experience either in ourselves or in others, that they may receive names from the thing itself, let us call, if you please, infusion and effusion. To which of these, I ask, does 'Your name is oil poured out' belong? Is it not to the effusion? For of an infusion he would rather have said 'poured in' than 'poured out.' Finally, on account of the good odor of the breasts steeped from without, the bride says: 'Your name is oil poured out,' ascribing the odor itself to the name of the bridegroom, as to oil poured out upon the breasts. And whoever feels himself steeped with the gift of an outward grace, by which he too can pour it back upon others, for him also there is reason to say: 'Your name is oil poured out.'
18.2: But one must surely beware in these things either of giving what we have received for ourselves, or of keeping what we have received to be spent. You keep for yourself, surely, what belongs to your neighbor, if, for example, though you are full of virtues, and adorned besides with the gifts of knowledge and of eloquence, by fear perhaps, or by sluggishness, or by a humility less discerning, you bind with a useless, nay, even a damnable silence the good word which could profit many; cursed, certainly, because you hide the wheat among the peoples (Prov. 11:26). Again, you scatter and lose what is yours, if, before you yourself have been wholly poured into, half full you hasten to pour out, plowing with the firstborn of the ox against the law, and shearing the firstborn of the sheep (Deut. 15:19). Surely you defraud yourself of the life and the salvation which you give to another, while, empty of a sound intention, you are puffed up by the wind of empty glory, or infected by the poison of earthly desire, and you perish, swelling with a deadly abscess.
18.3: Wherefore, if you are wise, you will show yourself a basin, and not a channel. For the latter almost at the same moment both receives and pours back; but the former waits until it is filled; and so it shares what overflows, without loss to itself, knowing that he is cursed who makes his own part worse. And lest you think my counsel contemptible, hear one wiser than I: 'The fool,' says Solomon, 'pours out all his spirit at once; the wise man reserves it for afterward' (Prov. 29:11). But we have many channels in the Church today, and very few basins. Of so great a charity are those through whom the heavenly streams flow to us, that they wish to pour out before they are poured into, readier to speak than to hear, and prompt to teach what they have not learned, and eager to be set over others, who do not know how to rule themselves. I think that no degree of piety unto salvation is to be set before that degree which the Wise Man set, saying: 'Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God' (Sir. 30:24). But if I have only a little oil with which to anoint myself, do you think I ought to give it to you, and remain empty? I keep it for myself, and I do not bring it out at all except at the prophet's command. If some of those press on with asking, who perhaps think of me above what they see in me, or hear something from me, it will be answered them: 'Lest perhaps there be not enough for us and for you, go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves' (Matt. 25:9). But charity, you say, does not seek what is its own (1 Cor. 13:5). And do you know for what reason? it does not seek what is its own, surely because those things are not lacking. Who, pray, seeks what he has? Charity never fails to have what is its own, that is, the things necessary for its own salvation; nor does it only have them, but it even abounds. It wishes to abound for itself, so that it may be able to do so for all; it keeps for itself as much as suffices, so that it may fail none. Otherwise, if it is not full, it is not perfect.
18.4: But you, brother, whose own salvation is not yet firm enough, whose charity is still either nothing, or so tender and reedy that it yields to every breath, believes every spirit, is carried about by every wind of doctrine; nay, whose charity is so great that, beyond the commandment indeed, you love your neighbor more than yourself: and again so small that, against the commandment, it melts with favor, fails with fear, is disturbed by sadness, is contracted by avarice, is drawn out by ambition, is disquieted by suspicions, is harried by insults, is gutted by cares, swells with honors, wastes with envy: you, I say, feeling yourself thus in your own affairs, with what madness, I ask, do you either strive to care for the affairs of others, or consent to it? But hear, indeed, what a cautious and watchful charity advises. 'Not that there should be relief for others,' he says, 'and tribulation for you, but by equality' (2 Cor. 8:13). 'Do not be righteous overmuch' (Eccl. 7:16). It is enough that you love your neighbor as yourself; for this is by equality. David says: 'Let my soul be filled as with fat and with richness, and my mouth shall praise with lips of exultation' (Ps. 63:5): wishing, surely, to be poured into first, and so to pour out; and not only to be poured into first, but also to be filled, so that he might pour forth from fullness, and not yawn from emptiness. Cautiously, indeed: lest what was relief for others should be tribulation for himself; and nonetheless chastely, imitating him of whose fullness we have all received. Learn you also to pour out only from what is full, nor wish to be more generous than God. Let the basin imitate the fountain. That one does not flow into a stream, nor is it extended into a lake, until it is sated with its own waters. Let the basin not be ashamed not to be more overflowing than its fountain. Finally, the fountain of life itself, full in itself, and full of itself, did it not first, boiling up and leaping into the nearest secret places of the heavens, fill all things with goodness; and then at last, the higher and more secret parts having been filled, burst forth to the earth, and from the overflow save men and beasts, according as he multiplied his mercy? First he filled the inner places; and so, overflowing in his many compassions, he visited the earth, and made it drunk, he multiplied to enrich it. Do you also, then, do likewise. Be filled first, and so take care to pour out. A kindly and prudent charity is accustomed to flow in abundance, not to flow away. 'My son, do not flow clean away,' says Solomon; and the Apostle: 'Therefore,' he says, 'we ought to attend to the things that are said, lest perhaps we drift away' (Heb. 2:1). What then? are you then holier than Paul, wiser than Solomon? Otherwise it does not please me, either, to be enriched from you emptied out. For if you are wicked to yourself, to whom will you be good? From your abundance, if you are able, help me; but if not, spare yourself.
18.5: But hear now what things, and how great, are necessary for one's own salvation, what things, and how great, ought to be poured in, before we presume to pour out, which, however, I shall be able for the present to gather briefly. For the hour has already climbed high, and presses the sermon to its end. The physician draws near to the wounded man, the spirit to the soul. For whom does he not find wounded by the sword of the devil, even after the wound of the ancient offense has been healed by the medicine of baptism? To that soul, then, which says: 'My scars have putrefied and are corrupted, from the face of my folly' (Ps. 38:5); when the spirit draws near, what is needed first? That the swelling, or the proud flesh, which has perhaps grown up over the wound, and can hinder healing, be cut away before all else. Let the sore of an inveterate habit, then, be cut off with the knife of sharp compunction. But the pain is bitter; let it therefore be soothed with the ointment of devotion, which is nothing else than the exultation conceived from the hope of pardon: this the faculty of continence brings forth, and victory over sin. Now she gives thanks, and says: 'You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise' (Ps. 116:16, 17). Then the medicine of penance is applied, a poultice of fasts, of vigils, of prayers, and whatever other exercises of penitents there are. In the labor he must be fed with the food of a good work, lest he fail. That a work is food, you are taught from this: 'My food is,' he says, 'that I may do the will of my Father' (John 4:34). Let the works of piety, then, which strengthen, accompany the labors of penance. 'Almsgiving,' he says, 'affords great confidence before the Most High' (Tob. 4:12). Food stirs thirst; he must be given drink. Let the drink of prayer come to the food of a good work, settling in the stomach of the conscience what has been well done, and commending it to God. By praying one drinks the wine that gladdens the heart of man, the wine of the spirit, which makes drunk, and pours in forgetfulness of carnal pleasures. It moistens the inward parts of a dry conscience, digests the foods of good acts, and leads them through certain members of the soul, strengthening faith, comforting hope, quickening and ordering charity, and fattening the manners.
18.6: Food and drink having been taken, what now remains, except that the sick man rest, and lie down to the quiet of contemplation after the sweats of action? Sleeping in contemplation, he dreams of God; for the time being, indeed, he looks through a mirror and in an enigma, but not face to face. Yet thus, of one not so much gazed upon as guessed at, and that suddenly and as if under a certain flashing of a spark passing by, barely and thinly touched, he catches fire with love, and says: 'My soul has desired you in the night, but my spirit also within my breast' (Isa. 26:9). Such love is jealous; this befits the friend of the bridegroom, with this the faithful and prudent servant, whom the Lord has set over his household, must needs burn. This fills, this glows, this boils over, this now pours out securely, overflowing and bursting forth, and saying: 'Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is scandalized, and I do not burn?' (2 Cor. 11:29.) Let him preach, let him bear fruit, let him renew signs, and change wonders: there is no place for vanity to mix itself in, where charity occupies the whole. For the fullness of the law and of the heart is charity (Rom. 13:10), if, however, it is full. Finally, God is charity (1 John 4:16), and there is nothing among things which can fill the creature made to the image of God, except charity, which is God, who alone is greater than that creature. He who has not yet attained it is promoted most dangerously, however great he may seem to be in other virtues. If he has all knowledge, if he has given all his substance to the poor, if he has delivered his body so that it burns, without charity he is empty. See how much must first be poured in, that we may dare to pour out, giving from fullness, not from want: first, indeed, compunction; then devotion; third, the labor of penance; fourth, the work of piety; fifth, the pursuit of prayer; sixth, the leisure of contemplation; seventh, the fullness of love. All these things one and the same Spirit works, according to the operation which is called infusion; so that that which has been called effusion may now be administered purely, and for this reason safely, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God unto ages of ages. Amen.

19.1: The loving bride still speaks, still goes on to pursue the praises of the Spouse at greater length; and she provokes grace, while she shows that what she had already received was not empty in her. 'Therefore,' she says, 'the young maidens have loved you exceedingly' (Song 1:2). As if she said: Not in vain nor emptily was your name emptied out, O Spouse, and poured out into my breasts; for therefore the young maidens have loved you exceedingly. For what reason? For the name poured out, and for the breasts steeped from it. For from that they were stirred up to the love of the Spouse; from that they took occasion to love. While the bride received the poured-in gift, they at once perceived the fragrance, who could not be far from the mother; and filled with that sweetness they say: 'The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us' (Rom. 5:5). Therefore the bride, commending their devotion: 'This,' she says, 'O Spouse, is the fruit of your name poured out, that therefore the young maidens have loved you.' For they perceive it poured out, which they were not able to receive whole; therefore they have loved you. For the pouring out makes the name receivable; the reception makes it lovable, but only to the young maidens. Those who are more capacious rejoice in the whole; they have no need of the poured-out.
19.2: The angelic creature beholds with unblunted keenness of mind the great abyss of the divine judgments, and, blessed with ineffable delight in their supreme equity, it glories moreover that they are consigned to effect through its ministry and made manifest; and therefore it deservedly loves the Lord Christ. 'Are they not all,' he says, 'ministering spirits, sent into ministry for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation?' (Heb. 1:14). Moreover the archangels (to attribute to them something more distinguished than those who are simply angels) delight, I believe, wonderfully, in that they are admitted more familiarly even to the counsels of eternal Wisdom, and that through them those counsels are administered, each in its own places and times, with the highest governance. And this is the reason why they too love the Lord Christ. Those blessednesses also, which are perhaps for that reason called virtues, in that they are divinely ordained, with a happy curiosity, to search out and admire the hidden and perpetual causes of virtues and prodigies, and to exhibit from all the elements of the earth, powerfully, whatever signs they wish, and when they wish: they too, therefore, not without merit, burn from that to love the Lord of virtues, and Christ, the power of God. For it is full of sweetness and grace to behold, in Wisdom herself, the uncertain and hidden things of wisdom; and none the less full of honor and glory that the workings of causes hidden in the Word of God, to be shown and admired to the world, are directed in their hand.
19.3: But those spirits also, who are called powers, while they delight to behold and magnify the divine omnipotence of our Crucified One, reaching mightily everywhere, receive power to drive out and conquer the contrary powers of demons and of men, on behalf of those who receive the inheritance of salvation. And do not these have the most just cause to love the Lord Jesus? And there are above these the principalities, who, contemplating him more deeply, and clearly discerning that he is the beginning of the universe and the firstborn of every creature, are for that reason endowed with so great a dignity of principality, that they have power over all the regions of the earth, as if from some supreme hinge of things, to change and order at their will kingdoms, and principalities, and whatever dignities they please; to make, according to each one's deserts, the first last, and the last first; to put down the mighty from their seats, and to exalt the humble. And this too is for these the reason for loving. But the dominions also love. Why? they are carried, with a certain praiseworthy presumption, to track down something more subtle and more sublime concerning the unending and unshakable lordship of Christ: namely, that everywhere in the universe, not only powerful but present, it compels, with a most beautiful order, the courses of times, the motions of bodies, the nods of minds to obey his most right will; and that with a care so vigilant, that not a point or a jot, as it is said, of all these may in any way be withdrawn from its due service; yet with so easy a labor, that the governor feels no disturbance or anxiety at all. Therefore, beholding the Lord of hosts judging all things with so great tranquility, carried away by the excessive but felt stupor of a most intent and sweet contemplation into that so vast sea of divine brightness, they withdraw into a more secret recess of wonderful tranquility, where they enjoy so great peace and security, that while they rest, the rest of the multitude, out of reverence for their prerogative, seems to minister and serve them, as to truly the dominions.
19.4: In the thrones God sits. And I think that for these spirits, above all who have been mentioned, there is both a more just cause and a richer matter of loving. For if you enter the palace of any king of men whatsoever, when it is full of stools, benches, and chairs, is not the royal seat seen set on high? And there is no need to ask where the king is wont to sit: surely his manifest seat at once occurs to you, higher and more adorned than the other seats. So also understand these spirits to surpass all the others in every adornment of beauty, in whom the divine Majesty has chosen to take residence by a certain special gift of stupendous condescension. But if sitting signifies a teaching office; I think that he, who is the one Master for us in heaven and on earth, the Wisdom of God, Christ, although elsewhere he reaches everywhere by reason of his purity, yet more specially and more principally illuminates these, as his own throne, with his presence, and from there, as from a solemn auditorium, teaches the angel, teaches man knowledge. From there to the angels the knowledge of the divine judgments; from there to the archangels, of the counsels; there the virtues hear when, and where, and what signs they are to bring forth. There at last all of them, whether powers, or principalities, or dominions, truly learn what they owe by duty, what they may presume by dignity, and, what is especially provided against for all, not to abuse, once power is received, their own will or glory.
19.5: Those hosts of heaven, however, which are called cherubim, if the interpretation of their name is kept for them, I judge to have nothing that they receive from others, or through others: since they may draw to the full from the very fountain, the Lord Jesus himself graciously introducing them by himself into all the fullness of truth, revealing most bountifully the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, which are all hidden in him. But neither do those which are called seraphim, which indeed Charity, that is God, has so drawn and absorbed into himself, and rapt into the same ardor of holy affection, that they seem to be one spirit with God; after the likeness, truly, of fire, which is seen to have made the air it inflames not ignited, but fire, while it presses all its heat into it and clothes it with its color. They love therefore to contemplate in God chiefly, those spirits, indeed, the knowledge of which there is no number; but these, the charity which never falls away. Whence they have also obtained these names, each from that in which they are seen to excel: for cherubim indeed is interpreted 'fullness of knowledge'; but seraphim are called 'the burning' or 'the burned.'
19.6: God is loved, therefore, by the angels on account of the supreme equity of his judgments; by the archangels, on account of the supreme governance of his counsels; moreover by the virtues, on account of his most kindly exhibition of miracles, through which he most worthily draws the unbelieving to faith; but by the powers, on account of that force of most just power, by which he is wont to drive away and ward off the cruelty of the wicked from the pious; truly by the principalities, on account of that eternal and original power, by which he gives being and the beginning of being to every creature, higher and lower, spiritual and corporeal, reaching mightily from end to end; by the dominions also, on account of his most peaceful will, by which, although he lords it everywhere in the strength of his arm, yet by a mightier virtue, for his inborn gentleness and untroubled calm, he disposes all things sweetly. He is loved also by the thrones, on account of the goodwill of the teacher Wisdom communicating herself without envy, and the unction which freely teaches concerning all things. But by the cherubim he is loved for this reason, because God is the Lord of the sciences; and knowing what is needful to each for salvation, he distributes, discreetly and providently, his gifts to those who worthily ask, as he knows it is expedient; by the seraphim also, because he is charity, and hates nothing of the things he has made, and wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
19.7: All these, then, love according as they are able to receive. But the young maidens, since they have less wisdom, receive less, nor do they at all suffice for such sublime things: for they are little ones in Christ, to be nourished with milk and oil. Therefore they must needs take from the breasts of the bride that whence they may love. The bride has the oil poured out, at whose odor they are stirred up to taste and perceive how sweet the Lord is. And when she shall perceive them blazing with love, turning to the Spouse: 'Your name is oil poured out,' she says, 'therefore the young maidens have loved you exceedingly.' What is 'exceedingly'? Greatly, vehemently, ardently. Or rather, it is you, who have recently come, whom the spiritual sermon touches more obliquely, rebuking that less discerning vehemence of yours, indeed your utterly too obstinate intemperance, which we also have often tried to restrain. You are not willing to be content with the common life. The regular fast does not suffice for you, nor the solemn vigils, nor the imposed discipline, nor the measure which we share out to you in clothing and food; you prefer private things to the common. You who have once entrusted the care of yourselves to us, why do you again take charge of yourselves? For that by which you have so often offended God, your consciences bearing witness, namely, your own will, behold, now again you have it as your teacher, not me. It teaches you not to spare nature, not to acquiesce to reason, not to comply with the counsel or example of your elders, not to obey us. Or are you ignorant that obedience is better than victims? (1 Sam. 15:22) Have you not read in your Rule, that whatever is done without the will or consent of the spiritual father shall be imputed to vainglory, not to reward? (Regul. S. Benedict, ch. 49.) Have you not read in the Gospel what form of obeying the boy Jesus gave to the holy boys? For when he had remained in Jerusalem, and had said that he ought to be in the things of his Father, his parents not acquiescing, he did not disdain to follow them into Nazareth, the Master his disciples, God men, the Word and Wisdom the craftsman and the woman. What? Indeed the sacred history adds: 'And he was,' it says, 'subject to them' (Luke 2:43-51). How long will you be wise in your own eyes? God entrusts and subjects himself to mortals; and do you still walk in your own ways? You received a good spirit; but you do not use it well. I fear lest you receive another in its place, who under the appearance of good may trip you up: and you, who have begun in the spirit, may be consumed in the flesh. Or do you not know that an angel of Satan often transforms himself into an angel of light? (2 Cor. 11:14). God is Wisdom, and he wills to be loved not only sweetly, but also wisely. Whence the Apostle: 'Your reasonable service,' he says (Rom. 12:1). Otherwise the spirit of error will very easily mock your zeal, if you neglect knowledge; nor does the crafty enemy have a more effective device for removing love from the heart, than if he can bring it about that one walk in it incautiously, and not with reason. Wherefore I think to deliver to you certain ways, which it is worth while for those who love God to observe. But because this sermon calls for an end, tomorrow, if God shall have preserved life for me and the leisure which we now have for discoursing, I shall endeavor to explain them. For then, our senses refreshed by the quiet of the night, and, what is chief, with prayer sent before, more eager, as is right, we shall come together to the sermon on love, our Lord Jesus Christ granting it, to whom be honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

20.1: That the sermon may take its beginning from the Master's words: 'If any man love not the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema' (1 Cor. 16:22). He is altogether greatly to be loved by me, through whom I am, I live, and I have understanding. If I am ungrateful, I am also unworthy. Plainly worthy of death is he who refuses to live for you, O Lord Jesus, and is dead; and he who has no understanding for you has lost his understanding; and he who cares to be for any reason save for you is as nothing, and is nothing. After all, what is man, except that you have made yourself known to him? (Ps. 143:3.) 'For yourself,' O God, you have made all things; and he who wills to be for himself and not for you, begins to be nothing among all things: 'Fear God, and keep his commandments; this is,' he says, 'the whole of man' (Eccl. 12:13). Therefore if this is the whole of man, without this man is nothing. Bow down to yourself, O God, that little which you have deigned that I be; and from my wretched life receive, I beseech you, the remnant of my years; but for those which I have lost in living, because I have lived ruinously, 'a contrite and humble heart, O God, you will not despise.' My days have declined like a shadow, and have passed without fruit. It is impossible that I should recall them; may it please you that I reconsider them to you in the bitterness of my soul. Now concerning wisdom, all my desire is before you, and the resolution of my heart; if there were any in me, I would keep it for you. But, O God, you know my foolishness; unless perhaps this itself is to be wise, that I too acknowledge it, and indeed by your gift. Increase it to me, not indeed ungrateful for the little gift, but anxious for that which is lacking. For these things, then, I am so loving you, as much as I am able.
20.2: But there is something that moves me more, urges me more, kindles me more. Above all, I say, the cup which you drank, the work of our redemption, renders you lovable to me, good Jesus. This altogether easily claims all our love for itself. This, I say, is that which both more soothingly entices our devotion, and more justly demands it, and binds it more tightly, and moves it more vehemently. For in it the Savior labored much, nor did he take upon himself so much weariness in the whole fabric of the world. For that world, finally, he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps. 32:9). But this one, on the other hand, endured contradictors in his words, spies on his deeds, mockers in his torments, and reproachers in his death. Behold how he loved. Add that this very love he did not repay, but added. For who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? (Rom. 11:35.) But as Saint John the evangelist says: 'Not because we have loved God, but because he first loved us' (1 John 4:10). Finally, he loved even those who did not exist; but he adds that he loves those who resist, according to Paul's testimony saying: 'Since when we were yet enemies, we were reconciled to God by the blood of his Son' (Rom. 5:10). Otherwise, if he had not loved enemies, he would not yet have possessed friends, just as there would not yet be those whom he would so love, if he had not loved those who did not yet exist.
20.3: But he loved sweetly, wisely, mightily. Sweet, I should say indeed, that he put on flesh; careful, that he shunned fault; mighty, that he underwent death. For those whom he visited in the flesh, he nevertheless by no means loved carnally, but in the prudence of the spirit. For 'Christ the Lord is a spirit before our face' (Lam. 4:20), jealous over us with the jealousy of God, not of man, and certainly a sounder one than the first Adam felt for his Eve. And so those whom he sought in the flesh, he loved in the spirit, he redeemed in power. It is altogether full of every sweetness of delight, to see man, the Creator of man. But while he prudently separated his nature from fault, he also mightily drove death away from nature. In the taking on of flesh he condescended to me, in the shunning of fault he consulted for himself, in the undergoing of death he satisfied the Father; a sweet friend, a prudent counselor, a mighty helper. To him I confidently entrust myself, who wills, knows, and is able to save me. Whom he sought, him he has also called by his grace; surely he will not cast out one who comes? But neither violence nor fraud do I fear at all, I say, that could snatch me out of his hand; who both conquered death conquering all things, and deceived the serpent, the deceiver of the universe, with a holier art indeed; more prudent than the one, mightier than the other. He indeed took on the truth of the flesh, but only the likeness of sin; showing in the former a wholly sweet consolation to the weak, and in the latter prudently hiding from the devil the snare of his deception. Moreover, that he might reconcile us to the Father, he strongly undergoes and overcomes death, pouring out the price of our redemption, his blood. Therefore unless he had loved sweetly, that Majesty would not have sought me in prison; but to his affection he joined wisdom, by which he might deceive the tyrant; he joined also patience, by which he might appease the offended God the Father. These are the ways which I had promised you; but I have put them before you in Christ, that you might hold them the more commendable.
20.4: Learn, O Christian, from Christ, how you are to love Christ. Learn to love sweetly, to love prudently, to love mightily. Sweetly, lest enticed; prudently, lest deceived; mightily, lest oppressed, we be turned away from the love of the Lord. Lest you be led away by the glory of the world or the pleasures of the flesh, let Christ, the Wisdom of God, grow sweet to you above these; lest you be deceived by the spirit of lying and error, let Christ, the Truth, shine upon you; lest you be wearied by adversities, let Christ, the Power of God, strengthen you. Let charity inflame your zeal, knowledge inform it, constancy strengthen it. Let it be fervent, let it be circumspect, let it be invincible. Let it have no lukewarmness, let it not lack discernment, let it not be timid. And see lest perhaps these three things have been handed to you also in the Law, God saying: 'You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole strength' (Deut. 6:5). It seems to me (if no other more fitting sense occurs in this threefold distinction) that the love of the heart indeed pertains to a certain zeal of affection; but the love of the soul, to the diligence or judgment of reason; while the love of strength can be referred to the constancy or vigor of the mind. Love therefore the Lord your God with the whole and full affection of your heart; love him with all the vigilance and circumspection of reason; love him also with your whole strength, so that you neither fear to die for his love, as it is written in what follows: 'For love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell' (Song 8:6). Let the Lord Jesus be gentle and sweet to your affection, against, of course, the evilly sweet allurements of the carnal life; and let sweetness overcome sweetness, just as one nail drives out another. But let him be none the less a light going before your understanding and a guide to your reason, not only for avoiding the snares of heretical fraud, and for keeping the purity of the faith from their wiles, but also that you may be cautious to shun an excessive and indiscriminate vehemence in your behavior. Let your love also be strong and constant, neither yielding to terrors, nor succumbing to labors. Therefore let us love affectionately, circumspectly, and valiantly, knowing that the love of the heart, which we call affectionate, apart from that which is called of the soul, is indeed sweet, but seducible; and that the latter, apart from that which is of strength, is rational, but fragile.
20.5: And see in manifest examples that it is so as we say. When the disciples took it ill that they had heard from the Master himself about his departing who was about to ascend, they heard: 'If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice that I go to the Father' (John 14:28). What then? did they not love him at whose departure they grieved? But they loved in a certain way, and they did not love. They loved sweetly, but less prudently; they loved carnally, but not rationally; finally, they loved with their whole heart, but not with their whole soul. Their love was against their salvation; whence he also said: 'It is expedient for you that I go' (John 16:7), blaming their counsel, not their affection. Again, when speaking of his future death, he checked Peter, who loved him dearly, trying to oppose him, rebuking him thus, as you remember; what else in him did he reprove but imprudence? Finally, what is: 'You do not perceive the things that are of God' (Mark 8:32, 33), but: you do not love wisely, following a human affection against the divine counsel? And he called him Satan, for the reason that he, although unknowing, opposed salvation, he who would forbid the Savior to die. Whence also, being corrected, he no longer forbade him to die, repeating afterward the sad word, but promised that he himself would die with him. But he did not fulfill it, because he had not yet attained to the third degree, in which one is loved with one's whole strength. He was taught to love with his whole soul, but he was still weak; well instructed, but little aided; not ignorant of the mystery, but fearful of martyrdom. Plainly that love, strong as death, was not yet then, which yielded to death; but it was afterward, when, clothed with power from on high according to the promise of Jesus Christ, he at length began to love with such great might, that, forbidden in the council to preach the holy name, he answered the forbidders constantly: 'We ought to obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). Then at last he loved with his whole strength, when he spared not his own life for love. For greater charity has no man, than that one lay down his life for his friends (John 15:13): which although he did not then lay down, yet he had already offered it. Therefore not to be led away by blandishments, nor to be deceived by deceits, nor to be broken by injuries, is to love with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength.
20.6: And note that the love of the heart is in a certain way carnal, in that it moves the human heart more toward the flesh of Christ, and toward what Christ did or commanded in the flesh. Filled with this love, one is easily pricked to compunction at every sermon about such things. He hears nothing more willingly, reads nothing more studiously, recalls nothing more often, meditates on nothing more sweetly. From there he fattens the holocausts of his prayers, as it were, with the fat of a fatted calf. Before one praying stands the sacred image of the Man God, whether born, or sucking, or teaching, or dying, or rising again, or ascending; and whatever of the sort occurs, it must needs either draw the soul into love of the virtues, or drive out the vices of the flesh, put the allurements to flight, and still the desires. I judge this to have been the principal reason with the invisible God, that he willed to be seen in the flesh, and as a man to converse with men, namely that he might first draw back to the saving love of his flesh all the affections of the carnal, who were not able to love otherwise than carnally, and so lead them gradually to spiritual love. Did not they, after all, still stand on this degree, who said: 'Behold, we have left all things, and have followed you'? (Matt. 19:27.) Certainly by the love of his bodily presence alone they had left all things, so that they would not even bear to hear a word of his future saving passion and death with equanimity, nor afterward look upon the glory of the ascending one except with deep sorrow. For this is what he said to them: 'Because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart' (John 16:6). And so in the meantime he suspended them from the love of all flesh by the grace alone of his flesh then present.
20.7: But he afterwards showed them a higher degree of love, when he said: 'It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing' (John 6:64). I think he had already climbed this one, who said: 'Although we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer' (2 Cor. 5:16). Perhaps, and none the less, the prophet stood on this very one, when he said: 'Christ the Lord is a spirit before our face.' For that he subjoins: 'Under his shadow we shall live among the nations' (Lam. 4:20), he seems to me to have added from the person of beginners, that those who feel themselves too weak to bear the heat of the sun may rest at least in the shadow; and that they may be nourished by the sweetness of the flesh, while they are not yet able to perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. For the shadow of Christ, I think, is his very flesh, by which Mary also was overshadowed (Luke 1:35), so that by its interposition the fervor and splendor of the Spirit might be tempered to her. Let him, then, who does not yet have the life-giving Spirit be comforted in the meantime in the devotion of the flesh, in that manner only, in which those have it who say: 'Christ the Lord is a spirit before our face'; and again: 'Although we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer.' For otherwise indeed Christ is by no means loved even in the flesh without the Holy Spirit, although not in that fullness. Yet the measure of this devotion is this, that that sweetness occupy the whole heart, and claim for itself the whole of it away from the love of all flesh and of carnal allurement. For this is to love with one's whole heart. Otherwise, if by chance I prefer any kinship or pleasure of my own flesh to the flesh of my Lord, on account of which it happens that I less fulfill those things which, abiding in the flesh, he taught me by word and example; does it not plainly stand clear that I by no means love him with my whole heart, since, having that heart divided, I seem to spend one part on his flesh, and to turn the other to my own? Finally he says: 'He who loves father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me, is not worthy of me' (Matt. 10:37). Therefore, to say it briefly, to love with one's whole heart is to postpone to the love of his sacrosanct flesh everything that flatters from one's own or another's flesh. In which I likewise comprehend the glory of the world, because the glory of the world is the glory of the flesh, and that those who delight in it are carnal is not doubtful.
20.8: Although devotion of this sort toward the flesh of Christ is indeed a gift, and a great gift, of the Spirit; yet I should call this love carnal, at any rate in respect of that love by which one tastes, not so much the Word made flesh, as the Word Wisdom, the Word justice, the Word truth, the Word holiness, piety, virtue; and if there be any other thing, it can be called of this kind. And these are surely all Christ, who has been made unto us wisdom from God, and justice, and sanctification, and redemption (1 Cor. 1:30). Do the two seem affected to you equally and in one way: the one who piously suffers with the suffering Christ, is pricked to compunction, and is easily moved at the memory of the honors he bore, and is fed by the sweetness of this devotion, and is strengthened to everything wholesome, honorable, and pious; and again the one who is always enkindled with zeal for justice, who everywhere burns for the truth, who glows with zeal for wisdom; to whom the holiness of life is a friend, and the discipline of morals; whose manners blush at boasting, abhor detraction, know not envy, detest pride, not only flee all human glory, but loathe and despise it; who abominate and persecute most vehemently in themselves all impurity of flesh and heart; who at last, as it were naturally, reject everything evil, and embrace what is good? If you compare the affections of both, does it not stand clear that in a certain way the former, in respect indeed of this latter, loves as it were carnally?
20.9: Nevertheless that carnal love is good, by which the carnal life is shut out, the world is despised and conquered. But one makes progress in it when it becomes also rational; it is perfected when it is made also spiritual. Moreover it is rational then, when in all things which must be believed about Christ, the reason of faith is held so firmly, that by no appearance of truth, by no heretical or diabolical circumvention, one may be anywise deviated from the purity of the ecclesiastical sense. And likewise when in one's own behavior that caution is observed, that the limit of discernment be exceeded by no superstition or levity, or by the vehemence of a, so to speak, more fervent spirit. And that this is to love God with one's whole soul we have already said above. But if the vigor of the aiding Spirit also comes to it so great, that by no fear of labors or torments, nor even of death, is justice ever forsaken; in this also God is loved with one's whole strength, and it is spiritual love. Which name, of course, I think belongs especially to this love, on account surely of the prerogative of the fullness of the Spirit, by which it excels. And let these things suffice for what the bride says: 'Therefore the young maidens have loved you exceedingly' (Song 1:2). In the things which follow, may he deign to open to us the treasures of his mercy, he himself, the keeper of them, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, through all ages of ages. Amen.

21.1: 'Draw me after you; we will run in the odor of your ointments' (Song 1:3). What? does the bride, then, have need to be drawn, and that after the Spouse? As though, indeed, she follows him unwilling, and not gladly. But not everyone who is drawn, is drawn unwillingly. Nor is it irksome that the infirm and feeble man, namely he who cannot go by himself, be drawn to the bath, or to dinner, although it may be irksome that the guilty be drawn to judgment, or to punishment. Finally, she who asks even this wills to be drawn: but she would not ask, if she were able to follow the Beloved by herself, as she would wish. But why is she not able? shall we confess that the bride, too, is weak? If any one of the young maidens called herself weak, and asked to be drawn, we would by no means wonder. But concerning the bride, who, as strong and perfect, seemed to be able to suffice for drawing others too: to whom does it not sound harsh, that she herself also has need to be drawn, as one weak or feeble? Concerning what soul shall we now trust that it is strong and sound, if we consent that she be called weak, who for her singular perfection and more excellent virtue is named the bride of the Lord? Or perhaps the Church said this, when she beheld the Beloved ascending, eager to follow him, and to be taken up with him in glory? And yet a soul of whatsoever perfection, so long indeed as it groans under the body of this death, and is held shut up in the prison of this evil age, bound with necessities, torn with crimes, needs must rise more slowly and slackly to contemplating sublime things, nor has it altogether the freedom to follow the Spouse wherever he has gone. Hence that tearful voice of one groaning: 'Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?' (Rom. 7:24.) Hence that suppliant prayer: 'Bring forth my soul out of prison' (Ps. 141:8). Let the bride, therefore, say, let her say even with a groan: 'Draw me after you; because the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind thinking many things' (Wis. 9:15). Or does she say this, desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ, especially while she sees those, for whom it seemed necessary that she remain in the flesh (Phil. 1:23, 24), now making good progress to love the Spouse, and to stand in the safety of charity? Surely she had sent this before: 'Therefore,' saying, 'the young maidens have loved you.' Now, therefore, as if she said: Behold, the young maidens love you, and loving, firmly cleave to you, and have no further need of me at all; there is no cause for me to remain longer in this life; therefore she says, 'Draw me after you.'
21.2: I should feel this, if she had said, 'Draw me to you.' But now, because she says, 'after you,' she seems to me to ask rather this, that she may be able to follow the footsteps of his manner of life, that she may be able to emulate his virtue, and hold the rule of his life, and be able to grasp the discipline of his manners. For in these help is especially needed, by which she may be able to deny herself, and take up her cross, and so follow Christ. Here indeed the bride must needs be drawn, and surely drawn by no other than by him who says: 'Without me you can do nothing' (John 15:5). 'I know,' she says, 'that I cannot at all come to you, unless by walking after you; but not even this, unless aided by you: and therefore I pray that you draw me after you.' Blessed, surely, is he whose help is from you; he has disposed ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears (Ps. 83:6), about to arrive some time at you, in the mountains of joys. How few, O Lord Jesus, are willing to go after you! although yet there is no one who is unwilling to come to you, all knowing this, because 'pleasures are in your right hand even to the end' (Ps. 15:11). And therefore all wish to enjoy you, but not likewise to imitate you; they desire to reign with you, but not to suffer with you. Of these was that one who said: 'Let my soul die the death of the just, and let my last end be like theirs' (Num. 23:10). He wished for himself the last end of the just, but not likewise their beginnings. Even the carnal wish for themselves the death of the spiritual, though they abhor their life, knowing the death of the saints to be precious: because 'when he has given sleep to his beloved, behold, it is the inheritance of the Lord' (Ps. 126:2, 3); and because 'blessed are the dead who die in the Lord' (Rev. 14:13): while on the contrary, according to the prophet's sentence, 'the death of sinners is most evil' (Ps. 33:22). They care not to seek, whom yet they desire to find; desiring to obtain, but not likewise to follow. Not so those to whom he said: 'You are they who have continued with me in my temptations' (Luke 22:28). Blessed are they who have been counted worthy of your testimony, gracious Jesus! They in truth went after you, both with their feet and with their affections. You made known to them the ways of life, calling them after you, because you are the Way and the Life, and you say, 'Come after me, I will make you fishers of men' (Matt. 4:19); again: 'He who ministers to me, let him follow me: and where I am, there also my minister shall be' (John 12:26). Therefore they said, glorying: 'Behold, we have left all things, and have followed you' (Matt. 19:27).
21.3: So, therefore, also your beloved, having left all things for your sake, always longs to go after you, always to cling to your footsteps, and to follow you wherever you have gone: knowing that your ways are beautiful ways, and all your paths are peaceable; and that he who follows you does not walk in darkness. But she prays to be drawn, because your justice is like the mountains of God, nor does she suffice for it by her own strength. She prays to be drawn, as is her wont; because no one comes to you, unless your Father has drawn him (John 6:44). Moreover, whom the Father draws, you also draw. For the works which the Father does, these the Son also does in like manner. But more familiarly she asks to be drawn by the Son, as by her own spouse, whom the Father sent to meet her as a leader and a teacher, who should go before her in the way of morals, and prepare the path of virtues, and instruct her as it were himself, and teach her the way of prudence, and deliver to her the law of life and of discipline; and so deservedly he himself would desire her beauty.
21.4: 'Draw me after you; we will run in the odor of your ointments.' For that reason I have need to be drawn, because the fire of your love has grown a little cold in us; nor can we now run from the face of this coldness, as yesterday and the day before. But we will run afterward, when you have restored to me the joy of your salvation, when the better temperature of grace returns, when the Sun of justice has grown hot again, and the cloud of temptation, which is seen to cover him for a while, has passed over, and at a gentle breath of a softer breeze the ointments begin to melt as usual, and the perfumes to flow, and to give their odor. Then we will run; in that odor we will run. With the ointments breathing, I say, we will run, because the sluggishness which now is will depart, and devotion will return, and there will no longer be need for us to be drawn, since we are stirred up by the odor to run of our own accord. But now, in the meantime, draw me after you. Do you not see that he who walks in the spirit by no means remains in one state, nor always advances with the same ease, and that his way is not in man; but as the Spirit, the moderator, dispenses to him as it wills, now more slowly, now more briskly, to forget the things that are behind, and to stretch himself to the things that are before? I think that, if you attend to this very thing, your own experience answers within you what I speak without.
21.5: When, therefore, you feel yourself affected with sluggishness, acedia, or weariness, do not for that reason lose confidence or desist from the spiritual pursuit; but seek the hand of the one who helps, beseeching to be drawn, after the example of the bride, until, being roused again by grace and made more prompt and eager, you run, and say: 'I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart' (Ps. 118:32). But in this way, as long as grace is present, delight in it, so that you do not think yourself to possess the gift of God by a hereditary right, so sure of it, namely, as if you could never lose it: lest suddenly, when he perhaps withdraws his hand, and takes away the gift, you fall in spirit, and become sadder than you ought. Finally, do not say in your abundance, 'I shall not be moved forever'; lest you be compelled to say also that which follows, indeed with a groan: 'You have turned your face from me, and I have been troubled' (Ps. 29:7, 8). You will rather take care, if you are wise, according to the counsel of the Wise Man, in the day of evils not to be forgetful of good things, and in the day of good things not to be forgetful of evils (Sir. 11:27).
21.6: Therefore in the day of your strength do not be secure, but cry to God with the Prophet, and say: 'When my strength fails, do not forsake me' (Ps. 70:9). Moreover, in the time of temptation comfort yourself, and say with the bride: 'Draw me after you; we will run in the odor of your ointments.' Thus hope will not forsake you in evil time, nor will providence be lacking in good; and you will be, amid the adversities and prosperities of mutable times, holding a certain image of eternity, namely this inviolable and unshaken equanimity of a constant mind, blessing the Lord at all times, and thereby also claiming for yourself, even amid the doubtful events and certain failings of this tottering age, in a certain way the state of perpetual unchangeableness, while you begin to renew and reform yourself into that ancient mark of the likeness of the eternal God, with whom there is no transmutation, nor shadow of alteration (James 1:17). For just as he is, so also you will be in this world, neither fearful in adversities, nor dissolute in prosperities. In this, I say, the noble creature, made to the image and likeness of him who made it, shows itself to receive, and even now and again to recover, the dignity of its ancient honor, when it judges itself unworthy to be conformed to this slipping age, striving rather to be reformed, according to Paul's teaching, in the newness of its mind (Rom. 12:2), into that likeness in which it knows itself to have been created; and by this also, as is fitting, compelling this age, which was made for its sake, in turn, in a wondrous way, to be conformed to it, while all things begin to work together for it unto good, as in their own and natural form, laying aside their degenerate appearance and recognizing their Lord, for serving whom they were created.
21.7: Whence I judge that that saying, which the Only-begotten said of himself, namely, that if he were lifted up from the earth, he would draw all things to himself, can also be common to all his brothers, namely to those whom the Father foreknew and predestined to be made conformable to the image of his Son, that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers. And I, therefore, if I be lifted up from the earth, I boldly say, will draw all things to myself (John 12:32). For I do not rashly usurp to myself, my brothers, the word of which I put on the likeness. But if it is so, let not the rich of this age think that the brothers of Christ possess only heavenly things, because they hear him saying: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven' (Matt. 5:3). Let them not think, I say, that those possess only heavenly things, who hear those alone in the promise. They possess earthly things also, and indeed as having nothing, but possessing all things: not begging, like the wretched, but possessing as lords, all the more certainly lords, the less covetous they are. Finally, to the faithful man the whole world is a store of riches. The whole, plainly: because both the adversities and the prosperities of his own all equally serve him, and work together for good.
21.8: Therefore the avaricious man hungers for earthly things as a beggar; the faithful man despises them as a lord. The former, by possessing, begs; the latter, by despising, preserves. Ask of any one of those who gape with insatiable heart after temporal gains, what he thinks of those who, selling their goods and giving to the poor, purchase the kingdoms of heaven in exchange for earthly substance, whether they act wisely or not. He will without doubt answer: Wisely. Ask, again, why he himself does not do what he approves? 'I cannot,' he will say. Why? Truly because the mistress avarice does not permit; because he is not free; because those things which he seems to possess are not his own; but neither is he himself his own master. If they are truly yours, lay them out to gain, and in exchange for earthly things secure the heavenly. If you cannot, confess that you are not the lord of your money, but its servant; its keeper, not its possessor. Finally, you are also conformed to your purse, as a servant to his mistress, since, just as the one necessarily both rejoices together with it when it rejoices, and grieves with it when it grieves, so you likewise grow in mind together with your growing purse, and dwindle with its dwindling. For you are also contracted with sadness, when it is emptied; and you are loosened with joy, or at least puffed up with pride, when it is filled. So much for him. But let us take care, rather, to emulate the freedom and constancy of the bride, who, as one well instructed in all things, and taught in heart in wisdom, knows both how to abound, and how to suffer want. When she asks to be drawn, she shows what is lacking to herself, not of money, but of virtue. Again, when she none the less comforts herself with the hope of grace about to return; although she proves herself to faint, yet she proves herself not to despair.
21.9: She says, therefore: 'Draw me after you; we will run in the odor of your ointments.' And what wonder if she has need to be drawn, who runs after the giant, who strives to overtake him who 'leaps upon the mountains, skips over the hills'? 'Swiftly,' he says, 'does his word run' (Ps. 147:15). She cannot run on equal footing, she cannot contend with him at equal speed, who 'rejoices as a giant to run his way' (Ps. 18:6); she cannot by her own strength, and therefore she asks to be drawn. 'I am weary,' she says, 'I faint; do not desert me, but draw me after you, lest I begin to wander after other lovers, lest I run as it were in uncertainty.' 'Draw me after you; because it is better for me that you draw me, namely that you inflict some force upon me, either by frightening me with threats, or by exercising me with scourges, than that, sparing me, you leave me in my sluggishness, evilly secure.' Draw her in a certain way unwilling, that you may make her willing; draw her torpid, that you may restore her running. There will be a time when I shall not need a drawer, because we will run willingly and with all eagerness. I shall not run alone, although I have asked that I alone be drawn: the young maidens also will run with me. We shall run equally, we shall run together; I by the odor of your ointments, they stirred up by my example and exhortation: and by this all of us shall run in the odor of your ointments. The bride has her imitators, just as she herself is of Christ, and therefore she does not say in the singular, 'I shall run'; but 'we shall run.'
21.10: But a question arises, why, in like manner, when she asked to be drawn, she did not also join the young maidens, so as to say, not 'Draw me,' but 'Draw us.' For what? is the bride, then, in need of being drawn, and do the young maidens not need it? O beautiful one, O happy, O blessed! expound to us the reason of this distinction. 'Draw me,' you say. Why 'me,' and not 'us'? Or do you grudge this good thing to us? God forbid! For you would not have straightway said that the young maidens would run with you, if you had wished to go alone after the Spouse. Why, then, having soon subjoined 'we shall run' in the plural, did you ask that you alone be drawn? 'Charity,' she says, 'so demanded.' Learn through this word from me, in your spiritual exercise, to hope for a twofold help from above: correction, and consolation. The one exercises you without; the other visits you within. That one represses insolence, this one lifts up to confidence; that one works humility, this one comforts faintheartedness; that one makes men cautious, this one devout. That one teaches the fear of the Lord; this one tempers that very fear with infused saving joy, as it is written: 'Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name' (Ps. 85:11); and again: 'Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice unto him with trembling' (Ps. 2:11).
21.11: We are drawn, when we are exercised with temptations and tribulations; we run, when, visited with inward consolations and inspirations, we breathe again as it were among sweet-smelling ointments. Therefore what seems austere and hard, I keep for myself, as one strong, as one sound, as one perfect, and I say in the singular, 'Draw me.' What is sweet and delightful, I share with you as with one weak, and I say, 'We shall run.' I know that the young maidens are delicate and tender, and less fit to suffer temptations: and therefore I wish that they run with me, but not that they be drawn with me; I wish to have companions of consolation, but not also of labor. Why? Because they are weak, and I fear lest they fail, lest they succumb. 'Me,' she says, 'O Spouse, correct, exercise me, try me, draw me after you; because I am ready for scourges, and strong to endure.' But we shall run together: I alone shall be drawn, but we shall run together. We shall run, we shall run, but in the odor of your ointments, not in the confidence of our own merits: nor do we trust to run in the greatness of our own strength, but in the multitude of your mercies. For even if at any time we have run and were willing, it was not of the willing, nor of the running, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. 9:16). Let mercy return, and we shall run. You indeed run in your strength, as a giant and a mighty one: but we, unless your ointments breathe, shall not run. You, whom the Father has anointed with the oil of gladness above your fellows (Ps. 44:8), run in that very anointing; we shall run in its odor: you in fullness, we in the odor. It would be time for me to pay what I remember I promised long above concerning the ointments of the Spouse, if the length of this sermon did not forbid. I put it off, therefore: for the dignity of the matter does not suffer to be cramped by a troublesome brevity. Ask the Lord of anointing, that he deign to make the free-will offerings of my mouth well-pleasing, to insinuate into your desires the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness, which is in the Spouse of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

22.1: If the ointments of the bride were found so precious, so magnificent, as you heard when they were treated of; what kind are those of the Spouse? And if we are not sufficient to unfold these worthily, as they are; yet there is no doubt but that the virtue of these is more excellent, and the grace more efficacious, of which the odor alone excites not only the young maidens, but also the bride herself, to run. For if you attend, she dared to promise nothing such concerning her own ointments. And indeed she glories that those are best; but she does not say, nevertheless, that she would have run in them, or would run; which she promises in the sole odor of these. What, if she should feel the anointing itself poured out upon her, by the so slight fragrance of which, being cheered, she is moved so that she runs? It would be a wonder if she should not also fly. But someone says: Cease now to commend; it is enough, when you shall begin to assign them, it will appear what they are. Nay. By no means do I promise that. Indeed whether even these be those which are suggested to the mind to be spoken, believe me, I confess that I do not yet know. For I think that the Spouse has various kinds of spices and of ointments, and not few: and that some indeed are those in which the bride especially delights, as one nearer and more familiar; others truly which reach even to the young maidens; others which reach even to those placed afar off and strangers, so that there is no one who hides himself from his heat. But although the Lord is sweet to all, yet especially to those of his household; and the more familiarly anyone draws near to him on account of the merits of his life and the purity of his mind, by so much do I think that he perceives the fragrance of fresher spices and of a sweeter anointing.
22.2: Moreover, in such things understanding does not grasp, except as much as experience reaches. But I truly would by no means rashly arrogate to myself the prerogative of the bride. The Spouse knows with what delights he cherishes the spirit of the beloved, with what inspirations he singularly refreshes her senses, and soothes her with perfumes. Let there be to you your own fountain, in which a stranger does not share with him, nor does one unworthy drink from it; for it is a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain (Song 4:12). But the waters are derived thence into the streets. I confess that I have these at hand, provided nevertheless that no one be troublesome or ungrateful to me, if from the public I draw and pour out. For that I may commend for a little while my ministry in this part, it is indeed of no small fatigue and labor, namely daily to go out, and to draw even from the manifest streams of the Scriptures, and from them to serve the necessities of each one, so that without his own labor each one of you may have at hand spiritual waters for every work; for example, for washing, for drinking, for cooking foods. The divine discourse is surely the saving water of wisdom, not only drinking, but also washing, the Lord saying: 'And you are clean by reason of the word which I have spoken to you' (John 15:3). But the divine eloquence, the fire of the Holy Spirit kindling, cooks also the raw thoughts of the flesh, and turns them into spiritual senses and foods of the mind, so that you may say: 'My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall burn out' (Ps. 38:4).
22.3: Those who with a mind indeed purer are sufficient by themselves to apprehend sublimer things, than they are set forth by us, I not only do not forbid, but also much congratulate, while they indeed tolerate us to minister simpler things to the simpler. Who will grant me that all may prophesy? Would that it were not necessary for me to be occupied in these things! Would that either this care lay upon another, or certainly, which I would prefer, there were no one among you who needed these things, and all were taught of God, and I could be at leisure and see that the Spouse is God! But now him whom in the meantime it is by no means permitted, I do not say to behold, but even to inquire into (which I do not speak without tears), the King seated in his beauty upon the cherubim, seated upon a high and elevated throne, in that form in which, equal to the Father in the splendors of the saints, he was begotten before the day-star, in which the angels also always desire to look upon him, God with God: at least him as man I, a man, speak to men according to that form, in which, that he might show himself manifest by his exceeding condescension and love, being made a little lower than the angels, he placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself as a bridegroom coming forth out of his chamber (Ps. 18:6). I speak him sweet rather than sublime, and anointed, not lofty, such finally as the Spirit of the Lord anointed, and sent to evangelize to the poor, to heal the contrite of heart, to preach to the captives indulgence, and to the closed an opening, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord (Ps. 61:1, 2).
22.4: Therefore, saving to each one that which perhaps, by a special gift, it has been granted to him to feel and experience for himself concerning the Spouse's ointments more sublimely and more subtly, I bring forth into common that which I have received from the common. For he himself, the fountain of life, he himself, the sealed fountain, bursting forth from within the enclosed garden, through the mouth of Paul his pipe, as truly that wisdom which according to the sentence of blessed Job is drawn from hidden things (Job 38:18), poured himself out into four streams, and derived them into the streets, where indeed he also assigns to us that he is made by God unto us wisdom, and justice, and sanctification, and redemption (1 Cor. 1:30). From these indeed four streams, as from most precious ointments (for nothing hinders both to be understood, both the water and the anointing; water, because they cleanse; anointing, because they are fragrant): from these, I say, four aforesaid, as from most precious ointments made upon the mountains of spices from heavenly kinds, so great a sweetness of odor filled the nostrils of the Church, that soon, being stirred up from the four parts of the world by that sweetness, she hastened to the Spouse above, as truly that queen of the south hastening from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, being provoked indeed by the odor of his reputation (1 Kings 10:1-7).
22.5: Assuredly neither was the Church able to run in the odor of her Solomon before, until he who from eternity was wisdom from the Father, was made unto her in time wisdom from the Father, by which she could perceive his odor. Thus he was made unto her justice, thus sanctification, thus also redemption none the less, that she could run in the odor of these too, since he was all these alike in himself before all things. For in the beginning indeed was the Word (John 1:1); but then at last did the shepherds come hastening to see him, when it was announced that he had been made. Finally they also say to one another: 'Let us pass over even to Bethlehem, and let us see this word which is made, which the Lord has made, and has shown to us.' And it follows, that they came hastening (Luke 2:15, 16). Before, they did not move themselves, while the Word was only with God. But when the Word, which was, was made; when the Lord did and showed this; then they came hastening, then they ran. As therefore in the beginning was the Word, but the Word was with God, yet was made in order that he might begin to be also with men: so none the less in the beginning wisdom was, justice was, sanctification and redemption was, but to the angels; that he might be also to men, the Father made him all these things, and he did that which the Father. Finally, 'He who is made,' he says, 'unto us wisdom from God' (1 Cor. 1:30). He does not say simply, 'who is made wisdom'; but, 'who is made unto us wisdom': because that which he was to the angels, he is made also to us.
22.6: But to the angels, you say, how he was redemption, I do not see. For neither does the authority of the Scriptures anywhere seem to assent, that they at any time were either captives to sin, or liable to death, so that they would have necessary redemption, except only those who, falling by the irremediable lapse of pride, do not thereafter deserve to be redeemed. If therefore the angels were never redeemed, some indeed not needing, others not deserving; some indeed, because they did not even fall; but these, because they are irrevocable; in what manner do you say that the Lord Jesus Christ was unto them redemption? Hear briefly. He who raised up man fallen, gave to the standing angel that he might not fall, thus freeing him from captivity, as defending this one from captivity. And by this reason he was equally unto each redemption, loosing him, and preserving this one. It is evident, therefore, that the Lord Christ was unto the holy angels redemption, as justice, as wisdom, as sanctification: and none the less that he was made these same four things for men, who can, the invisible things of God being understood, behold them only through those things which are made (Rom. 1:20). So therefore he is made unto us everything that he was to the angels. What? Wisdom, justice, sanctification, redemption. Wisdom in his preaching, justice in the absolution of sins, sanctification in the conversation, which he had with sinners; redemption in the passion, which he endured for sinners. Where therefore he was made these by God; then the Church perceived the odor, then she ran.
22.7: See now the fourfold anointing, see the most abundant and inestimable sweetness of him whom the Father anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows. You were sitting, O man, in darkness and in the shadow of death through ignorance of the truth; you were sitting bound with the chains of your offenses. He descended to you into the prison, not that he might torment you, but that he might snatch you out of the power of darkness. And first indeed the teacher of truth drove away the shadow of your ignorance with the light of his wisdom. Then through justice, which is of faith, he loosed the cords of your sins, freely justifying the sinner. By which twofold benefit he fulfilled that saying of holy David: 'The Lord looses the fettered, the Lord enlightens the blind' (Ps. 145:7, 8). He added also to live holily among sinners, and so to deliver a form of life, as of a way, by which you might return to your country. At last, for the summit of piety, he delivered his soul unto death, and from his own side brought forth the price of satisfaction, by which he might appease the Father; through which he plainly drew that verse to himself: 'With the Lord is mercy, and with him is plenteous redemption' (Ps. 129:7). Plainly plenteous; because not a drop, but a wave of blood flowed forth abundantly through the five parts of the body.
22.8: What ought he to have done for you, and did not? He enlightened the blind, loosed the bound, led back the erring, reconciled the guilty. Who would not run after him willingly and eagerly, who both frees from error, and dissembles errors; who then delivers merits by living, and seeks rewards by dying? What excuse has he who does not run in the odor of these ointments, except him to whom perhaps the odor has by no means reached? But truly into all the earth the odor of life has gone out; because the mercy of the Lord fills the earth, and his compassions are above all his works. Therefore he who does not perceive this vital fragrance scattered everywhere, and for this reason does not run, is either dead, or putrid; the odor of report excites to run, leads to the experience of the anointing, to the prize of vision. One voice of those rejoicing, of all attaining: 'As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts' (Ps. 47:9). Altogether on account of the meekness, which is preached in you, we run after you, Lord Jesus, hearing that you do not despise the poor, that you do not abhor the sinner. You did not abhor the thief confessing, not the woman sinner weeping, not the Canaanite woman suppliant, not her taken in adultery, not the one sitting at the toll-booth, not the publican praying, not the denying disciple, not the persecutor of the disciples, not your very crucifiers. In the odor of these we run. Moreover we perceive the odor of your wisdom from this, that we have heard that if anyone is in need of wisdom, he may ask it of you, and you will give it to him. For they say that you give to all abundantly, and do not upbraid (James 1:5). But truly so great a fragrance of your justice is scattered everywhere, that you are called not only just, but even justice itself, and justice justifying. In fine you are as strong to justify, as you are abundant to forgive. Wherefore whosoever, pricked for his sins, hungers and thirsts after justice, let him believe in you who justify the impious, and, justified through faith alone, he shall have peace with God. Your conversation also, and not only your conversation but also your conception, exudes sanctity most sweetly and most abundantly. For you did not commit sin, nor contract it. Those therefore who are justified from sins desire and resolve to follow sanctity, without which no one shall see God; let them hear you crying: 'Be holy, because I am holy' (Lev. 19:2). Let them consider your ways, and learn from you that you are just in all your ways, and holy in all your works (Ps. 144:17). Now how many does the odor of redemption make to run? When you are lifted up from the earth, then you truly draw all things to yourself. Your passion is the last refuge, the singular remedy.
