With wisdom failing, justice not sufficing, with the merits of sanctity yielding, it comes to the rescue. For who would presume for himself sufficiency for salvation from his own wisdom, or justice, or sanctity? 'Not that we are sufficient,' he says, 'to think anything of ourselves as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God' (2 Cor. 3:5). And so when my strength has failed, I am not troubled, I do not distrust. I know what I shall do: I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord (Ps. 115:13). 'Enlighten my eyes, O Lord, that I may know what is acceptable before you at all times' (Wis. 9:10), and I am wise. 'Remember not the offenses of my youth, and my ignorances' (Ps. 19:7), and I am just. 'Lead me, O Lord, in your way' (Ps. 85:11), and I am holy. Nevertheless unless your blood intercede for me, I am not saved. For all these we run after you: dismiss us not, because we cry after you.
22.9: Nor do we all run equally in the odor of all the ointments: but you may see some burn more vehemently in the studies of wisdom, others be more animated to repentance by the hope of indulgence, others be more provoked to the exercise of virtues by the example of his life and conversation, others be more kindled to piety by the memory of the passion. Do we think that we can find examples of each? They ran in the odor of wisdom, who had been sent by the Pharisees, when, returning, they said: 'Never did a man speak' (John 7:46); indeed admiring the doctrine, and confessing the wisdom. Saint Nicodemus ran in this very odor, who came to Jesus by night (John 3:2), in much splendor of wisdom: for instructed and taught about many things he departed. But Mary Magdalene ran in the odor of justice, to whom many sins were forgiven, because she loved much (Luke 7:47). Just indeed and holy, and no longer a sinner, as the Pharisee upbraided, not knowing that the justice or sanctity of God is a gift, not the work of man; and because he is not only just, but also blessed, to whom the Lord will not impute sin. Had he forgotten how, by touching, he had driven away either his own or another's corporal leprosy, and had not contracted it? So, being touched by the woman sinner, the just man imparts justice, does not lose it; nor does he defile himself with the filth of sin, with which he cleanses her. The Publican also ran, who when he humbly implored propitiation for his sins, went down justified, justice itself being witness (Luke 18:14). Peter ran, who, having fallen, wept bitterly (Luke 22:62), that he might wash away the fault, and recover justice. David ran, who, acknowledging and confessing his guilt, deserved to hear: 'And the Lord has transferred from you your sin' (2 Sam. 12:13). Moreover Paul testifies that he runs in the odor of sanctification, when he glories that he is an imitator of Christ, saying to the disciples: 'Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ' (1 Cor. 11:1). And all ran who said: 'Behold, we have left all things, and have followed you' (Matt. 19:27). For by the desire of following Christ they had left all things. That sentence exhorts all generally to the same odor: 'He who says that he abides in Christ, ought to walk even as he walked' (1 John 2:6). Now, if you wish to hear, take all the martyrs as those who ran in the odor of the passion. Behold, you have four ointments assigned; the first, of wisdom; the second, of justice; the third, of sanctification; the fourth, of redemption. Hold the names, receive the fruit; and seek not the manner of the composition, or the number of the species, with which they are made. For these cannot easily be at hand to us in the Spouse's ointments, as they were in those former ones of the bride. For in Christ is the fullness of things without number, and without measure. For neither is there number to his wisdom (Ps. 146:5); and his justice is like the mountains of God (Ps. 35:7), like everlasting mountains; and his sanctity is singular, and his redemption inexplicable.
22.10: This too must be said, that the wise men of this age have in vain disputed so many things about the four virtues, which yet they were altogether unable to apprehend, since they knew not him who is made unto us by God wisdom teaching prudence; and justice forgiving offenses; and sanctification, living continently as an example of temperance; and redemption, dying bravely as an example of patience. Perhaps someone says: The other things agree well, but sanctification seems to be referred to temperance less properly. To which it is answered first, that that which is continence is temperance. Then, it is customary in the Scriptures that sanctification be put for continence or cleanness. In fine, what were those so frequent sanctifications with Moses other than certain purifications of men tempering themselves from food, from drink, from sexual union, and things like these? But hear the Apostle himself especially, how familiar he has either to use, or to employ, sanctification in this sense. 'This is,' he says, 'the will of God, your sanctification, that each one of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification, and not in the passion of desire;' again: 'For God has not called us unto uncleanness, but unto sanctification' (1 Thess. 4:3-7). It is clear that he puts sanctification for temperance.
22.11: Having therefore brought into the light that which seemed somewhat obscure, I return to that from which I had digressed. What have you to do with virtues, who are ignorant of Christ, the virtue of God? Where, I ask, is true prudence, unless in the doctrine of Christ? Whence true justice, unless from the mercy of Christ? Where true temperance, unless in the life of Christ? Where true fortitude, unless in the passion of Christ? Therefore those alone who are imbued with his doctrine are to be called prudent; the just alone, who have obtained the pardon of sins from his mercy; the temperate alone, who study to imitate his life; the strong alone, who bravely hold the documents of his patience in adversities. In vain, therefore, does anyone labor in the acquisition of virtues, if he thinks they are to be hoped from elsewhere, than from the Lord of virtues: whose doctrine is the seed-plot of prudence; whose mercy, the work of justice; whose life, the mirror of temperance; whose death, the ensign of fortitude. To him be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

23.1: The king has brought me into his cellars. Behold whence the odor, behold whither we run. He had said that we must run, and in what we must run; but whither we must run, he had not said. Therefore we run to the cellars, and we run in the odor which proceeds from them, the bride with her accustomed sagacity perceiving him beforehand, and desiring to be brought into his fullness. But what do we think is to be understood of these cellars? Meanwhile let us think them certain places full of fragrance near the Spouse, full of spices, crammed with delights. For in a workshop of this sort whatever better things from the garden, or from the field, are to be preserved are stored away. Thither therefore they run alike. Who? Souls fervent in spirit. The bride runs, the young maidens run; but she who loves more ardently runs more swiftly, and arrives more quickly. Arriving, she suffers, I do not say rejection, but not even delay. Without delay it is opened to her, as to one of the household, as to one most dear, as to one especially beloved, and singularly pleasing. But the young maidens, what? They follow from afar; for neither, since they are still weak, can they run with equal devotion with the bride, nor wholly imitate her desire and fervor; and therefore arriving more slowly, they remain outside. But the charity of the bride does not rest, nor does it grow insolent, as is wont, with its successes, so as to forget them, consoling rather and exhorting to patience, that they may bear with equanimity both their own rejection and his absence. Finally she also announces to them the joy which she has received, not indeed for any other reason, unless that they may rejoice with her, while they trust that whatever grace has accrued to the mother will by no means be foreign to them. For neither does she care to advance so far that she neglects their care; nor does she think her own progress is to be aided to their harm. Wherefore by whatever prerogative of merits she may be taken away from them, by charity without doubt and by pious solicitude it is necessary that she always be with them. Finally she must imitate her Spouse, who indeed ascends to the heavens, and nevertheless promises that he will be on earth with his own even to the consummation of the age. So also she, however much she may advance, however much she may be promoted, by care, providence, and affection is never removed from those whom she begot in the Gospel, never forgets her own bowels.
23.2: Let her say therefore to them: Rejoice, be confident. 'The king has brought me into his cellars': think that you also have been brought in likewise. I seem to have been brought in alone; but it will not profit one alone. All my progress is yours: I profit for you, I will share with you whatever more perhaps I shall have merited for you. Do you wish to know without doubt that she spoke in this sense and affection? Hear what they answer. We shall exult and rejoice in you. In you, they say, we shall exult and rejoice: for in ourselves we do not yet merit. And they add, 'Mindful of your breasts,' that is, we bear with equanimity while you come, knowing that you will return to us with full breasts. Then we trust that we exult and rejoice, mindful in the meantime of your breasts. That which they add, 'above wine' (Song 1:3), signifies that they are indeed still struck, on account of their imperfection, by the recollection of carnal desires, which are designated by wine; yet that those desires are overcome by the memory of the abundance of sweetness, which they have already experienced flowing from the breasts. I would speak of the breasts, if I did not remember that I have said enough above (serm. 9). But now you see how they presume concerning the mother, how they reckon her gains and joys as their own, consoling the injury of their own rejection by her introduction. By no means would they trust so, unless they acknowledged her as mother. Let prelates hear this, who always wish to be a terror to those committed to them, rarely a benefit. Be instructed, you who judge the earth. Learn that you ought to be mothers of your subjects, not lords; strive rather to be loved than feared: and if sometimes there is need of severity, let it be fatherly, not tyrannical. By cherishing show yourselves mothers, by correcting, fathers. Grow meek, lay aside savagery; withhold the rods, put forth the breasts; let your breasts become fat with milk, not swell with vainglory. Why do you make your yoke heavy upon them, whose burdens you ought rather to bear? Why does the little one, bitten by the serpent, flee the conscience of the priest, to whom he ought rather to have run back as to the bosom of a mother? If you are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of gentleness; each one considering himself, lest he also be tempted (Gal. 6:1). Otherwise he will die in his sin: but his blood, he says, I will require from your hand (Ezek. 3:20). But these things elsewhere.
23.3: Now since the sequence of the letter is manifest from those things which we have set before, let us see now what we ought to understand spiritually concerning the cellars. In what follows mention is made also of the garden and of the chamber, which both I now join to these cellars, and take up into the present discussion: for treated together they will better be known one from the other. And let us seek, if it pleases, these three in the holy Scriptures, the garden, the cellar, the chamber. For in them the soul thirsting for God gladly busies and stays itself, knowing that it will without doubt find there him whom it thirsts for. Let the garden therefore be the simple and plain history; let the cellar be the moral sense; let the chamber be the secret of theoric contemplation.
23.4: And first indeed I think history is not undeservedly assigned to the garden, because in it are found men of virtues, as it were fruitful trees in the garden of the Spouse and in the paradise of God, of whose good deeds and manners as many examples as you take, so many fruits you pluck. Or does anyone perhaps doubt that a good man is a planting of God? Hear what holy David sings concerning the good man. He shall be, he says, as a tree that is planted near the running streams of waters, that shall give its fruit in its time, and its leaf shall not fall away (Ps. 1:3). Hear Jeremiah singing in harmony with the same spirit, and in almost the same words. He shall be as a tree, he says, that is planted near the running streams of waters, that sends its roots to the moisture, and shall not fear when the heat comes (Jer. 17:8). Likewise the Prophet: 'The just man shall flourish as the palm tree, he shall be multiplied as the cedar of Lebanon' (Ps. 91:13). And of himself: 'But I as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God' (Ps. 51:10). History is therefore the garden, and it is itself threefold. For in it are contained the creation, reconciliation, and reparation of heaven and earth. Creation indeed, as the sowing or planting of the garden. Reconciliation however, as the germination of the sown or planted. For in its own time, the heavens distilling dew from above, and the clouds raining the just one, the earth was opened and brought forth the Savior (Isa. 45:8), through whom the reconciliation of heaven and earth was made. For he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. 2:14), making peace through his blood in the things which are on earth, and which are in heaven (Col. 1:20). Moreover the reparation will be in the end of the age. For there shall be a new heaven, and a new earth: and the good shall be gathered from the midst of the wicked, as fruits from the garden, to be stored in the storehouses of God. In that day, as it is written, the bud of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth sublime (Isa. 4:2). You have therefore three times in the garden of the historical sense.
23.5: In the moral discipline likewise one is to note equally three things, as it were three cells in one cellar. And perhaps for this reason he said 'cellars' in the plural, and not 'cellar,' namely thinking of this number of cells. Finally below she glories that she has been brought into the wine cellar (Song 2:4). We therefore, because we read: 'Give occasion to the wise man, and he will be wiser' (Prov. 9:9): having occasion from the word which the Holy Spirit judged should be imposed upon this cellar, let us impose names also upon the other two, the spice-cellar upon one, and the ointment-cellar upon the other. We shall see the reasons of these words afterward. But now observe that all things with the Spouse are found healthful, all sweet; wine, ointments, spices. Wine, the Scripture bearing witness, makes glad the heart of man (Ps. 103:15). Nevertheless the face is made cheerful in the oil of the law (ibid.), with which indeed the powder of pigments is infused, that ointments may be made. Spices are useful not only by the pleasing sweetness of odor, but also by the power of healing. Justly does the bride exult that she has been brought thither, where so great an abundance of grace overflows.
23.6: But I have also other names, I think bearing a more evident reason of themselves. And that they may be named in their order, I should call the first of discipline; the second, of nature; the last, of grace. In the first you learn, according to the reason of the ethical part, to be inferior, in the next equal, in the last superior: that is, under another, with another, over another; or thus, to be under, to be with, to be over. First therefore you learn to be a disciple, secondly a companion, thirdly even a master. And indeed nature begot all men equal. But since, with the good of nature depraved in morals by pride, men have become impatient of equality, contending to be set over one another, and desiring to surpass one another, and greedy of vain glory, envying one another, provoking one another: first of all in the former cell, the insolence of manners is to be tamed by the yoke of discipline, until the stubborn will, worn down by the hard and long customs of the elders, is humbled and healed, and receives again by obeying the good of nature in itself, which it had lost by being proud; when it has learned, now by natural affection alone, not by fear of discipline, to bear itself socially, as far as in it lies, and quietly with all the companions of its nature, that is with all men, passing at length into the cell of nature, and experiencing what is written: 'Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity!' like ointment on the head (Ps. 132:1, 2). There certainly comes to disciplined manners, as to bruised spices, the oil of gladness, the good of nature; and there is made a good and pleasant ointment. By which, as it were anointed, the man is rendered sweet and mild, a man without complaint, circumventing no one, shaking no one, harming no one, not exalting or preferring himself over anyone, and moreover willingly sharing in the account of giving and receiving.
23.7: I think, if you have well understood the properties of each cell, you will testify that I have not unsuitably called this one the ointment-cellar, that one the spice-cellar. For in that one, as the violent crushing extracts and draws out by the pestle the strength and fragrance of the pigments, so the power of the Magisterium, and the strictness of discipline, somehow elicit and express the natural force of upright manners. But in this one the pleasant gentleness of a voluntary and as it were innate affection runs of its own accord, officious, plainly after the manner of the ointment that is on the head, descending and flowing through all at the light touch of warmth. And so in the cell of discipline, as it were dry and simple kinds of spices are contained, and hence I thought that one should be named the spice-cellar. But in that one which is called of nature, since now as it were already prepared ointments are laid up and kept, it also has taken its name from the thing, that it may be called the ointment-cellar. For I judge the wine cellar truly to bear no other reason of its name, save that in it is stored the wine of the zeal that fervently burns in charity. Nor ought he who has not yet merited to be brought into it to preside over others at all. He who presides over others must wholly burn with this wine, even as the Doctor of the Gentiles burned, when he said: 'Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is scandalized, and I am not burned?' (2 Cor. 11:29.) Otherwise you affect to preside over those whom you do not care to benefit, quite shamelessly; and of those whose salvation you do not zealously seek, too ambitiously you claim subjection for yourself. I have also named this cell of grace; not that anyone could obtain even the other two without grace, but on account of the fullness which is singularly received in this one. Finally, the fullness of the law is charity; and, he who loves his brother has fulfilled the law (Rom. 13:10, 8).
23.8: You have seen the reason of the names; see also the difference of the cells. For indeed it is not a matter of equal ease or of the same power, to curb wanton and wandering senses and the intemperate appetite of the flesh by the fear of a master, and to restrain them by the rigid censure of discipline; and to get on well with companions by a spontaneous affection; to live with manners corrected under the rod, and to show a pleasing manner to equals with the will alone as Mistress. For again let no one say it is of one merit, or of one virtue, to live socially, and to preside usefully. For how many live quietly under a teacher, whom if you set free from the yoke, you would see that they cannot be quiet, nor keep themselves in any way harmless to their equals? And likewise you will see countless men converse simply and without complaint among their brothers, while presiding over brothers not only uselessly, but also foolishly and wickedly. For those who are of this sort are content with a certain good mediocrity, even as God has divided to them the measure of grace; indeed in no way needing a master, yet not fit for the office of master. Therefore those who follow excel the former indeed in manners; but those who know how to be superiors exist superior to both. Finally those who preside well also receive in the promise that they be established over all the goods of their Lord (Matt. 24:48). But few indeed are they who preside usefully; fewer, who also preside humbly. Nevertheless he easily fulfills both, who, having perfectly obtained discretion the mother of virtues, is nonetheless inebriated with the wine of charity even to the contempt of his own glory, even to the forgetfulness of himself, and not to seeking the things which are his own; which is obtained only by the wonderful magisterium of the Holy Spirit within the wine cellar. For the virtue of discretion without the fervor of charity lies idle, and vehement fervor without the tempering of discretion rushes headlong. And therefore praiseworthy is he in whom neither is lacking: so that both fervor may raise up discretion, and discretion may rule fervor. Therefore it behooves him who presides to be thus disposed. But I should call it the best in manners, and to have perfectly grasped the sum of this discipline, to have been granted to run through and go around all these cells without hindrance: who in nothing at all either resists his superiors, or envies his equals, or either fails his subjects in care, or presides over them in pride; obedient to prelates, conforming to companions, usefully condescending to subjects: which indeed I should not doubt to grant to the bride as the mark of perfection. The word which she spoke also intimates this, that 'the king has brought me into his cellars,' since she shows herself brought not into some one cell, but into 'cellars' in the plural.
23.9: Now let us come to the chamber. And what is this? And do I presume to know what it is? By no means do I arrogate to myself the experience of so great a thing, nor do I glory in the prerogative, which is kept for the blessed bride alone, careful according to that saying of the Greeks, 'Know myself'; that I may know also with the Prophet what is wanting to me (Ps. 38:5). Yet if I knew nothing at all, I would say nothing. What I know, I do not grudge you, nor do I withhold it: what I do not know, may he teach you who teaches man knowledge (Ps. 93:10). I have said, and you remember, that in the secret of theoretical contemplation the chamber of the King is to be sought. But just as I know that I said concerning the ointments, namely that many and diverse ones are with the Spouse, nor are all at hand to all, but to each are granted according to the diversity of merits, so also I think not that there is one chamber to the King, but several. For truly neither is there one queen, but several: and the concubines are many, and of the young maidens there is no number. And each one finds a secret for herself with the Spouse, and says: 'My secret to me, my secret to me' (Isa. 24:16). It is not given to all to enjoy in one place the gracious and secret presence of the Spouse, but as it is prepared for each one by his Father. For we did not choose him, but he chose us, and placed us; and where each one has been placed by him, there he is. Finally, one woman, pricked with compunction, gained a place at the feet of the Lord Jesus (Luke 7:38), while the other found the fruit of her devotion at the head (Matt. 26:7), if indeed the other. Moreover Thomas in the side, John in the breast, Peter in the bosom of the Father, Paul in the third heaven, obtained the grace of this secret.
23.10: Who of us is sufficient worthily to distinguish these varieties of merits, or rather of rewards? Yet lest we seem altogether to have passed over what we ourselves know; the former woman laid a bed for herself in the haven of humility; the latter, on the throne of hope; Thomas, on the solid ground of faith; John, on the breadth of charity; Paul, in the depth of wisdom; Peter, in the light of truth. Thus, therefore, there are many mansions with the Spouse, and whether of the number of queen, or concubine, or even of the young maidens, each one receives there a place and a limit congruous to her merits, in so far as it is lawful for her to proceed by contemplating, and to enter into the joy of her Lord, and to search out the sweet secrets of the Spouse. Which, in its own place, I shall endeavor to show more distinctly, in so far as he himself shall deign to suggest. Now indeed let it suffice to know this, that to none of the young maidens, to none of the concubines, to none even of the queens is the access to that secret of the chamber at all open, which the Spouse keeps for his dove, beautiful, perfect, one. Whence neither do I indeed resent being, if I am not admitted to it, especially since it is evident to me that not even the bride herself as yet comes to every secret that she wishes. Finally she even earnestly asks that it be shown her, where he feeds, where he reclines at midday (Song 1:6).
23.11: But hear to what point I have arrived, or have thought myself to have arrived. For it is not to be attributed to boasting, that I lay open my progress to you. There is a place with the Spouse, from which he decrees his rights, and disposes his counsels, he himself the governor of the universe, establishing laws for every creature, weight, and measure, and number. And that place is high and secret, but by no means quiet. For although he himself, as far as in him lies, disposes all things sweetly, yet he disposes; and he does not permit the contemplator, who by chance has arrived at that place, to rest; but wonderfully, although delightfully, wearies him searching and admiring, and renders him restless. The bride beautifully expresses both in what follows, namely the delight of contemplation of this sort, and the restlessness, where she confesses both that she sleeps, and that her heart watches (Song 5:2). For in the sleep, indeed, of most sweet astonishment, and of peaceful admiration, she signifies that she feels rest; but in the vigils, of restless curiosity and laborious exertion, she signifies that she suffers weariness. Hence blessed Job: 'If I sleep,' he says, 'I say, When shall I arise? and again I shall wait for the evening' (Job 7:4). Do you perceive in these words the holy soul wishing sometimes to decline a certain troublesome sweetness, and again to desire that same sweet trouble? For it would not have said, 'When shall I arise,' if that rest of its contemplation had wholly pleased it: but if it had wholly displeased it, it would not again have awaited the hour of rest, that is, the evening. That place, therefore, is not one of the chamber, where rest is by no means had in every way.
23.12: There is likewise a place, from which the most secret and most severe censure of the just judge, God, watches immovably over a rational but reprobate creature, terrible in counsels over the sons of men. In this place, I say, God is beheld by the reverent contemplator, by his just but hidden judgment, neither washing away the evils of the reprobate, nor accepting their good things; moreover even hardening hearts, lest perhaps they grieve, and come to themselves, and be converted, and he heal them. And this is not without a certain and eternal reason, that which is the more fearful in that it stands fixed the more immovably in eternity. That is to be greatly feared which we read in the prophet concerning matters of this sort, where God, speaking to his angels, so says: 'Let us have mercy on the impious.' To these fearing and asking, 'Will he not, then, learn to do justice?' 'No,' he says; and adding the cause: 'In the land of the saints,' he says, 'he has wrought iniquity; and he shall not see the glory of the Lord' (Isa. 26:10). Let the clergy fear, let the ministers of the Church fear, who in the lands of the saints which they possess commit such iniquities, that, not at all content with the stipends which should suffice them, they impiously and sacrilegiously retain for themselves the surplus with which the needy were to be supported; and do not fear to consume the livelihood of the poor in the uses of their pride and luxury, sinning indeed with a double iniquity, because they both plunder what is another's, and abuse sacred things in their vanities and filthiness.
23.13: When, therefore, it is observed that he spares and has mercy on such as these for the present, lest he spare them forever, he whose judgments are a great deep; who would seek rest in this place? This vision has the tremor of judgment, not the security of the chamber. That place is terrible, and void of all rest. I shuddered wholly, whenever I was caught up into it, repeating to myself with trembling that sentence: 'Who knows whether he is worthy of love, or of hatred?' (Eccl. 9:1). Nor is it a wonder if I totter there, certainly a leaf which is snatched by the wind, and dry stubble (Job 13:25), where even that greatest contemplator confesses that his own feet were almost moved, his steps almost poured out; and he said: 'I was envious of the iniquitous, seeing the peace of sinners.' Why? 'In the labor of men they are not,' he says, 'and with men they shall not be scourged; and therefore pride held them (Ps. 72:3-6), lest they be humbled to penance, but be damned for pride with the proud devil and his angels.' For those who are not in the labor of men, shall surely be in the labor of demons, the judge saying: 'Go, accursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels' (Matt. 25:41). Yet this also is a place of God, plainly nothing other than the house of God, and the gate of heaven. Here, namely, God is said to be feared; here is his holy and terrible name, and as it were an entrance of glory: 'Plainly the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord' (Ps. 110:9, 10).
23.14: Nor let it move you, that I have given the beginning of wisdom to this place at last, and not to the former. For there, as in a certain auditorium of hers, we hear Wisdom, the teacher of all things, teaching; here we also receive it; there we are instructed indeed, but here we are affected. Instruction makes learned, affection makes wise. The sun does not also warm all to whom it shines; so Wisdom does not immediately enkindle to doing many whom it teaches what is to be done. It is one thing to know many riches, another to possess them; nor does the knowledge make one rich, but the possession. So entirely, so it is one thing to know God, and another to fear him; nor does knowledge, but fear make one wise, which also affects [the soul]. Would you then call wise him whom his own knowledge puffs up? Who but the most foolish would call those wise, who, when they had known God, did not glorify him as God, or give thanks? I rather feel with the Apostle, who manifestly pronounces their heart foolish (Rom. 1:21). And well is the fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom; because then God first savors to the soul, when he affects it to fear, not when he instructs it to know. You fear the justice of God, you fear his power; and a just and powerful God savors to you, because fear is a savor. Moreover the savor makes one wise, just as knowledge makes one knowing, just as riches make one rich. What, therefore, is the former place? It only prepares for wisdom. There you are prepared, that here you may be initiated. Preparation is the knowledge of things. But the swelling of pride very easily follows this, if fear does not repress it, so that it is rightly said: 'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,' which first opposes itself to the plague of foolishness. There, therefore, is a certain approach to wisdom, here also an entrance. Moreover neither here nor there is perfect rest to the one contemplating; because there God appears as it were solicitous, here as it were disturbed. You shall not, therefore, seek the chamber in these places, of which the one appears as it were the auditorium of one teaching, the other more the praetorium of a judge.
23.15: But there is a place where God is beheld truly resting and quiet; a place altogether, not of a judge, not of a master, but of a Spouse: and which to me indeed, for of others I know not, is plainly the chamber, if at any time it has happened that I be introduced into it. But, alas! a rare hour, and a short stay! There the mercy of the Lord is clearly acknowledged from eternity, and even to eternity, upon those who fear him. And happy is he who can say: 'I am a partaker of all them that fear you, and that keep your commandments' (Ps. 118:63). The purpose of God stands, the sentence of peace stands over those who fear him, both dissembling their evils, and rewarding their good things: so that in a wonderful way not only good things, but also evil things cooperate with them for good. O alone truly blessed, to whom the Lord will not impute sin! (Ps. 31:2). For he who has not had sin is no one. For all have sinned, and all need the glory of God (Rom. 3:23). Who, nevertheless, shall accuse against the elect of God? (Rom. 8:33). It suffices for me for all justice to have propitious him alone, against whom alone I have sinned. Everything which he himself has decreed not to impute to me, is as it were as if it had not been. Not to sin. Is the justice of God; the justice of man is the indulgence of God. I have seen these things, and I have understood the truth of that sentence: 'Every one who is born of God sins not; because the heavenly generation keeps him' (1 John 3:9). The heavenly generation is the eternal predestination, by which God loved his elect and graced them in his beloved Son before the constitution of the world, thus appearing to himself holy, that they might see his virtue and his glory, and be the sharers of that inheritance of which they would also appear conformed to the image. These, therefore, I have observed as if they had never sinned; because even if they seem to have failed in time, they do not appear so in eternity; because the charity of their Father covers the multitude of sins. And he called blessed those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered (Ps. 31:1); when suddenly so great confidence and infused joy arose in me concerning myself, as certainly in the place of horror, that is, in the place of the second vision, no fear had preceded, so that I seemed to myself to be like one of those blessed. O that it had lasted! Again and again visit me, O Lord, in your salvation, to see in the goodness of your elect, to rejoice in the joy of your people (Ps. 106:4, 5).
23.16: O place of true rest, and which I should by no means have deemed unworthy of the appellation of chamber! in which God is beheld not as it were disturbed with wrath, nor as it were stretched out with care; but his will is proved in it good, and acceptable, and perfect. This vision does not terrify, but soothes; it does not excite restless curiosity, but settles it; nor does it weary the senses, but calms them. Here rest is truly had. A tranquil God tranquilizes all things; and to behold the quiet one is to rest. It is to see the King after the diurnal as it were litigations of forensic causes, dismissing from himself the crowds, declining the troubles of cares, seeking lodging by night, entering the chamber with those of peace, whom he deigns [to honor] with this secret and this familiarity, resting certainly the more securely the more secretly; the more serenely disposing himself the more placidly he beholds those alone whom he loves. If it shall happen to any one of you to be so snatched away and so hidden at some hour in this secret and in this sanctuary of God, that neither the active sense, nor a pricking care, nor a biting guilt, nor those things certainly which are removed with more difficulty, the phantasms of corporeal images rushing in, may call him away or disturb him; he will be able indeed, when he has returned to us, to glory and say: 'The King has introduced me into his chamber' (Song 1:3). Whether, nevertheless, that is the very one concerning which the bride exults, I should not rashly affirm. It is nevertheless a chamber, and the chamber of the King; because certainly of the three, which we have assigned to a threefold vision, this place alone has been made in peace. For, as will openly be shown, in the former a small, and in the second no rest is perceived: since there he, appearing admirable, exercises the curiosity in zeal for searching; and here he, becoming known as terrible, shakes the infirmity. But indeed in this third place he deigns to appear not plainly terrible, nor so much admirable as lovable, serene and placid, sweet and mild, and of much mercy to all beholding him.
23.17: Now, that your memory may keep a compendium of those things which have been disputed at greater length concerning the cellar, the garden, and the chamber; remember the three times, the three merits, the three as it were rewards. In the garden observe the times, in the cellar the merits, in that threefold contemplation of one seeking the chamber the rewards. And concerning the cellar indeed let these suffice. Moreover concerning the garden or the chamber, if anything is to be added, or if anything perhaps other than those things which have been said shall occur to be observed; let us not pass it over in its place. But if not, let the things which have been said suffice, and let them by no means be repeated, lest those things ever come into loathing, which God forbid! which are brought forth to the praise and glory of the Spouse of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God blessed above all things for ever. Amen.

24.1: At length, brethren, on this our third return from the City, a more merciful eye from heaven has looked down upon us, and at last a more serene countenance has smiled upon us from above. The Leonine rage has been stilled, the malice has found its end, the Church has recovered peace. He who had troubled her for almost this whole space of eight years by a dire schism has been brought to nothing in his sight. Shall I indeed, for nothing, be restored to you out of so great perils? I have been granted to your desires, and I make myself ready for your advancement: by whose merits I live, I wish to live for their pursuits and their salvation. And that you would have me follow out what was long since begun in the Song, I indeed accept gladly, and I judge it more fitting to patch up the interrupted sermon than to begin anything new. But I fear lest the dignity of the subject matter, as it ought, fail to admit a mind that in that interval of time has grown unaccustomed, and has long been held drawn away — not only to things so different, but even to things so unworthy. But if I give you what I have, God can also, for my faithful service, give me to give even that which I have not. If not, let the talent surely be blamed, not the will.
24.2: The place, however, from which we must begin, if I am not mistaken, is this: 'The upright love you.' Before we begin to unfold it, let us see what it is, whose it is, who namely it is that says this. For that is required of us which the author himself does not utter. And perhaps we do better to attribute this to the young maidens, that in their own words they may also add this. For since they had said: 'We will exult and rejoice in you, mindful of your breasts above wine' (nor is there any doubt but that they were speaking to the mother), continuing the discourse they add this also: 'The upright love you' (Song 1:3). I think [this is said] for the sake of some of their number, who did not think the same, although they seemed to run equally; who seek their own things, and do not walk simply nor sincerely, but envy the mother's special glory, and seize an occasion of murmuring against her, from that, namely, that she alone had entered into the cellars. Which is nothing other than what the Apostle says: 'Peril from false brethren' (2 Cor. 11:26). These, in short, are they by whose reproaches she is again and again compelled to answer for herself, when she answers them thus: 'I am black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem' (Song 1:4). And so, on account of those that murmur and blaspheme, it is said by those who are good, who are simple, who are humble and meek; by these, I say, it is said to the bride for her consolation: 'The upright love you.' 'Let not,' they say, 'the unjust rebuke of these blasphemers be a care to you, since it is certain that the upright love you.' Good, truly, is the consolation, when, doing good, we are blasphemed by the wicked, if the upright love us. Against the mouth of those who speak iniquity, the good report of the good, together with the testimony of conscience, is altogether sufficient. 'In the Lord shall my soul be praised; let the meek hear, and rejoice.' 'Let the meek,' he says, 'rejoice' (Ps. 34:3). Let me please the meek, and I shall hear with an even mind whatever the envy of the lost shall have willed to cast at me.
24.3: In this sense, then, I think it was set down, 'The upright love you.' Nor absurdly, as I judge: since almost everywhere in the choir of the young maidens such are found, who observe with curiosity the doings of the bride, for the sake of detracting, not of imitating. They are tortured over the blessings of their elders, and are fed on evils. You may see them go apart, come together and sit together, and presently loose their saucy tongues into a detestable whispering. One joins herself to another, and not a breath passes among them; so great is the itch of detracting, or of hearing the detractor. They strike up a familiarity for slandering, being at one for discord. They patch up the most hostile friendships among themselves, and with an equal feeling of kindred malice the hateful conference is held. Not otherwise did Herod and Pilate once act, of whom the Gospel tells that they were made friends on that day (Luke 23:12), that is, on the day of the Lord's passion. For those who thus come together into one, it is not to eat the Lord's supper, but rather to pledge and to drink the cup of demons; while with importunate tongues they pour out to some the poison of perdition, and others gladly receive death entering through the ears. For so, according to the prophet, death enters through our windows (Jer. 9:21), when, itching in our ears and mouths, we strive to administer to one another the deadly cup of detraction. 'Let not my soul come into the council of the detractors,' since God hates them, the Apostle saying: 'Detractors are hateful to God' (Rom. 1:30). Hear how God himself, speaking in the psalm, confirms this sentence: 'The man who detracts his neighbor, him I pursued' (Ps. 101:5).
24.4: Nor is it any wonder, since this vice in particular is known to assault and persecute charity, which is God, and that more keenly than the rest, as you too may observe: every one who detracts, first of all indeed betrays himself as empty of charity; and then what else does he aim at by detracting, save that he whom he detracts may come into hatred or contempt with those before whom he detracts? He strikes, then, at charity in all who hear him with a slanderous tongue, and, so far as in him lies, kills and extinguishes it utterly: and not only that, but also in all the absent, to whom the word, flying quickly through those who are present, shall chance to find its way. You see how easily, and in a brief space, speech running swiftly can infect a huge multitude of souls with the corruption of this malice. For this reason the prophetic spirit says of such: 'Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood' (Ps. 14:3). Truly, as swift as speech runs swiftly on. There is one who speaks, and he utters but one single word; and yet that one word, in a single moment, while it infects the ears, kills the souls of the multitude of hearers. For the heart made bitter with the gall of envy can, through the instrument of the tongue, scatter nothing but bitter things, the Lord saying: 'Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks' (Luke 6:45). And there are kinds of this plague, while some indeed vomit out the poison of detraction nakedly and irreverently, as it comes to the mouth; but others strive to shadow over the conceived malice, which they cannot contain, with a certain coloring of feigned modesty. You may see deep sighs sent on before, and so, with a certain gravity and slowness, with a sad face, with downcast brows, and a plaintive voice, the curse go forth — and that the more persuasive in proportion as it is believed by those who hear to be uttered with a reluctant heart, and rather from the affection of one who sympathizes than of one who is malicious. 'I grieve,' he says, 'vehemently, for that I love him well enough, and could never correct him in this matter.' And another: 'For myself, indeed,' he says, 'I had well known this of him; but by me it would never have become known.' But since the matter has been laid open by another, I cannot deny the truth: saying it in sorrow, it is really so. And he adds: 'A great loss! for in other respects indeed he avails in many things; but in this part, to speak the truth, he can by no means be excused.'
24.5: Having recalled these few things against this most malignant vice, let us return to the order of the exposition, and show who in this place are to be understood by 'the upright.' For I do not think that any one of right understanding judges that they are called upright in body who love the bride. We must therefore show the spiritual rectitude, that is, of the mind or the heart. It is the Spirit who speaks, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. Therefore it was according to the mind, not according to the earthly and filthy matter, that God made man upright. For in his image and likeness he created him (Gen. 1:27). He himself, however, as you sing: 'The Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him' (Ps. 92:16). Upright, therefore, God made man upright and like to himself, that is, without iniquity, even as there is no iniquity in him. But iniquity is a vice of the heart, not of the flesh, so that by this you may know that in the spiritual portion of you, and not in the gross and clayey substance, the likeness of God is to be preserved or repaired. For God is a spirit, and those who would be like him, whether to persevere or to become so, must enter into the heart, and transact this business in the spirit: where, with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, they are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18).
24.6: Although God also gave man the upright stature of his body; perhaps that this bodily rectitude of the outward and meaner clay might remind the inner man, who was made in the image of God, of the spiritual rectitude that is to be kept by him, and that the comeliness of the clay might put to shame the deformity of the mind. For what is more unseemly, than to carry a crooked mind with an upright body? A perverse and foul thing it is, that the earthen vessel, which is the body from the earth, should have its eyes above, freely look up at the heavens, and delight its gaze with the luminaries of the heavens; while the spiritual and heavenly creature, on the contrary, should drag its eyes, that is, its inward senses and affections, downward into the earth; and she who ought to have been nourished in saffron should cling to the mud, like one of the swine, and embrace dung (Lam. 4:5). Be ashamed, my soul, that you have changed the divine likeness for that of the beast; be ashamed that you, who are from heaven, do wallow in the mire. Be ashamed, soul, says the body, in the contemplation of me. Created upright and like to your Creator, you also received me as a help like to yourself, namely according to the lineaments of bodily uprightness. Whithersoever you turn, whether to God above or to me below (for no one ever hated his own flesh), everywhere the figure of your comeliness meets you, everywhere for the state of your dignity you have, from the teaching of wisdom, a familiar admonition. Me, then, who keep and hold back the prerogative which I received for your sake — how is it that you are not ashamed to have lost your own? Why does the Creator behold in you his likeness blotted out, while he preserves and continually presents to you your own in me? Now every help that was owed to you from me you have turned into confusion for yourself; you abuse my service, you dwell unworthily in the human body, O brutish and beastly spirit.
24.7: Souls of this crooked kind, then, cannot love the bride, because they are not friends of the Bridegroom, since they are of the world. 'Whosoever,' he says, 'will be a friend of this world, is made an enemy of God' (James 4:4). Therefore to seek and to taste the things that are on the earth is the crookedness of the soul; and, on the other hand, to meditate on and long for the things that are above is uprightness. And that it may be perfect, let it be defined in sense and in consent. I would call you upright, if in all things you think aright, and do not dissent by your deeds. Let faith and action announce the state of the invisible soul. Deem one upright, if you prove him catholic in faith and just in work. If otherwise, do not hesitate to judge him crooked. For so you have it: 'If you offer rightly and do not divide rightly, you have sinned' (Gen. 4:7). Rightly, indeed, you offer whichever of these you offer, but you do not rightly divide them one from the other. Be not a right offerer and a wrong divider. Why do you divide the act from the faith? You divide iniquitously, slaying thereby your faith: for faith without works is dead (James 2:20). Do you offer a dead gift to God? For if in a certain soul devotion itself is the faith, what is faith that works not by love, but a senseless corpse? Do you well honor God with a fetid gift? do you well appease the murderer of your faith? How is that a peace-offering, where there is so fierce a discord? No wonder that Cain rose up against his brother, who had first killed his own faith. Why do you wonder, O Cain, if he who despises you looks not upon your gifts? (Gen. 4:5.) Nor is this a wonder, that he looks not upon you, who are so divided in yourself. If you give the hand to devotion, what do you give the mind but to envy? You do not reconcile God to you, being at variance with yourself; you do not please, but you sin; and that, not yet indeed by bearing impiously, but nevertheless by not dividing rightly. Although not yet a fratricide, you are nonetheless held a fidicide. Is he upright, even when he stretches out his hand to God, whose heart envy and brotherly hatred drag down to the earth? How is he upright, whose faith is dead, whose work is death, in whom there is no devotion but much bitterness? There was indeed faith in the offerer, but in the faith there was no love; a right offering, but a cruel division.
24.8: The death of faith is the separation of charity. Do you believe in Christ? do the works of Christ, that your faith may live. Let love quicken your faith, let action prove it. Let not an earthly work bend down him whom faith in heavenly things lifts up. You who say that you abide in Christ ought to walk even as he walked. But if you seek your own glory, envy the flourishing, detract from the absent, and repay him who hurts you — this Christ did not do. You confess that you know God, but in your deeds you deny him. Not rightly indeed, but impiously, you have given the tongue to Christ and the soul to the devil. Hear, then, what he says: 'This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me' (Isa. 29:13). You are surely not upright, who divide so unrightly. You cannot lift up a head that is pressed under the yoke of the devil. You cannot raise yourself up, over whom iniquity has dominion. Your iniquities have gone over your head, and like a heavy burden have weighed upon you (Ps. 38:5). Iniquity, moreover, sits upon a talent of lead (Zech. 5:7). You see that even right faith, which works not by love, does not make a man upright. But he who is without love has not wherewith to love the bride. But neither do works, however right, suffice to make an upright heart without faith. For who would call a man upright who does not please God? But without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11:6). He who does not please God, to him God cannot be pleasing. For he to whom God is pleasing cannot displease God. Moreover, to him to whom God is not pleasing, neither is his bride. How, then, is he upright, who neither loves God nor the Church of God, to whom it is said: 'The upright love you'? If, then, neither faith without works, nor works without faith, suffice for the uprightness of the soul, let us, brethren, who believe in Christ, study to make straight both our ways and our pursuits. Let us lift up our hearts together with our hands to God, that we may be found altogether upright, proving the uprightness of our faith by upright acts, as lovers of the bride, beloved of the Bridegroom, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

25.1: Behold what I said in the sermon, that the bride is compelled to make answer when her rivals provoke her — those who, though in body they seem to be of the number of the young maidens, are far from it in mind. She says indeed: 'I am black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem' (Song 1:4). It is plain that they were detracting from her, upbraiding her blackness. But mark the patience and the gentleness of the bride. For not only did she not render evil for evil, but she even blessed them, calling them daughters of Jerusalem, who for their own wickedness had rather deserved to be called daughters of Babylon, or daughters of Baal, or if any other name of reproach had occurred. She had indeed learned from the prophet, nay from that very anointing which teaches gentleness, that a bruised reed is not to be broken, and smoking flax is not to be quenched (Isa. 42:3). Wherefore she did not think that those already sufficiently stirred up were further to be provoked, nor that anything was to be added to the goads of the envy with which they were tormented. Rather, with those who hate peace, she studied to be at peace, knowing that she was a debtor even to the foolish. She chose, therefore, to soothe them with a favorable name, because her care was rather to give attention to the salvation of the weak than to her own vengeance.
25.2: This perfection, indeed, is to be wished for by all; but properly it is the form of the best, that is, of prelates. For good and faithful superiors know that the care of languishing souls, not pomp, has been committed to them. And when by the sign of a complaining voice they detect the inward murmuring of any of them, even bursting out against themselves up to revilings and insults; recognizing themselves as physicians and not as masters, they forthwith prepare against the frenzy of the soul not vengeance, but medicine. This, then, is the reason why the bride calls daughters of Jerusalem those very ones whom she endures as evil-minded and slanderous: namely, that in a gentle speech she may soothe the murmurers, settle their commotion, and heal their envy. For it is written: 'A peaceful tongue restrains quarrels' (Prov. 25:15). In another way, moreover, those who are of this sort are in a certain manner truly daughters of Jerusalem, nor does the bride name them so falsely. For whether on account of the sacraments of the Church, which they indeed receive indifferently together with the good; or on account of the confession of faith, which is in like manner common to all; or on account of at least the bodily fellowship of the faithful; or even on account of the hope of future salvation, from which they are by no means excluded, so long as they live here, nor are such even to be despaired of, however desperately they may live — they are not incongruously called daughters of Jerusalem.
25.3: Let us see now what it was to say: 'I am black, but beautiful.' Is there no contradiction in these words? Far be it! I say this for the sake of the simple, who do not know how to distinguish between color and form, since form pertains to the composition, and blackness is a color. In short, not everything that is black is straightway deformed. Blackness, for example, is no blemish in the pupil; and certain black pebbles please in ornaments; and black hair even adds comeliness and grace to fair countenances. So, too, you may readily observe in innumerable things. Although without number are those which on the surface, indeed, you will find discolored, but in the composition comely. In such a way, perhaps, may the bride, with the beauty, to be sure, of the composition, not be free from the blemish of blackness; but that, plainly, is in the place of her pilgrimage. Otherwise it will be when the Spouse of glory shall present her to himself in the fatherland as glorious, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing. But now, if she should say that she had no blackness, she would seduce herself, and the truth would not be in her. Wherefore do not wonder that she said: 'I am black,' and yet, nonetheless, glories that she is beautiful. For how is she not beautiful, to whom it is said: 'Come, my beautiful one'? (Song 2:10.) But to whom it is said: 'Come,' she had not yet come — lest perhaps anyone think that this was said, not indeed to this black one, who is still toiling by the way in coming, but to that blessed one who already, wholly without blackness, reigns in the fatherland.
25.4: But hear whence she called herself black, and whence beautiful. Was it black, indeed, on account of the foul manner of life which she formerly had under the prince of this world, still bearing the image of the earthly man; and beautiful, from the heavenly likeness which she afterward put on, already walking in the newness of life? But if this is so, why does she not rather speak in the past, 'I was black,' and not 'I am black'? If, however, this sense pleases anyone, what follows — 'like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon' (Song 1:4) — must be so understood, that she called herself a tent of Kedar indeed from the old manner of life, but of Solomon from the new. For that 'skins' is the same as 'tent,' the prophet shows, saying: 'Suddenly my tents are laid waste, suddenly my skins' (Jer. 4:20). First, therefore, she was black, like the most worthless tents of Kedar; afterward, beautiful, like the skins of the glorious king.
25.5: But let us see how both look rather to the state of a better life. If we consider the outward habit of the saints, that which is in the face — how humble and abject it surely is, and neglected with a certain carelessness; when yet, again and again, within, with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, they are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18): will not any one soul whatsoever of this sort seem to us deservedly able to answer those who upbraid her blackness: 'I am black, but beautiful'? Do you wish me, then, to show you a soul at once black and beautiful? 'The letters,' they say, 'are weighty; but the presence of the body is weak, and the speech contemptible' (2 Cor. 10:10). This was Paul. And so, O daughters of Jerusalem, you judge Paul by the presence of the body, and despise him as discolored and deformed, because you see the little man afflicted in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in many labors, in stripes beyond measure, in deaths often (2 Cor. 11:23, 27)? These are the things which blacken Paul. For such things the doctor of the nations is reputed inglorious, ignoble, black, obscure; in short, like the offscouring of this world. For is not he himself the one who is caught up into paradise, who, passing through the one and the other, reaches by the purity of his life even to the third heaven? O truly most beautiful soul! whom, though inhabiting a weak little body, heavenly beauty did not disdain to receive, angelic sublimity did not reject, divine brightness did not repulse. Do you call this one black? She is black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem. Black by your judgment, beautiful by the divine and angelic judgment. Even if she is black, it is only from without. But to herself it is a very small thing to be judged by you, or by those who judge according to the face. For man sees in the face, but God looks upon the heart (1 Sam. 16:7). Therefore, though black without, she is yet beautiful within, that she may please him to whom she has approved herself. Not indeed to you: for to whom, if she had still pleased. She would not be a servant of Christ. Happy blackness, which brings forth the whiteness of the mind, the light of knowledge, the purity of conscience!
25.6: Hear, in fine, what God promises through the prophet to black ones of this sort, whom either the humility of repentance, or the zeal of charity, like the heat of the sun, seems to have discolored. 'If your sins,' he says, 'be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if they be red as crimson, they shall be as white wool' (Isa. 1:18). Not at all, truly, is that outward blackness of the saints to be despised, which works the inward whiteness, and, accordingly, prepares a seat for wisdom. For wisdom is the brightness of eternal life, as the Wise Man defines (Wis. 7:26); and it is fitting that the soul in which she has elected a seat be white. But if the soul of the just man is the seat of wisdom, without doubt I would say that the soul of the just man is white. And perhaps justice itself is whiteness. But Paul was just, for whom a crown of justice was laid up (2 Tim. 4:8). Therefore Paul's soul was white, and wisdom sat in it, so that he spoke wisdom among the perfect — wisdom hidden in a mystery, which none of the princes of this world knew. Moreover, that outward blackness, of the weak presence of the body, of many labors, of many fastings and watchings, either wrought or merited in him that whiteness of wisdom and justice. And therefore what is black in Paul is more beautiful than every outward adornment, than every regal attire. There shall not be compared to it any beauty of the flesh whatever, no, not a shining skin that must soon burn, not a painted face that is near to corruption, not a precious garment subject to decay, not the look of gold, or the splendor of gems, or any such things, which are all for corruption.
25.7: Rightly, therefore, does all the care of the saints — the adornment and superfluous culture of their outward man being spurned, which certainly is corrupted — give and devote itself with all diligence to cultivating and adorning that inner man, who is to the image of God, and is renewed from day to day. For they are certain that nothing can be more acceptable to God than his image, if it were restored to its own comeliness. And therefore all their glory is within, not without; that is, not in the flower of the grass, or in the mouth of the crowd, but in the Lord. Whence they also say: 'This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience' (2 Cor. 1:12): that God alone is the judge of the conscience, to whom alone they desire to please; and to please whom is the only true and highest glory. Not a mean glory, plainly, is that which is within, in which even the Lord of glory deigns to glory, David saying: 'All the glory of the king's daughter is from within' (Ps. 45:14). And each one's own glory is the safer, while he has it in himself and not in another. But perhaps one must glory not only in inner whiteness, but also in the outward blackness as well as the exterior, lest anything at all should be lost to the saints, but all things cooperate unto good. Not only, therefore, in hope, but also [one must] glory in tribulations. 'Gladly,' he says, 'will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me.' An infirmity to be wished for, which is compensated by the power of Christ. Who will give me, not only to be infirm, but also to be destitute and to fail utterly from myself, that I may be strengthened by the power of the Lord of hosts? For power is perfected in infirmity. Finally he says: 'When I am weak, then am I strong and powerful' (2 Cor. 12:9, 10).
25.8: Which being so, the bride beautifully turns to her own glory that which is hurled at her as a reproach by her rivals; glorying that she is not only beautiful, but also black. For she does not blush at the blackness, which she knows went before also in the Spouse: to be likened to whom, how great a glory it is! She thinks, therefore, that nothing is more glorious for her than to bear the reproach of Christ. Whence that voice altogether of exultation and salvation: 'Far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ'! (Gal. 6:14.) Welcome is the ignominy of the cross to him who is not ungrateful to the Crucified. It is blackness, but it is the form and likeness of the Lord. Go to holy Isaiah, and he will describe to you how he saw him in the spirit. For whom else does he call the man of sorrows, and one acquainted with infirmity; and that there was no beauty nor comeliness in him? And he added: 'We esteemed him as a leper, and as one struck by God, and afflicted.' But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our crimes; and by his bruise we are healed (Isa. 53:3, 5). Behold whence he is black. Join to this also that of holy David: 'Fair in form above the sons of men' (Ps. 45:3); and you have in the Spouse all that the bride has here testified of herself.
25.9: Does it seem to you, too, that he, according to the things that have been said, could rightly answer the rival Jews: 'I am black, but handsome, O sons of Jerusalem'? Black, plainly, he to whom there was no beauty, nor comeliness; black, because he is a worm and no man, the reproach of men, and the outcast of the people (Ps. 22:7). Finally, he made himself to be sin (2 Cor. 5:21): and should I fear to call him black? Look, surely, at one foul with rags, livid with stripes, bedaubed with spittle, pale with death; and even then, truly, you will confess him black. Ask also the apostles, how they looked upon him on the mount; or certainly the angels, upon whom they long to look; and nonetheless you will marvel that he is beautiful. Therefore he is beautiful in himself, black for your sake. How beautiful I acknowledge you, even in my own form, O Lord Jesus! not only on account of the divine miracles with which you shine, but also on account of the truth, and meekness, and justice. Blessed is he who, diligently observing you, a man conversing among men in these things, offers himself, according to his powers, as your imitator. Your beautiful one has already received this gift of blessedness as the first-fruits of her dowry; neither is she slow to imitate what is beautiful in you, nor confounded to bear what is black in you. Whence she also said: 'I am black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem'; and she added the similitude: 'Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.' But that is obscure, and by no means to be touched by the weary. You have time to knock. If you do not dissemble, he who reveals mysteries will be at hand; nor will he delay to open, who even invites you to knock. For it is he who opens, and no one shuts (Rev. 3:7), the Spouse of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

26.1: 'Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon' (Song 1:4). Here we must begin, because here the former sermon ended. You are waiting to hear what this is, and how it squares with the chapter treated last, because it is a comparison. For it may have been added in this way, that both parts of the comparison answer to that alone which had gone before there: 'I am black.' Or it may be so, that to those two these two are referred, that is, each to each. That sense is the simpler, this one the more obscure. But let us try both: and first, indeed, that one which appears more difficult. Yet the difficulty is not in the two first, but in the two last only. For Kedar indeed, which is interpreted 'darkness,' seems to agree plainly enough with blackness; but the skins of Solomon do not so agree with beauty. Moreover, who does not see that the tents likewise fall into the same fittingness? For what are tents, but our own bodies, in which we sojourn? For we have no lasting city here, but we seek the one that is to come (Heb. 13:14). But we also wage war in them, as in tents; violent, indeed, toward the kingdom. In fine, the life of man upon earth is a warfare (Job 7:1); and so long as we serve in this body, we sojourn away from the Lord, that is, from the light. For the Lord is light; and to the extent that any one is not with him, to that extent he is in darkness, that is, in Kedar. Let him, therefore, acknowledge as his own that lamentable voice: 'Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner' (Ps. 120:5, 6). This, then, is the dwelling of our body, not the mansion of a citizen or the home of a native; but either the tent of a soldier, or the stable of a traveler. This body, I say, is a tent, and a tent of Kedar, which indeed, by the interposition of itself, for the present defrauds the soul of the spectacle of the uncircumscribed light; nor does it allow it to see it at all, save through a glass indeed and in an enigma, not face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).
26.2: Do you see whence the blackness of the Church, whence also some rust has clung to even the most beautiful souls? From the tent of Kedar, truly, from the exercise of the toilsome warfare, from the length of the wretched sojourning, from the straits of the sorrowful exile, from the body, at last, weak and heavy; because the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind that thinks of many things (Wis. 9:15). Therefore they also long to be dissolved, that, being lifted above the body, they may fly away into the embraces of Christ. 'O wretched man that I am! who will deliver me from the body of this death?' (Rom. 7:24.) She who is of this sort knows, surely, that in the tent of Kedar she cannot, to the very purity, be without spot or wrinkle, nor without some blackness, however small; and she longs to depart, that she may put it off. And this is the reason why the bride called herself black, like the tents of Kedar. But how is she beautiful, like the skins of Solomon? But I feel in these skins something sublime and sacred wrapped up, which by no means I would dare to touch at all, save, to be sure, at the nod of him who laid it up and sealed it. For I have read: 'He who searches the majesty will be overwhelmed by the glory' (Prov. 25:27). I desist, then, and put it off. Meanwhile it will be your care to obtain, as usual, the favor by your prayers; that we may return to that which needs more attentive minds, the more cheerfully, the more confidently. And perhaps the devout knocker will find what the rash searcher could not. Although, in truth, both grief bids an end, and the calamity which I suffer.
26.3: For how long shall I dissemble, and the fire which I hide within myself burn my sad breast, and feed upon my inmost parts? Shut in, it creeps the more widely, rages the more fiercely. What have I to do with this song, who am in bitterness? The force of grief takes away my attention, and the indignation of the Lord drinks up my spirit. For, he being taken away, through whom my studies in the Lord were wont to be free in whatever way, at the same time my heart also forsook me. But I did violence to my spirit, and dissembled up to this hour, lest the affection should seem to conquer the faith. In fine, while others wept, I, as you could observe, followed that detested funeral with dry eyes, with dry eyes I stood at the tomb, until all the solemnities of the burial were accomplished. Clothed in the sacerdotal vestments, I myself finished the wonted prayers over him with my own mouth, and with my own hands, after the custom, I cast the earth upon the body of my beloved, myself, too, soon to be earth. Those who looked upon me wept, and wondered that I did not weep myself, since all pitied not him indeed, but me rather, who had lost him. For whose heart, even of iron, would not be moved over me there, seeing me survive Gerard? It was a common loss; but it was not reckoned against my own misfortune. But I, with what strength of faith I could, struggled against the affection, striving, even against my will, not to be moved in vain by the debt of nature, the due of the universe, the usage of our condition, the command of the mighty, the judgment of the just, the scourge of the terrible, the will of the Lord. For such reasons always, from then on and thereafter, I demanded of myself not to give way to much weeping, yet was much disturbed and sad. Nor could I command sorrow, though I could command tears; but, as it is written: 'I was troubled, and I did not speak' (Ps. 77:5). But suppressed grief took root the deeper within, made, as I feel, the more bitter in that it was not allowed to go out. I confess, I was overcome. It must needs go forth, what I suffer within. Let it go forth, then, to the eyes of the sons, who, knowing the trouble, may judge the lamentation more humanely, and console more sweetly.
26.4: You know, O sons, how just my grief is, how to be lamented is my wound. You see, certainly, how faithful a companion has deserted me in this way in which I walked, one not slow for work, how sweet in manners. Who was so altogether necessary to me? to whom was I equally dear? He was my brother by blood, but more truly a brother in religion. Mourn, I pray, for my state, you to whom these things are known. I was weak in body, and he carried me; I was little of heart, and he strengthened me; I was sluggish and negligent, and he stirred me up; I was improvident and forgetful, and he reminded me. Where are you torn from me? where snatched from my hands, O man of one mind, O man after my own heart? We loved one another in life; how are we separated in death? Most bitter separation! and one that nothing but death could at all have brought about. For when would you, living, have deserted me, living? It is altogether the work of death, a horrible divorce. For who would have spared so sweet a bond of our mutual love, unless death, the enemy of all sweetness? A good death was that, which by snatching away one, in its fury slew two. Was it not death to me also? Nay, more to me, to whom, surely, a life unhappier than every death has been preserved. I live, that I may die living; and shall I call this life? How much more gently would you have deprived me, O stern death, of the use of life than of its fruit! for life without fruit is a heavier death. In fine, a twofold evil is prepared for the unfruitful tree, the axe and the fire (Matt. 3:10). Envying, therefore, my labors, you have taken far from me a friend and a neighbor, through whose zeal chiefly my works were, when they were, fruitful. It would, therefore, have been better for me to put my life in peril than to have lost your presence, O Gerard, who were the solicitous promoter, the faithful helper, the cautious examiner of my studies in the Lord. Why, I pray, have we either loved, or lost, one another? It is a hard condition, but my fortune is to be pitied, and not his! For you, dear brother, if you have lost loved ones, have surely received more loved ones. But what consolation now remains for me, wretched, after you, my only comfort? The companionship of bodies for the concord of our manners was equally pleasing to both; but the division has wounded me alone. That which pleased was common; that which is sad and mournful is mine: upon me have the wrathful [affections] passed over, upon me is the fury confirmed. To both of us was the presence of each other welcome, the companionship sweet, the converse pleasant; but all those delights of both, I have lost, you have gained. And indeed, for those exchanged, the recompense is great.
26.5: With how great a usury of joys and a heap of blessings are you lacking to us today, most dear brother! You have, certainly, in return for me, so little a one, Christ's presence laid up for you; nor do you feel the loss of your absence from us, being mingled with the choirs of angels. There is no reason, then, that you should complain of our presence being, as it were, withdrawn from you, to whom the Lord of majesty has vouchsafed in abundance the plenty of himself and his own. But I, what for you? How I would wish to know what you now feel about me, your only one, faltering amid cares and pains, deprived of you, the staff of my weakness! if yet it is allowed me still to think of the wretched, now that you have entered the abyss of light, and are swallowed up in that sea of eternal happiness. For perhaps, although you have known us according to the flesh, yet now you know us no longer: and since you have entered into the powers of the Lord, you are mindful of his justice alone, forgetful of us. For the rest, he who cleaves to God is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17), and is wholly changed into a certain divine affection, nor can he now feel or taste anything but God, and what he feels and tastes is God, being full of God. But God is charity, and the more one is joined to God, the fuller he is of charity. Moreover, God is impassible, but not without compassion, to whom it is proper always to have mercy and to spare. You, then, also must needs be merciful, who cling to the Merciful One, although you are now no longer wretched: and you who do not suffer, yet compassionate. Your affection, therefore, is not diminished, but changed; nor, because you have put on God, have you put off the care of us; for he himself has care of us (1 Pet. 5:7). What is weak you have cast away, but not what is pious. For charity never fails (1 Cor. 13:8): you will not forget me to the end.
26.6: Methinks I hear my brother saying: 'Can a mother forget the son of her womb?' 'Even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you' (Isa. 49:15). By no means is it expedient. You know where I am, where I lie, where you have left me; there is no one to stretch out a hand. At whatever has come up, I look to Gerard as I was wont, and he is not. Alas! then do I, wretched, groan, like a man without help. Whom shall I consult in my doubts? in whom trust in adversities? who will bear the burdens? who will drive away the dangers? Did not Gerard's eyes go before my steps everywhere? Did they not keep your breast, O Gerard, more known to my care than my own, assault it more familiarly, press it more keenly? Did not your tongue, that so winning and powerful one, very often rescue mine from the speeches of the world, and restore it to a friendly silence? The Lord had given him an erudite tongue, that he might know when he ought to bring forth speech. So, in fine, in the prudence of his answers, and in the grace given him from above, he satisfied both those of the household and the strangers, so that almost no one required me, to whom Gerard had perhaps first come. He came to meet, however, those arriving, opposing himself, lest they should suddenly break in upon my leisure.
