If there were any, certainly, whom he could not satisfy by himself, these he led to me, and sent the rest away. O the industrious man! o the faithful friend! and he both did his friend's pleasure, and did not fail in the offices of charity. Who went away from him with an empty hand? If [he was] rich, he carried back counsel; if poor, support. Nor did he seek the things that were his own, who thrust himself into the midst of the cares, that I might be free. For he hoped, as he was most humble, a greater fruit from our quiet, than if he himself were free. Sometimes, however, he asked to be released and to yield to another, as one who would provide better. But where would such a one be found? Nor was he held in that office by any overweening affection, as is wont, but by the sole regard of charity. For he labored more than all, and received less than all; so that often, while he ministered necessaries to others, he himself lacked in many, for example, food or clothing. In fine, when he felt himself drawing near to his departure: 'God,' he said, 'you know that, as far as was in me, I always wished for quiet; to attend to myself, to be free for you.' But your fear, the will of the brethren, and the zeal of obedience, held me entangled; above all, the genuine love of the abbot, at once brother and father. It is so. Thanks to you, brother, for all the fruit of my studies in the Lord, if there is any. To you I owe it, if I have profited, if I have been of use. You were entangled, and I, by your kindness, sat at leisure for myself, or was more holily occupied in the divine offices, or more usefully attended to the teaching of the sons. For why should I not be secure within, when I knew you acting without, my right hand, the light of my eyes, my heart, and my tongue? And indeed an unwearied hand, a single eye, a heart of counsel, a tongue speaking judgment, as it is written: 'The mouth of the just man will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment' (Ps. 37:30).
26.7: But what did I say, that he acted without? as if Gerard were ignorant of what is within, and were without a share in spiritual gifts. Those know who know him, how much his words savored of the spirit. His fellows in the cloister know how his manners and his pursuits savored not of the flesh, but burned with the spirit. Who was more rigid than he in the keeping of discipline? who more severe in chastising his body, more raised up or more sublime in contemplating, more subtle in disputing? How often, disputing with him, did I learn what I did not know; and I who had come to teach, went away rather taught? Nor is it a wonder about me, since great and wise men likewise testify that this same thing happened to them from him. He did not know letters; but he had the sense that is the inventor of letters, and he had the illuminating Spirit. Nor only in the greatest things, but in the least also, was he greatest. What, for example, in buildings, in fields, gardens, waters, in fine in all the arts or works of rustics? what, I say, in this kind of things also, escaped the skill of Gerard? For masons, smiths, farmers, gardeners, shoemakers, and weavers, he was easily a master. And when by the judgment of all he was wiser than all, only in his own eyes he was not wise. Would that that curse did not touch many, even if less wise: 'Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes' (Isa. 5:21)! To those who know, I speak these things, and as yet more and greater than these about him, to those who have found them out. I spare, however, because he is my flesh and my brother. This, however, I add with confidence: he was useful to me in all things, and above all; he was useful in small things and great, in private and public, without and within. Rightly did I hang wholly upon him, who was all to me. He had left me, almost alone, the honor and the name of provider: for he did the work himself. I was called abbot, but he was in charge of the solicitude. Rightly did my spirit rest in him, by whom it was allowed me to delight in the Lord, to preach more freely, to pray more securely. Through you, I say, my brother, have I had a sober mind and a grateful quiet, a more effectual speech, a richer prayer, a more frequent reading and a more fervent affection.
26.8: Alas! you are taken away, and all these things together. With you have all my delights and my joys equally departed. Now the cares rush in, now the annoyances knock on this side and that, and the straits on every side have found me alone, they alone have remained to me at your departure, alone under the burden do I groan. Either to lay it down, or to be crushed, is necessary, because you have withdrawn your shoulders. Who will grant me to die soon after you? For I would not wish it for your sake, nor to defraud you of your glory. Moreover, to survive you is labor and grief. I will live, as long as I live, in bitterness; I will live in mourning: and let this be my consolation, that I am afflicted by mourning. I will not spare myself; and I will help the hand of the Lord: for the hand of the Lord has touched me. Me, I say, it has touched and struck, not him, whom it has called to rest; it has killed me, when it cut down him. For who would call him killed, whom he has planted in life? But what was to him the gate of life, is plainly death to me; and I would say that I am dead by that death, not he who has fallen asleep in the Lord. Come forth, come forth, O tears, long since desiring it; come forth, because he who had blocked your passage has departed. Let the floodgates of my wretched head be opened; and let the fountains of waters burst forth, if perhaps they may suffice to wash away the filth of the sins with which I have deserved wrath. When the Lord has consoled me, then perhaps I also may deserve to be consoled, if yet I do not spare myself from mourning: for they who mourn, they shall be comforted (Matt. 5:5). Wherefore let every holy man condescend to me, and let him who is spiritual sustain me, a mourner, in the spirit of gentleness. Let my mourning, I pray, be weighed by human feeling, not by usage. For we see the dead daily mourned by their dead: much weeping, and no fruit. We do not blame the affection, unless it exceeds the measure; but the cause. That one, indeed, is of nature, and its disturbance is the punishment of sin: this one is vanity and sin. For there, if I am not mistaken, only the losses of the glory of the flesh, the discomforts of the present life, are mourned. And they are to be mourned who so mourn. Do I weep in such a way? My affection is like, but the cause is other, and the intention unlike. I have, truly, no complaint about all the things that are of the world. In those things, indeed, which are of God, I grieve that faithful help, that saving counsel, has been taken away. I mourn Gerard: Gerard is the cause — a brother in flesh, but nearest in spirit, a companion in purpose; my soul has cleaved to his soul, and of the two it has made one, not blood-relationship, but unanimity. The kinship of the flesh, indeed, was not lacking; but the fellowship of the spirit, the agreement of minds, the conformity of manners, joined [us] more. When, therefore, we were one heart and one soul, this sword passed through my soul likewise and his, and dividing, placed one half in heaven, and left the other half in the mire. I, I am that wretched portion lying in the mud, bereft of a part of myself, and that the better part; and it is said to me: 'Will you not weep?' My bowels are torn from me; and it is said to me: 'Have you not felt?' I feel, I feel, even against my will, because neither is my strength the strength of stones, nor is my flesh of brass; I feel, at any rate, and I grieve, and my grief is always before my eyes. Not indeed will he who strikes be able to accuse us of hardness and insensibility, as the one did of those of whom he says: 'I have struck them, and they have not grieved' (Jer. 5:3). I have confessed my affection, and I have not denied it. Anyone may call it carnal: I do not deny that it is human, even as neither do I deny that I am a man. If this does not suffice, neither will I deny that it is carnal. For I too am carnal, sold under sin, doomed to death, liable to pains and miseries. I am not, I confess, insensible to pains: I dread my death and the death of mine. He was my Gerard, truly mine. Was he not mine, who was a brother by blood, a son by profession, a father by solicitude, a companion in spirit, my inmost in affection? He has withdrawn from me; I feel it, I am hurt, and grievously.
26.10: Forgive me, O sons: nay, if you are sons, grieve in your turn for the father's lot. Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, at least you my friends, who surely consider how heavy things, for my sins, I have received from the hand of the Lord. With the rod of his indignation he has struck me, worthily for my merits, harshly for my strength. Who would call it a light thing to live without Gerard, but one who does not know what bond I had with Gerard? Yet I do not gainsay the words of the Holy [One]; nor do I blame the judgment by which each one receives what he is worthy of: he, the crown which he merited; I, the punishment which I owed. Do I, because I feel the punishment, blame the sentence? That is human, this impious. Human, I say, and necessary, to be affected toward our dear ones, whether delightfully when they are present, or distressfully when they are absent. Social converse will not be without fruit, especially among friends: and what mutual love has wrought in those present to one another, the horror of separation indicates, and the grief of those separated from one another. I grieve for you, dearest Gerard, not because you are to be grieved for, but because you are taken away. And therefore, perhaps, I should rather grieve for myself, who drink the cup of bitterness. And I alone am to be grieved for, because I alone drink: for you do not [drink]. I alone suffer what those are wont to suffer in common who love one another, when they lose one another.
26.11: Would that I had not lost you, but sent you on before! would that, even late, at some time I may follow you wherever you have gone! For there is no doubt that you have gone to those whom, about the middle of your last night, you were inviting to praise, when, in countenance and voice of exultation, you suddenly burst into that [verse] of David, while those who stood by were astonished: 'Praise the Lord from the heavens, praise him in the heights' (Ps. 148:1). Now for you, my brother, while it was still midnight, the day was dawning, and the night was being lit up as the day; truly that night was your illumination in your delights. I was summoned to that miracle, to see a man exulting in death, and insulting death. Where is, O death, your victory? where is, O death, your sting? Now it is not a sting, but a jubilee. Now a man dies singing, and dying, he sings. You, mother of sorrow, are usurped for joy; you, enemy of glory, are usurped for glory; you, gate of hell and pit of perdition, are usurped for the entrance of the kingdom and for the finding of salvation: and that by a sinful man. Rightly, indeed, because you iniquitously usurped rash power over an innocent and just man. You are dead, O death, and pierced with the hook which, unwary, you swallowed, whose voice is that in the prophet: 'O death, I will be your death; I will be your sting, O hell' (Hos. 13:14). Pierced, I say, with that hook, you open to the faithful, passing through the midst of you, a broad and glad exit to life. Gerard fears you not, you ghostly phantom. Gerard passes through the midst of your jaws to the fatherland, not only secure, but even rejoicing and praising. When, therefore, I had come up, and he had finished with a clear voice, in my hearing, the last [words] of the psalm, looking up to heaven, he said: 'Father, into your hands I commend my spirit' (Luke 23:46). And repeating that same speech, and frequently redoubling it: 'Father, Father,' turning to me, with a face, to be sure, made cheerful: 'How great,' he said, 'is the condescension of God, to be the Father of men! how great the glory of men, that they should be sons of God, and heirs of God!' For if sons, then heirs. So sang he whom we mourn: in which, I confess, he turned my mourning, almost, into a song, while, intent on his glory, I almost forget my own misery.
26.12: But a piercing grief calls me back to myself, and an anxiety that agitates me, as from a light sleep, easily recalls me from that serene contemplation. I will mourn, then, but over myself, because over him reason now forbids. For I think that, if an opportunity were given, he would say to us now: 'Do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves.' David rightly mourned over his parricidal son (2 Sam. 19:1), for whom he knew that the exit from the belly of death was forever blocked by the mass of his crime. Rightly over Saul and over Jonathan (2 Sam. 1:17); who, being alike swallowed up once, no emergence is now hoped for. And indeed they will rise again, but not to life; nay, to life, that, living, they may die the more unhappily in death. Although concerning Jonathan the sentence may not undeservedly remain doubtful. But to me, even if that reason for mourning is not at hand, yet it is not none. First I mourn over my own wound, and the loss of this house; then I mourn over the needs of the poor, of whom Gerard was the father; I mourn, certainly, also over the whole state of our order and of our profession, which drew from your zeal, counsel, and example, O Gerard, no small strength; lastly I mourn, even if not over you, yet because of you. Hence, wholly from hence, am I grievously affected, because I vehemently love. And let no one be troublesome to me, saying that I ought not to be so affected; since kind Samuel over a reprobate king (1 Sam. 16:1), and pious David over a parricidal son, satisfied their affection, and not to the injury of the faith, not to the disparagement of the judgment from above. 'Absalom, my son,' says holy David, 'my son Absalom' (2 Sam. 18:33): and behold, one greater than Absalom is here. The Savior also, seeing the city of Jerusalem, and foreseeing that it would fall, wept over it (Luke 19:41). And shall I not feel my own desolation, which is present? Shall I not grieve my wound, fresh and heavy? He wept in compassion, and do I not dare [to weep] in suffering? And certainly, at the tomb of Lazarus, he neither reproved the weepers, nor forbade the weeping; nay, he even wept with the weepers: 'And Jesus wept,' it says (John 11:35). Those tears were, truly, witnesses of nature, not signs of distrust. In fine, he presently came forth at the voice of him who was dead, lest you should at once think that the mourner's affection was a prejudice to the faith.
26.13: So neither is our weeping a sign of unbelief, but an indication of our condition; nor, because I, being struck, weep, do I reprove the one who strikes, but I call upon his mercy, and I endeavor to bend his severity. Whence my words are full of grief, but not at all of murmuring. Have I not brought forth words full of justice, since by the completion of one sentence both he who owed it was punished, and he who merited it was crowned? And I still say: the sweet and upright Lord has done both well. I will sing to you, O Lord, mercy and judgment. Let mercy, which you have shown to your servant Gerard, sing to you; and let the judgment also sing, which we bear. In the one you will be praised as good, in the other as just. Is the praise only of goodness? There is also [the praise] of justice. You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right (Ps. 119:137). Gerard you gave, Gerard you have taken away: and if we grieve that he is taken away, yet we do not forget that he was given, and we give thanks that we have merited to have him, whom we are so unwilling to lack, in so far as it is not expedient.
26.14: I remember, Lord, my covenant and your mercy, that you may be justified in your words, and may overcome when you are judged. When, for the cause of the Church, we were at Viterbo last year, he fell sick, and, the languor growing strong, when the summons already seemed near, I, taking it sorely that the companion of my pilgrimage, and that such a companion, should be left in a strange land, and not resign [him] to those who had entrusted him to me, since he was loved by all, as he was very amiable; turned to prayer with weeping and groaning: 'Wait,' I said, 'Lord, until the return.' Restored to your friends, take him now, if you will, and I will not complain. You heard me, O God: he recovered, we accomplished the work you had enjoined, we returned with exultation, bearing the sheaves of peace. But I almost forgot my covenant, but you did not. I am ashamed of these sobs, which accuse me of transgression. What need of more? You have asked again what was committed, you have received what was your own. The tears put an end to the words; do you, Lord, put an end and a measure to them.

27.1: Since with the duties of human kindness we have attended our friend as he returned to his fatherland, I return, brethren, to the work of edification which I had interrupted. For it is unbecoming to weep long for one who is rejoicing; and it is importunate to press many tears upon one sitting at the feast. But even if we bewail our own hardships, we ought not to do even that too much, lest we seem not so much to have loved him as to have sought our own advantage from him. Let the joy of the Beloved, surely, temper the sadness of the desolate; and let it become more tolerable for us that he is not with us, because he is with God. Relying, therefore, on your prayers, I wish, if I can, to bring to light whatever that is which I feel to be hidden beneath those skins which have been brought forward as an example of the bride's beauty. This, if you remember, was touched upon, but remained undiscussed: but let it be discussed and explained how she is black like the tents of Kedar. How, then, [is she] beautiful like the skins of Solomon (Song 1:4), as if Solomon in all his glory had anything equal to the beauty of the bride and to the glory of her array? And indeed if we should say that these skins, I know not what they are, like the tents of Kedar also, look rather to blackness than to the beauty of the bride, perhaps it would fit, nor would there be wanting whence we might show that it agrees, as also we shall show. But if, on the other hand, we think that the beauty of any skins whatsoever is to be compared to the brightness of the bride, here indeed we have need of the help of him to whom you have knocked, that we may be able fitly to open this mystery. For of those things which shine in the countenance, if [any] be compared to the inward beauty of some holy soul, what will not appear vile and foul to a right judge? What, I say, does the figure of this world, which passes away, show in itself such, that it could equal the beauty of that soul which, having put off the oldness of the earthly man, has put on the comeliness of him who is from heaven, adorned with the best morals in place of necklaces, purer and more exalted than the very aether, more splendid than the sun? Do not, therefore, look to that Solomon, when you desire to search out after what manner the bride glories that she is like, in beauty, to skins.
27.2: What, then, is that which she says: 'I am beautiful like the skins of Solomon'? A great and wonderful thing, as I judge: if at least we attend here not to this one, but to that one of whom it is said: 'Behold, a greater than Solomon is here' (Matt. 12:42). For he is so far my Solomon that he is called not only the Peaceful One — for that indeed is what Solomon means — but even peace itself, Paul bearing witness that he himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14). With that Solomon I do not doubt that there can be found that which I should not doubt to compare at all to the beauty of the bride. And especially concerning his skins, mark it in the Psalm: 'Spreading out,' he says, 'the heaven like a skin' (Ps. 104:2). Not that Solomon, for all his great wisdom and great power, stretched out the heaven like a skin; but rather he who is not so much wise as Wisdom itself — he it is who stretched it out and established it. For his is that voice, and not that one's: 'When he was preparing the heavens — no doubt [it was] God the Father — I was present.' There was present, without doubt, to him preparing the heavens his power and his wisdom. Nor should you think that she stood by idle, and as it were only to look on, because he said 'I was present,' not also 'I was preparing.' Look a little lower down, and you will find him plainly adding: 'I was with him, composing all things' (Prov. 8:27-30). Finally he says: 'For whatsoever the Father does, these the Son also does in like manner' (John 5:19). And he, therefore, also stretches out the heaven like a skin. A most beautiful skin, which, after the manner of some great tent, covering the whole face of the earth, delights human eyes with the so sightly variety of the sun, the moon, and the stars. What is more beautiful than this skin? what more adorned than the heaven? Yet by no means is even this at all to be compared to the glory and beauty of the bride, yielding in this very point, that even this figure of it passes away, as being bodily and subject to bodily senses. For the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal (2 Cor. 4:18).
27.3: But there is a certain rational beauty of the bride, and a spiritual image; and it is itself eternal, because it is the image of eternity. Her beauty, for example, is charity; and charity, as you read, never fails (1 Cor. 13:8). There is, certainly, justice also: 'And his justice,' he says, 'remains for ever and ever' (Ps. 111:3). There is also patience; and you likewise read that the patience of the poor shall not perish forever (Ps. 9:18). What of voluntary poverty? what of humility? Does not the one merit the eternal kingdom (Matt. 5:3), and the other likewise eternal exaltation? (Luke 14:11.) To that also the holy fear of the Lord looks, which endures for ever and ever (Ps. 19:9). Thus prudence, thus temperance, thus fortitude, and whatever other virtues there are, what are they but certain pearls in the bride's array, glittering with perpetual splendor? Perpetual, I say, because [they are] the seat and foundation of perpetuity. For neither is there at all a place in the soul for the perpetual and blessed life, save with virtues intervening, as it were, in the midst. Whence the Prophet [says] to God, who indeed is the blessed life: 'Justice and judgment,' he says, 'are the preparation of your throne' (Ps. 89:14). And the Apostle says that Christ dwells, not indeed in every way, but signally, by faith in our hearts (Eph. 3:17). To the Lord, too, about to sit upon the ass, the disciples spread their garments (Matt. 21:7, 8); signifying that the Savior, that is salvation, by no means sits upon a naked soul, which he did not, to be sure, find clothed with the doctrine and morals of the Apostles. And therefore the Church, having the promise of future happiness, takes care in the meantime to prepare and adorn herself in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety (Ps. 45:9) of graces and virtues, that she may be found worthy and capable of the fullness of grace.
27.4: But to this spiritual and so beautiful variety, which in the meantime she has received from the first robe, in a certain garment of her sanctification, I would by no means compare in beauty this visible and bodily heaven, although in its own kind, indeed, most beautiful with starry variety. But there is the heaven of heavens, of which the Prophet [says]: 'Sing to the Lord,' he says, 'who ascends above the heaven of heavens to the east' (Ps. 68:33, 34). And this heaven is intellectual and spiritual: and he who made the heavens in understanding (Ps. 136:5) created it and established it for ever, and dwells in it himself. But lest you should think that the bride's devotion remains short of that heaven in which she knows her Beloved to dwell: for where her treasure is, there is her heart also (Matt. 6:21). She emulates, indeed, those who stand before the face to which she sighs, and with whom, for the present, she cannot associate herself by seeing, she studies to conform herself by living, crying out more by her conduct than by her words: 'Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place of the habitation of your glory' (Ps. 26:8).
27.5: From this heaven, indeed, she thinks it by no means unworthy of herself to draw a similitude. This [heaven] is stretched out like a skin, not, however, in the spaces of places, but in the affections of minds; this distinguished by the wonderful and various works of the craftsman. But the divisions are not of colors, but of beatitudes. For some, indeed, he placed as angels; others as archangels; others as virtues; others as dominations; others as principalities; others as powers; others as thrones; others cherubim, and others seraphim. Thus is this heaven starry; thus is this skin painted. This is one of the skins of my Solomon, and this is the chief in all the array of his manifold glory. But this great skin contains in itself very many skins of Solomon as well, since every blessed and holy one who is there is, to be sure, a skin of Solomon. For they are kindly and stretched out in charity, reaching even to us, to whom they do not grudge the glory which they have, but wish [it for us]; so that, for the sake of this very thing, they do not disdain to sojourn among us, being busy about us, and having care of us, all ministering spirits, sent into ministry for the sake of those who are to obtain the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1:14). Wherefore, as that whole assembled multitude of the blessed is in a singular way called the heaven of heavens; so also they are named the heavens of heavens on account of each single one, who indeed is a heaven, and to each single one pertains what is said: 'Spreading out the heaven like a skin' (Ps. 104:2). You see, I believe, what those skins are, and whose Solomon's they are, from the likeness of which the bride glories.
27.6: Now, then, behold her glory, who compares herself both to heaven, and to that heaven which is so much the more glorious as it is the more divine. Nor does she without reason claim for herself a similitude from that whence she derives her origin. For if, on account of the body, which she has from the earth, she likens herself to the tents of Kedar, why should she not also, on account of the soul, which is from heaven, glory that she is in like manner like to heaven, especially since her life bears witness to her origin, bears witness to the dignity of her nature and of her country? She adores and worships one God, as the angels [do]; she loves Christ above all things, as the angels [do]; she is chaste, as the angels [are] — and that in the flesh of sin and in a fragile body, which is not [the case with] the angels; finally she seeks and relishes the things which are with them, not the things which are upon the earth. What more evident badge of a heavenly origin, than to retain the inborn likeness, even in the region of unlikeness, to claim the glory of the celibate life on earth, and by an exile, and, finally, in a body almost bestial, to live an angel? These are things of heavenly power, not of earthly; and they openly show that the soul which can do these things is truly from heaven. But hear more openly: 'I saw,' he says, 'the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven, prepared of God, as a bride adorned for her husband'; and he added: 'And I heard a great voice from the throne saying: Behold, the tabernacle of God with men, and he will dwell with them' (Rev. 21:2, 3). To what end? I believe, that he might acquire for himself a bride from among men. A wonderful thing! He was coming to the bride, and he did not come without the bride. He was seeking a bride, and the bride was with him. Were they then two? God forbid! 'For one,' he says, 'is my dove.' But as he willed to make one from the different flocks of sheep, that there should be one fold and one shepherd (John 10:16), so, since he had a bride cleaving to him from the beginning — the multitude of angels — it pleased him also to call together a Church from among men, and to unite her to that which is from heaven, that there should be one bride and one bridegroom. Therefore, by this one being added, she is perfected, not doubled; and she recognizes that it is said of herself: 'One is my perfect one' (Song 6:8). Moreover, conformity makes them one, now indeed in a like devotion, but afterwards in equal glory.
27.7: You have, then, both of them from heaven: the bridegroom, that is, Jesus, and the bride, Jerusalem. And he, indeed, in order to be seen, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man (Phil. 2:7). But in what form or appearance, we ask, or in what dress did he who saw her see her descending? Or perhaps in the multitude of the angels, whom he saw descending and ascending upon the Son of man? (John 1:51.) But we say better that he then saw the bride, when he saw the Word in the flesh, recognizing two in one flesh. For while that holy Emmanuel brought to the earth the teaching of heavenly discipline, while a certain visible image of that heavenly Jerusalem, which is our mother, and the form of its beauty, expressed through him and in him, was made known to us: what did we behold in the bridegroom but the bride, admiring one and the same Lord of glory — the bridegroom crowned with a crown, and the bride adorned with her necklaces? He, therefore, who descended, he himself is also he who ascended, that no one may ascend into heaven save him who descended from heaven, one and the same Lord, and bridegroom in the head, and bride in the body. Nor was the heavenly man seen on earth in vain, since from earthly men he made very many heavenly, like to himself, that there might be that which is read: 'As is the heavenly, such also are they that are heavenly' (1 Cor. 15:48). From that time, therefore, life is lived on earth after the manner of the heavenly, while, after the pattern of that heavenly and blessed creature, this one too, who has come from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, cleaves to her heavenly spouse with a no less chaste love; and although not yet joined to him, as that one, by sight, she is nevertheless espoused by faith, according to the promise of God saying through the prophet: 'I will espouse you to me in mercy and in compassions, and I will espouse you to me in faith' (Hos. 2:19). Whence she strives more and more to be conformed to the form which came from heaven, learning from her to be modest and sober, learning to be chaste and holy, learning to be patient and compassionate, and, finally, learning to be meek and lowly of heart. And therefore, with manners of this sort, she strives, even while absent, to please him into whom the angels long to look, that while she burns with angelic desire, she may prove herself thereby a citizen of the saints and a member of God's household, may prove herself beloved, may prove herself a bride.
27.8: I think that every soul of this sort is not only heavenly on account of its origin, but may also, not without reason, be itself called heaven on account of its imitation. And then it clearly shows that its origin is truly from the heavens, when its conversation is in the heavens. Therefore a holy soul is a heaven, having the sun — understanding; the moon — faith; the stars — the virtues. Or, to be sure, the sun is the zeal of justice or fervent charity; and the moon, continence. For as the brightness of the moon, as they say, comes only from the sun, so without charity or justice the merit of continence is none. Hence, finally, the Wise Man: 'O how beautiful,' he says, 'is a chaste generation with charity!' (Wis. 4:1.) Moreover, I do not repent of having called the virtues stars, considering the fitness of the likeness. For just as stars shine in the night and are hidden in the day, so true virtue, which often does not appear in prosperity, stands out in adversity. That, indeed, is a matter of caution; this of necessity. Therefore virtue is a star, and a man of virtues is a heaven. Unless, perhaps, when one reads that God said through the prophet: 'Heaven is my seat' (Isa. 66:1), one thinks that this revolving and visible heaven is to be understood, and not rather that of which Scripture elsewhere more openly makes mention: 'The soul of the just man,' it says, 'is the seat of wisdom.' But he who, from the teaching of the Savior, knows that God is a spirit, and is to be adored in spirit (John 4:24), does not hesitate to assign him also a spiritual seat. For my part, indeed, I would confidently do this, no less in the soul of a just man than in the angelic spirit. In this sense, especially, that faithful promise confirms me: 'I and the Father,' says the Son, 'will come to him' — that is, to the holy man — 'and will make our abode with him' (John 14:23). I also think that the Prophet said this of no other heaven: 'But you dwell in the holy place, O praise of Israel' (Ps. 22:3). But the Apostle manifestly says that Christ dwells by faith in our hearts (Eph. 3:17).
27.9: Nor is it a wonder if the Lord Jesus gladly dwells in this heaven, which indeed, not as the others, he did not so much say that it should be made, as fought that he might acquire it, died that he might redeem it. Therefore, even after his labor, having obtained his desire, he says: 'This is my rest for ever and ever; here will I dwell, for I have chosen her' (Ps. 132:14). And blessed is she to whom it is said: 'Come, my chosen one, and I will place my throne in you.' Why are you sad now, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Do you think, then, that you too can find within yourself a place for the Lord? And what place is there for us within ourselves fit for this glory, sufficient for the majesty? Would that I might at least deserve to adore in the place where his feet have stood. Who will give me at least to cleave to the footsteps of some holy soul which he has chosen for himself as a dwelling? Yet, if he deigns to pour into my soul too the unction of his mercy, and so to stretch it out like a skin — which indeed, when it is anointed, is dilated — so that I too may be able to say: 'I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart' (Ps. 119:32); I too shall perhaps be able to show in myself, if not a large upper room made ready, where he may recline with his disciples, yet at least [a place] where he may rest his head. From afar I look up to those certainly blessed [ones], of whom it is said: 'And I will dwell in them, and will walk about in them' (2 Cor. 6:16).
27.10: O how great is the breadth of that soul, and how great the prerogative of merits, which is found both worthy to receive, and sufficient to contain, in itself the divine presence! What [of] that one, to which spacious walks are at hand, for the work, indeed, of the majesty? She is not, indeed, entangled in forensic causes or in worldly cares, nor is she given to the belly and to luxury; but neither is she curious to behold, nor desirous at all of ruling, nor even swollen with lordship. For, first of all, the soul must be empty of all these things, that it may become a heaven and the habitation of God. Otherwise how will it be able to be at leisure, and to see that he himself is God? But neither is any indulgence at all to be given to hatred or envy or rancour, since wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul (Wis. 1:4). Then it is necessary for her to grow and be enlarged, that she may be capable of God. Moreover, her breadth is her love, as the Apostle says: 'Be you enlarged in charity' (2 Cor. 6:13). For although the soul, since it is a spirit, by no means receives bodily quantity, yet grace bestows on it what nature has denied. It grows, indeed, and is extended, but spiritually; it grows not in substance, but in virtue; it grows also in glory; it grows, too, into a holy temple in the Lord; finally, it grows and advances into a perfect man, into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4:13). Therefore let the quantity of each soul be estimated from the measure of charity which it has, so that, for example, that which has much charity may be great; that which has little, small; but that which has none, nothing — Paul saying: 'If I have not charity, I am nothing' (1 Cor. 13:3). But if it has begun to have ever so little, so as at least to take care to love those who love it, and to salute even its brothers and those who salute it; I would now call that soul something, which, in the reckoning of giving and receiving, retains at least a social charity. Nevertheless, according to the word of the Lord, what more does it do? (Matt. 5:47.) Neither, therefore, would I judge ample nor great, but plainly narrow and small, the soul which I have known to be of so small a charity.
27.11: But if it should grow and advance, so that, passing the limit of this narrow and blameworthy love, it may grasp with all the freedom of the spirit the broad bounds of gratuitous goodness, so far as to take care, in a certain wide bosom of good will, to extend itself to every neighbor, loving each one as itself; will it not now rightly be said to it: 'What more do you do?' seeing that it makes itself so broad. It bears, I say, a broad bosom of charity, which embraces all, even those to whom it knows itself bound by no tie of the flesh, allured by no hope of receiving any advantage, bound by no return of what has been received, and, finally, bound by no debt at all, save, to be sure, that of which it is said: 'Owe no man anything, but to love one another' (Rom. 13:8). But if you add that it should do violence, even everywhere, to the kingdom of charity, so that, as a pious invader, you may prevail to occupy it even to its farthest bounds, while you think that even to enemies the bowels of pity are not to be closed; that you should do good also to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and calumniate you, and study, moreover, to be at peace even with those who hate peace: then indeed the breadth of heaven is the breadth of your soul; and the height is not unequal, nor the beauty unlike; and it is then at last fulfilled in her what is said: 'Spreading out the heaven like a skin' (Ps. 104:2): in which heaven, already of wonderful breadth, height, and beauty, the supreme and infinite and glorious one not only dwells condescendingly, but even walks about at large.
27.12: Do you see what heavens the Church has in herself, since she is, nevertheless, in her whole universality, a certain vast heaven, stretched from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth? See, also, consequently, to what you may liken her even in this very thing, if at least that has not slipped from you which was mentioned a little before as the example of this matter — namely, concerning the heaven of heavens and the heavens of heavens (see above, n. 9). Therefore, by the example of that [city] which is above, our mother, this one also, which still sojourns, has her heavens — spiritual men, conspicuous by life and repute, pure in faith, firm in hope, broad in charity, suspended in contemplation. And these, raining the salutary rain of the word, thunder with rebukes, flash with miracles. These declare the glory of God; these, stretched out like skins over all the earth, show in themselves the law of life and discipline, written, indeed, by the finger of God, to give to his people the knowledge of salvation: they show also the Gospel of peace, because they are the skins of Solomon.
27.13: Recognize now in these skins the image of those heavenly ones, which were described not long above in the adornment of the bridegroom (see above, n. 3). Recognize likewise the queen standing at his right hand, clothed about with like, yet not equal, ornaments (Ps. 45:9). For although even in this place of her pilgrimage, and in the day of her power, in the beauties of the saints, there is no small portion of brightness and beauty; yet differing is that which crowns her — the integrity and consummation of the glory of the blessed. Although I would also call the bride perfect and blessed, but in part. For in part [she is] a tent of Kedar; yet beautiful, whether in that portion of herself which already reigns blessed; or even in the illustrious men, by whose wisdom and virtues, even in this night, she is adorned, as heaven by its stars. Whence the Prophet: 'Those who have been taught,' he says, 'will shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who teach many unto justice, like the stars, forever and ever' (Dan. 12:3).
27.14: O humility, O sublimity! Both a tent of Kedar and a sanctuary of God; both an earthly dwelling and a heavenly palace; both a house of clay and a royal hall; both a body of death and a temple of light; and, finally, a contempt to the proud, and the bride of Christ. She is black, but beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem: whom though the toil and grief of a long exile discolor, yet the heavenly beauty adorns her, the skins of Solomon adorn her. If you shrink from the black, marvel also at the beautiful; if you despise the lowly, look up to the sublime. How cautious is this very thing, how full of counsel, full of discretion and of fitness, that in the bride this dejection and this exaltation are tempered together to one another, according to the time, with such moderateness, that amid the changes of this world the sublimity may raise up the humble, lest he fail in adversities; and humility may repress the sublime, lest he vanish away in prosperity? Both things, altogether beautifully, although they are contrary one to another, nevertheless work together equally for the good of the bride, and serve for her salvation.
27.15: And these things [have been said] because the bride seems to bring in a similitude from the skins of Solomon. It remains, nevertheless, that that sense on the same chapter be opened, which I mentioned and promised at the beginning — namely, in what way the whole similitude is to be referred to blackness alone: by which, indeed, you are not to be defrauded of the promise. But this is to be put off to another beginning of a sermon; both because the length of this one already demands it, and also that, as is customary, the prayer may go before those things which are to be referred to the praise and glory of the Spouse of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

28.1: You recall, I believe, to what, and to which skins of Solomon, I meant the beauty of the bride to be compared, if at least the similitude taken from them be referred to the showing forth and the commending of her beauty. But if it be thought that it should rather be referred to blackness, like that also [taken] from the tents of Kedar: then indeed nothing else occurs to me of skins of this sort of Solomon, save those which perhaps the king was wont to take for the use of the tabernacle, if ever it pleased him to dwell in tents; which indeed, if there were any such, must needs have been dark and squalid, as being daily exposed to the sun and to the injuries of frequent rains. Nor was this in vain, but that the ornament stored up within might be kept the more shining. By this example the bride does not deny her blackness, but excuses it; nor does she count it a reproach, whatsoever that garb be which charity forms and the judgment of truth does not disapprove. Finally, who is weak, and I am not weak with him? who is made to stumble, and I am not burned? (2 Cor. 11:29). She puts on the stain of compassion, that she may lighten or heal in another the malady of passion; she grows black from zeal for whiteness, for the gain of beauty.
28.2: The blackening of one makes many white, not when it is dyed with guilt, but when it is touched with care. 'It is expedient,' he says, 'that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not' (John 11:50): it is expedient that one be blackened for all in the likeness of the flesh of sin, and that the whole nation be not condemned in the blackness of sin: that the splendor and figure of the substance of God be veiled in the form of a servant for the life of the servant: that the whiteness of eternal life grow black in the flesh, for the purging of the flesh: that he who is beautiful in form above the sons of men, for the enlightening of the sons of men, be obscured in the passion, be disfigured on the cross, grow pale in death: that in all things he have no beauty nor comeliness, that he may win for himself a beautiful and comely bride, the Church, without spot and without wrinkle. I recognize the skin of Solomon; nay, I embrace Solomon himself in a black skin. Solomon, too, has blackness, but in the skin; black without, black on the surface, not within: otherwise all the glory of the king's daughter is from within (Ps. 45:3, 14). Within is the whiteness of the divinity, the comeliness of the virtues, the splendor of glory, the purity of innocence: but this the more despicable color of infirmity covers; and, as it were, his face was hidden and despised, while he was tempted in all things, for the likeness, without sin. I recognize the form of a blackened nature; I recognize those garments of skin, the dress of the first-created sinners (Gen. 3:21). Finally, he blackened himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man (Phil. 2:7). I recognize, beneath the skin of the kid, which signifies sin, the hand that did not commit sin, and the neck through which no evil thought passed; and therefore no guile was found in his mouth (Isa. 53:9). I know that you are gentle by nature, meek and lowly of heart, pleasant to look upon, sweet in spirit, and indeed anointed with the oil of gladness above your fellows (Ps. 45:7). Whence, then, is it that now, after the manner of Esau, you are hairy and rough? Whose wrinkled and squalid image is this, and whence these hairs? They are mine: for hairy hands express the likeness of a sinner. I recognize these hairs as mine; and in my own skin I see God, my Savior.
28.3: Yet it was not Rebecca that clothed him thus, but Mary; so much the worthier was he to receive the blessing, as she that bore him was the holier. And for good reason in my raiment; because the blessing is claimed for me, for me the inheritance is sought. For he had heard: 'Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession' (Ps. 2:8). 'Your inheritance,' he says, 'and your possession will I give you.' How will you give it him, if it is his own? And how do you bid him ask for his own? or how is it his own, if he must needs ask for it? For me, therefore, he asks, who to this end put on my form, that he might undertake my cause. For the chastisement of our peace was upon him, as the prophet says, and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isa. 53:5, 6): whence he ought to be made like his brethren in all things, as the Apostle says, that he might become merciful (Heb. 2:17). Therefore 'the voice indeed is the voice of Jacob; but the hands are the hands of Esau' (Gen. 27:22). That which is heard from him is his own: that which is seen in him is ours. What he speaks is spirit and life: what appears is mortal and death. One thing is seen, and another is believed. Sense reports him black; faith proves him white and beautiful. He is black, but to the eyes of the foolish: for to the minds of the faithful he is very beautiful: he is black, but beautiful: black in the estimation of Herod, beautiful in the confession of the thief, in the faith of the centurion.
28.4: How beautiful he had perceived him to be, who cried out: 'Truly this man was the Son of God!' But in what he perceived it is to be noted. For if he had regarded what appeared, how [was he] beautiful, how the Son of God? What met the eyes of the beholders but what was deformed and black, when, with hands stretched out on the cross, in the midst of two malefactors, he gave laughter to the spiteful, tears to the faithful? And he alone was the object of scorn, who alone could have been an object of terror, and alone had been owed honor. Whence, then, did he perceive the beauty of the Crucified, and that he is the Son of God, who was reckoned among the wicked? (Isa. 53:12.) It is neither lawful nor needful for me to answer anything to this; for the Evangelist's diligence did not pass it over. For thus you have it: 'But the centurion who stood over against him, seeing that he had so cried out and expired, said: Truly this man was the Son of God' (Mark 15:39). Therefore it was at his voice that he believed; from the voice he recognized the Son of God, and not from his face. For perhaps he was of his sheep, of which he said: 'My sheep hear my voice' (John 10:27).
28.5: Hearing found what sight did not; the appearance deceived the eye, truth poured itself into the ear. The eye pronounced him weak, the eye foul, the eye wretched, the eye condemned to a most shameful death; to the ear the Son of God, to the ear the beautiful one was made known; but not to the ears of the Jews, because they were uncircumcised in ears. Rightly did Peter cut off the servant's ear, that he might make a way for the truth, and the truth might set him free, that is, make him free. That centurion was uncircumcised, but not in ear, who, at the one voice of the dying man, amid so many signs of infirmity, recognized the Lord of majesty. And therefore he did not despise what he saw, because he believed what he did not see. But he did not believe from what he saw; but beyond doubt from what he heard, because faith comes by hearing (Rom. 10:17). It had indeed been fitting that truth should enter the soul through the higher windows of the eyes; but this is reserved for us, O soul, for the time to come, when we shall see face to face. But now, from the place where the disease crept in, let the remedy enter, and by the same footsteps let life follow death, light the darkness, the antidote of truth the serpent's venom; and let the eye that was troubled be healed, that it may serenely see him whom, when troubled, it could not. The ear, the first door of death, let it be first opened also to life; let hearing, which took away, restore sight; since unless we believe, we shall not understand. Therefore hearing [belongs] to merit, sight to the reward. Whence the Prophet: 'You will make me hear of joy and gladness' (Ps. 51:8): because the faithful reward of hearing is the blessed vision, and the merit of the blessed vision is faithful hearing. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt. 5:8). Moreover, by faith must the eye that is to see God be cleansed, as you have it: 'Purifying their hearts by faith' (Acts 15:9).
28.6: Meanwhile, therefore, while sight is not yet ready, let hearing be roused, let hearing be exercised, let hearing receive the truth. Blessed is he to whom Truth bears witness, saying: 'He obeyed me at the hearing of the ear' (Ps. 18:44). Worthy am I to see, if, before I see, I shall be found to have obeyed; secure shall I see, unto whom the gift of my obedience shall have gone before. How blessed is he who said: 'The Lord God has opened my ear, and I do not contradict, I have not gone back' (Isa. 50:5). Wherein you have both the pattern of voluntary obedience and the example of long-suffering. For he who does not contradict is spontaneous; and he who has not gone back perseveres. Both are necessary; because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7), and he who perseveres to the end, he shall be saved (Matt. 10:22). Would that the Lord would open my ear too, that the word of truth may enter my heart, cleanse my eye, and prepare it for the glad vision, that I too may say to God: 'Your ear has heard the preparation of my heart' (Ps. 10:17); that I too may hear from God, with the rest of the obedient: 'You are clean through the word which I have spoken to you' (John 15:3). Nor are all who hear cleansed, but those who obey: 'Blessed are they who hear and keep it' (Luke 11:28). Such hearing does he require who commands, saying: 'Hear, O Israel' (Deut. 6:3); such does he offer who says: 'Speak, Lord, for your servant hears' (1 Sam. 3:9); such does he promise who says: 'I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me' (Ps. 85:8).
28.7: And that you may know that the Holy Spirit, too, observes this order in the spiritual progress of the soul, so that he forms hearing before he gladdens sight: 'Hear,' he says, 'O daughter, and see' (Ps. 45:10). Why do you turn your eye? Prepare your ear. Do you desire to see Christ? You must first hear him, hear of him, that when you have seen you may say: 'As we have heard, so we have seen' (Ps. 48:8). The brightness is immense, the sight august, and you cannot attain to it. You can [attain] by hearing, but not by sight. Finally, when God was crying aloud, 'Adam, where are you?' (Gen. 3:9), I, now a sinner, did not see, yet I heard. But hearing will restore sight, if it has gone before pious, watchful, faithful. Faith will purge that which impiety troubled; and that which disobedience closed, obedience will open. Finally: 'From your commandments,' he says, 'I have gotten understanding' (Ps. 119:104): that the keeping of the commandments restores the understanding which transgression took away. Mark still, in holy Isaac, how, beyond the other senses, hearing flourished in him now old. The eyes of the patriarch grow dim, the palate is deceived, the hand is deceived; the ear is not deceived. What wonder, if the ear perceives the truth, since faith [comes] by hearing, hearing by the word of God (Rom. 10:17), and the word of God is truth? 'The voice,' he says, 'is the voice of Jacob.' Nothing more true. But the hands are the hands of Esau (Gen. 27:22). Nothing more false. You are deceived: the likeness of the hands has deceived you. Nor is there truth in taste, though there is sweetness. For how has he truth who thinks he eats venison, when he is fed on the flesh of the household kids? Much less the eye, which sees nothing. There is no truth in the eye, nor wisdom. 'Woe to you who are wise,' he says, 'in your own eyes!' (Isa. 5:21.) Not good is the wisdom over which a curse is uttered. It is of the world, and therefore foolishness before God (1 Cor. 3:19).
28.8: Good and true wisdom is drawn from hidden things, as blessed Job judges (Job 28:18). Why do you seek it outwardly in a bodily sense? Taste is in the palate; in the heart is wisdom. Do not seek wisdom in the eye of the flesh, because flesh and blood does not reveal it, but the Spirit (Matt. 16:17). Not in the taste of the mouth: for neither is it found in the land of those that live pleasantly (Job 28:13). Not in the touch of the hand, when the saint says: 'If I have kissed my hand with my mouth, which is the greatest iniquity, and a denial of God' (Job 31:27, 28). Which I think is then done, when the gift of God, which is wisdom, is ascribed not to God, but to the merits of actions. Isaac was wise, yet he erred in his senses. Hearing alone has the truth, which perceives the word. Rightly is the woman wise after the flesh forbidden to touch the risen flesh of the Word, giving indeed more to the eye than to the oracle, that is, to the sense of the flesh than to the word of God. For him whom she saw dead, she did not believe risen, though he himself had promised this. Finally, her eye did not rest, until her sight was filled; because there was no consolation of faith, nor any ratified promise of God. Do not heaven and earth, and whatever at all the eye of the flesh can reach, first have to pass away and perish, before one iota or one point [fail] of all the things that God has spoken? And yet she ceased from weeping at the sight of her eye, she who would not be comforted in the word of the Lord; valuing experience more than faith. But experience is deceitful.
28.9: She is therefore sent on to the surer knowledge of faith; which indeed takes hold of what sense does not know, and experience does not find. 'Touch me not,' he says: that is: 'Unlearn this deceptive sense; lean upon the word, accustom yourself to faith.' Faith, that cannot be deceived, faith that comprehends things invisible, does not feel the penury of sense; finally it passes beyond even the limits of human reason, the use of nature, the bounds of experience. Why do you ask the eye for that to which it does not suffice? And why does the hand try to search out what is above itself? Less is whatever the one or the other reports. Let faith, rather, pronounce of me, which takes nothing away from the majesty. Learn to hold that as more certain, and to follow that as safer, whatever she shall have counseled. 'Touch me not, for I have not yet ascended to my Father' (John 20:17). As if, when he has already ascended, he would then wish or be able to be touched by her. And indeed he will be able, but by affection, not by hand; by longing, not by eye; by faith, not by senses. 'Why,' he says, 'do you now seek to touch me, who judge the glory of the resurrection by the sense of the body?' Do you not know that, at the time of my mortality, the eyes of the disciples could not sustain for an hour the glory of the transfigured body that was to die? (Matt. 17:6.) As yet indeed I humor your senses, thrusting in the form of a servant, which you may recognize from your use. But my glory, made wonderful and strengthened from you, you will not be able to reach. Defer therefore the judgment, suspend the sentence, and do not entrust the definition of so great a matter to sense, but reserve it to faith. She will define it more worthily, she will define it more certainly, who shall comprehend it more fully. Finally, she comprehends, in that mystical and deep bosom of hers, what is the length, breadth, height, and depth. What the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor has ascended into the heart of man, that she carries in herself, shut up as it were in a certain covering, and keeps sealed.
28.10: She, then, will touch me worthily, who will receive me seated at the right hand of the Father, no longer in a lowly garb, but in a heavenly one: in the same flesh, indeed, but in another guise. Why do you wish to touch him deformed? Wait until you touch him beautiful. For he who is deformed now, then beautiful; deformed to the touch, deformed to the sight; deformed, finally, to you that are deformed, who cleave more to the senses, less to faith. Be beautiful, and touch me; be faithful, and you are beautiful. Beautiful [as you are], you will touch the Beautiful one both more worthily and more happily. You will touch with the hand of faith, with the finger of desire, with the embrace of devotion; you will touch with the eye of the mind. But is it black still? God forbid! Your beloved is white and ruddy. Beautiful indeed is he whom the flowers of roses and the lilies of the valleys surround; that is, the choirs of martyrs and of virgins: and I, who sit in the midst, am not at variance with either choir, being virgin and martyr. How, then, do I not match the white choirs of virgins, I who am a virgin, the son of a Virgin, and the spouse of a virgin? How [do I not match] the roseate [choirs] of martyrs, being the cause, the virtue, the fruit, and the form of martyrdom? Such a one, even I, and in such wise, touch, and say: 'My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands' (Song 5:10). Thousands of thousands are with the beloved, and ten hundred thousand about the beloved, and none to the beloved. Will it then be a fear to you, lest, seeking him whom you love, you fall by some error upon some one of the multitude? You will not at all doubt whom to choose. The one chosen out of thousands, more conspicuous than all, will readily meet you, and you will say: 'This is he, beautiful in his robe, walking in the greatness of his strength' (Isa. 63:1). Not, then, in the black skin, which indeed up to now had to be thrust before the eyes of the persecutors, that they might despise him as one to be slain; or also of friends, that they might recognize him risen again. Not, I say, will he now meet [you] in a black skin, but in a white robe, beautiful in form, not only above the sons of men, but even above the faces of angels. Why do you wish to touch me in a lowly garb, in a servant's form, in a contemptible guise? Touch him adorned with heavenly beauty, crowned with glory and honor; to be dreaded, indeed, in his divine majesty, but gracious and calm in his inborn serenity.
28.11: Amid these things mark the prudence of the bride, and the depth of her discourses, who, under the figure of the skins of Solomon — that is, in the flesh — searched out God, in death life; the height of glory and honor amid reproaches, and, under the black dress, finally, of the Crucified, the whiteness of innocence and the splendor of the virtues; just as those skins, to be sure, since they were black and despised, kept within themselves the precious and most white ornaments of the rich king. Rightly she does not despise blackness in the skins, marking the beauty which is beneath the skins. And therefore some despised her, because they did not at all know him: for had they known [him], they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8). Herod did not know [him], and therefore despised [him]; the Synagogue did not know [him], which, upbraiding him with the blackness of the passion and of infirmity, says: 'He saved others, himself he cannot save.' 'Christ the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him' (Matt. 27:42). But the thief on the cross knew [him], even while [he was] on the cross, who also confessed the purity of [his] innocence. Saying, 'But this man, what evil has he done?' he likewise at the same time bore witness to the glory of royal majesty: 'Remember me,' he said, 'when you come into your kingdom' (Luke 23:41, 42). The centurion knew [him], who cries out the Son of God (Matt. 27:54); the Church knows [him], which even emulates blackness, that it may share in the beauty. She is not ashamed to be seen black, to be called black, that she may say to her Beloved: 'The reproaches of those that reproached you have fallen upon me' (Ps. 69:9). But indeed black like the skins of Solomon, that is, on the outside, and not within: for my Solomon has no blackness within. Finally, he does not say: 'I am black like Solomon'; but, 'like the skins of Solomon': because the blackness of the true Peaceful One is only on the surface. The blackness of sin is within; and guilt stains the inner parts first, before it comes forth to the eyes. Finally, out of the heart come forth evil thoughts, thefts, murders, adulteries, blasphemies: and these are what defile a man (Matt. 15:19, 20); but God forbid that [they should] Solomon! By no means will you find defilements of this sort in the true Peaceful One. For it behooves him who takes away the sins of the world to be without sin, so that, being found fit to reconcile sinners, he may rightly claim for himself the name of Solomon.
28.12: But there is the blackness of afflicting penitence, when lamentation is taken up for sins. This, perhaps, Solomon will not abhor in me, if I yet willingly put it on for my sins; because a broken and contrite heart God will not despise (Ps. 51:17). There is also [the blackness] of affecting compassion, if you grieve with the afflicted, and a brother's mishap should discolor you. Nor indeed does our Peaceful One think even this to be rejected, seeing that he himself deigned to put it on for us, who bore our sins in his body upon the tree (1 Pet. 2:24). There is also [the blackness] of persecution: which is even counted for the highest ornament, if indeed it be undergone for justice and truth. Whence is that: 'The disciples went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus' (Acts 5:41); finally: 'Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake' (Matt. 5:10). With this especially I judge the Church to glory; this she more willingly imitates from the skins of the Spouse. Finally, she has it also in the promise: 'If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you' (John 15:20).
28.13: Whence the bride also adds: 'Do not consider me that I am brown, because the sun has discolored me' (Song 1:5), that is: 'Do not mark me as it were deformed, because you see me, on account of the persecution that presses on, less flourishing, less colored according to the glory of the world.' Why do you upbraid me with the blackness, which the heat of persecution, not the shame of [evil] conduct, has brought upon me? Or does she call the sun the zeal of justice, by which one is lifted up and girds oneself against the wicked, saying to God, 'The zeal of your house has consumed me' (Ps. 69:9)? and that: 'My zeal has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words'; that also: 'Horror has taken hold of me, for the sinners that forsake your law' (Ps. 119:139, 53); likewise: 'Do I not hate those that hate you, O Lord, and waste away over your enemies?' (Ps. 139:21). She also carefully observes that saying of the Wise Man: 'Have you daughters?' he says, 'do not show a cheerful countenance to them' (Sir. 7:26): namely, that to those who are remiss, and soft, and shunning discipline, she shows not the whiteness of serenity, but the darkness of severity. Or to be discolored by the sun is to glow with fraternal charity, to weep with those that weep, to grow weak with those that are weak, to burn at the scandals of individuals. Or thus: 'The sun of justice, Christ, has discolored me, of whose love I languish.' That languor is a certain wasting of color, and a failing in the desire of the soul: whence she also says: 'I remembered God, and was delighted, and I was exercised, and my spirit failed' (Ps. 77:3). Therefore, like a burning sun, the ardor of desire discolors one journeying in the body, while, gaping after the face of glory, repulse makes him impatient, and delay torments the lover. Who of us burns with holy love in such a way that, for the desire of seeing Christ, he loathes and lays aside every color of present glory and joy, testifying to him with that prophetic voice: 'And I have not desired the day of man, you know' (Jer. 17:16); likewise with holy David: 'My soul refused to be comforted' (Ps. 77:2); that is, [that he] scorns to be colored with the empty joy of present goods? Or indeed the sun has discolored me, to wit, by the comparison of its own splendor, while, drawing near to it, I find myself dark from it, find myself black, despise myself as foul. But otherwise I am indeed beautiful; why do you call me brown, succumbing to the beauty of the sun alone? But to the former sense those things which follow seem more to assent. For, adding: 'The sons of my mother have fought against me,' she openly signifies that she has suffered persecution. But from this point we shall begin another beginning of a sermon, since what we have received on this occasion can suffice, concerning the glory of the Spouse of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, by his gift, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

29.1: The children of my mother have fought against me (Song 1:5). Annas and Caiphas, and Judas Iscariot, were children of the Synagogue: and these fought most bitterly against the Church, equally a daughter of the Synagogue, at its very beginning, hanging on the wood her gatherer Jesus. For already then God fulfilled through them what he had formerly foreshadowed through the prophet, saying: 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered' (Zech. 13:7). And perhaps that voice of Hezekiah's song is his: 'My life is cut off, as by a weaver; while I was yet beginning, he cut me off' (Isa. 38:12). Concerning these, then, and others, who are known to have contradicted the Christian name from that nation, the bride is to be understood as saying: 'The children of my mother have fought against me.' And she beautifully calls them children of her mother, not also of her father, who had not God as father, but were of their father the devil; murderers, certainly, as he also was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44). Therefore she does not say: 'My brothers'; or: 'The children of my father'; but 'The children,' she says, 'of my mother have fought against me.' Otherwise, if she did not so distinguish, even the apostle Paul would seem to be included among those of whom she complains, because he too once persecuted the Church of God (1 Cor. 15:9), but he obtained mercy, because he did this ignorantly in unbelief (1 Tim. 1:13); and he proved that he has God for his father, being a brother of the Church as much from the father as from the mother.
29.2: But observe how she accuses by name the children of her mother, and them alone, as though they alone are at fault. How much has she suffered even from those without? according to that [word] in the prophet: 'Often have they fought against me from my youth'; and: 'Upon my back the sinners have built' (Ps. 129:1, 2). Why, then, do you especially plead the children of your mother, who are by no means ignorant that you have been most often attacked also by other and yet other nations? Called to the table of the rich man, 'consider carefully,' he says, 'what is set before you.' Brethren, we sit at the table of Solomon. Who is richer than Solomon? I do not speak of earthly riches, although in them too Solomon abounded; but look at the present table, how it is filled with heavenly delights. Spiritual and divine are the things that are set before us on it. 'Consider carefully, then,' he says, 'what is set before you, knowing that you ought to prepare such things' (Prov. 23:1, 2). I indeed, as far as in me lies, carefully observe that there is set before me in these words of the bride, and that it looks to my instruction and caution, that the persecution from one's household is expressed so expressly and alone; while so many and so grave things are passed over in silence that she is known to have borne everywhere on the earth, from every nation that is under heaven, from the unbelieving, from heretics and schismatics, all the same. I know the prudence of the bride; nor would I think that she passed these over by chance, or as though forgetful. But surely she laments the more expressly what she feels the more differently, and what she judges the more carefully to be guarded against by us. What, then, is this? An evil, certainly, inward and domestic. This is clearly expressed to you in the Gospel by the very mouth of the Savior, when he says: 'And a man's enemies will be those of his own household' (Matt. 10:36). This also in the prophet: 'The man of my peace,' he says, 'who ate my bread, has magnified his supplanting against me' (Ps. 41:9); likewise: 'For if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have borne it; and if he who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would perhaps have hidden myself from him.' But you, O man of one mind, my guide and my acquaintance, who took sweet food together with me (Ps. 55:13, 14), that is: 'What I suffer from you, my table-companion and messmate, that I feel the more grievously, I bear the more hardly.' You know whose complaint this is, and concerning whom.
29.3: Recognize, then, the bride also complaining of the children of her mother with the same affection, since [she does so] in the same spirit, when she says: 'The children of my mother have fought against me.' Whence also she says elsewhere: 'My friends and my neighbors have drawn near against me and stood' (Ps. 38:11). Far from you, I pray, do you always make this so abominable and detestable evil, you who have experienced and daily experience how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity (Ps. 133:1), if yet in unity, and not in offense. Otherwise it is plainly neither pleasant nor good, but most evil and most troublesome. Woe, however, to that man through whom the pleasant bond of unity is troubled! He will surely bear judgment, whoever he is. Let it happen rather to me to die, than to hear among you anyone justly crying out: 'The children of my mother have fought against me.' Are not you all children, as it were, of the present congregation of one mother, each one brothers to one another? What, then, from without could trouble or grieve you, if you are well within, and rejoice in brotherly peace? Finally, 'who,' he says, 'will be able to harm you, if you shall be zealous of good' (1 Pet. 3:13)? Wherefore be zealous of the better gifts (1 Cor. 12:31), that you may prove yourselves good imitators. Charity is the best gift; plainly incomparable, which the heavenly bridegroom was at pains to inculcate so often into his new bride, now indeed saying: 'By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love one to another'; now: 'A new commandment I give you, that you love one another' (John 13:35, 34); and: 'This is my commandment, that you love one another' (John 15:12); and likewise praying that they be one, as he himself and the Father are one (John 17:11). And see if not Paul himself, who invites you to the better gifts, among the rest places charity at the summit, whether when he says with faith and hope that it is greater and more excellent than knowledge; or when, after enumerating many and wonderful gifts of heavenly grace, he at length sends us to the more excellent way; surely no other than that, which he defines as charity. Finally, what are we to think comparable to her, who is preferred even to martyrdom and to faith that removes mountains (1 Cor. 12:31; 13:3)? This, then, is what I say: Let peace be to you from yourselves; and everything that seems to threaten from without does not terrify, because it does not harm. For, on the contrary, whatever from without may appear to flatter, there is certainly no consolation, if within — which God forbid! — the seedbed of discord has sprouted.
29.4: Wherefore, most beloved, have peace among yourselves, and be unwilling to hurt one another, not by deed, not by word, not by any sign: and let no one, perhaps exasperated and forestalled by faint-heartedness of spirit and by a storm, be forced to call upon God against those who have hurt or grieved him, and let it happen that he break out into a grave word: 'The children of my mother have fought against me.' For so sinning against a brother, you sin against Christ, who says: 'What you have done to one of the least of my brethren, you have done to me' (Matt. 25:40, 45). Nor must one guard only against the graver offenses, for example, against open insult or curse, but also against any clandestine and venomous whispering. It does not suffice, I say, to guard the mouth from these and such like; the light things too must be guarded against: if yet that may be called light which you have presumed against a brother with the will of hurting; since by this alone, if you are angry with him, you are held guilty of the divine judgment (Matt. 5:22). And deservedly: for what you think light, and on that account estimate more lightly, another often takes differently, as a man who sees in the face, and judges according to the face, ready to suspect a bean to be a beam, and to think a spark a furnace. For not all have that charity which believes all things (1 Cor. 13:7). But the senses of man and his thoughts are prone to suspect evil rather than to believe good: especially where the discipline of silence neither permits you, who are in the case, to excuse yourself, nor him to open the wound of suspicion which he suffers, that it may be cured. So he burns and dies of a closed and deadly wound, groaning within himself, while, wholly occupied in anger and disputation, he can in silence turn over in his mind nothing else but the injury he has received. He cannot pray, he cannot read, he cannot meditate on anything holy or spiritual: and so, the vital spirit being intercepted, while the soul for which Christ died, destitute of its supports, goes to death, what, meanwhile, I pray, is your disposition? What does your prayer, or whatever work you have meanwhile done, taste like to you, against whom Christ manifestly cries out from the breast of your brother whom you have grieved: 'The child of my mother,' he says, 'fights against me, and he who took sweet food together with me has filled me with bitterness'?
29.5: But if you should say that he ought not to have been so gravely troubled for so light a cause, I answer: The lighter it is, the more lightly you could have refrained from committing it. Although I know not how you call anything light, as I have said, whatever is more than to be angry, since you have received from the very mouth of the judge that even this very thing is subject to judgment. For what? Will you call it light, in which Christ is offended, whence you must be dragged to the judgment of God, since it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God? (Heb. 10:31.) You, then, having perhaps received an injury (which indeed is sometimes hard not to happen in these gatherings), do not presently, after the manner of the worldly man, hasten to strike back your brother with an oblique answer; but neither, under the appearance of rebuking, dare in any way to transfix with a sharp and burning word the soul for which Christ deigned to be fastened to the cross; neither grunt as if reproving, nor mutter with the lips as if murmuring, neither draw in the nostril nor guffaw as if scoffing, neither wrinkle the brow as if inveighing or threatening. Surely let your emotion die there where it arises, nor be allowed to go out that which carries death, lest it destroy; that you too may be able to say with the Prophet: 'I was troubled, and I did not speak' (Ps. 77:5).
29.6: I have understood some to feel this more deeply, as if it were said of the devil and his angels, who, having been themselves also children of that Jerusalem which is above, our mother, since they fell, do not cease to attack their sister the Church. But neither do I contend, if anyone also uses this in a good signification, according to which the spiritual, who are in the Church, fight against their carnal brethren with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6:17), wounding them unto salvation, and advancing them to spiritual things by attacks of this kind? Would that the just one would correct me in mercy and rebuke me, striking and healing, killing and making alive, that I too may dare to say: 'I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me' (Gal. 2:20). 'Be,' he says, 'agreed with your adversary, while you are with him on the way, lest he deliver you to the judge, and the judge to the torturer' (Matt. 5:25). A good adversary, to whom if I am agreed, there will be no occasion either for the judge to calumniate me, or the torturer [to torment me]. I indeed, if I have at any time grieved any of you for a cause of this kind, do not repent; for they have been grieved unto salvation. And indeed I know not whether I have ever done it without my own great sadness also, according to that: 'A woman, when she gives birth, has sadness' (John 16:21). But God forbid that I should now remember the distress, holding the fruit of my grief, while I see Christ, as it were, formed in the offspring.
