I know not, however, how those who, after rebukes and through rebukes, have at length recovered from weakness, are bound to me more tenderly than those who have remained strong from the beginning, not needing a medicine of this kind.
29.7: In this sense, then, the Church, or the soul loving God, can say that the sun has discolored her, by sending and arming from the children of her mother those who would healthfully attack her, and lead her captive to faith in and love of him, pierced, certainly, with many of those arrows of which it is written: 'The arrows of the mighty are sharp' (Ps. 120:4); and likewise: 'Your arrows are fixed in me.' And therefore it follows, and she says: 'For there is no soundness in my flesh' (Ps. 38:3), that, made sound and accordingly stronger in soul, she may say: 'The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak' (Matt. 26:41); and with the Apostle: 'For when I am weak, then I am powerful and strong' (2 Cor. 12:10). Do you see that the weakness of the flesh increases strength to the spirit, and supplies it with powers? So, on the contrary, know that the strength of the flesh works the weakness of the spirit. And what wonder, if the enemy being weakened, you are made stronger? Unless perhaps you most insanely take for your friend her who does not cease to lust against the spirit (Gal. 5:17). See, then, whether the holy one does not wisely ask to be shot and healthfully attacked, when he says in prayer: 'Pierce my flesh with your fear' (Ps. 119:120). That fear is the best arrow, which pierces and kills the desires of the flesh, that the spirit may be safe. But also he who chastises his body, and brings it into subjection, does he not seem to you to help also the hand of the one fighting against himself?
29.8: There is also the arrow, the word of God, living and effectual, and more piercing than any two-edged sword (Heb. 4:12), of which the Savior: 'I did not come,' he says, 'to send peace, but a sword' (Matt. 10:34). There is also the chosen arrow, the love of Christ, which not only transfixed the soul of Mary, but even passed through it, that it might leave no part of the virginal heart empty of love, but that she would love with her whole heart, with her whole soul, with her whole strength, and would be full of grace. Or certainly it passed through her, that it might come even to us, and that from that fullness we might all receive, and she would become the mother of charity, whose father is charity, God, giving birth and setting in the sun her tabernacle, that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: 'I have given you for a light to the gentiles, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth' (Isa. 49:6). For this was fulfilled through Mary, who brought forth in the flesh the visible one, whom, being invisible, she conceived neither from the flesh, nor with the flesh. And she indeed received in her whole self a great and sweet wound of love: but I would think myself happy, if at least I should feel myself pricked with the very point, as it were, of this sword, that, having received even a small wound of love, my soul also may say: 'I am wounded with charity' (Song 2:5). Who will grant me to be wounded in this manner — not only wounded, but even wholly attacked even to the destruction of that color and heat which fights against the soul?
29.9: If the daughters of this world should reproach that soul which is of this sort, saying that she is pale and without color, will she not seem to you to be able fitly to answer: 'Do not consider me that I am brown, because the sun has discolored me'? And if she remembers that she has come to this by the exhortations or rebukes of certain servants of God, emulous of her with God's emulation, will she not consequently and truly be able to infer, that 'the children of my mother have fought against me'? The sense will therefore be, according to what has been said, that the Church or any diligent soul says this, not as groaning or complaining, but as rejoicing and giving thanks, and moreover glorying, that for the name and love of Christ she is worthy to be and to be called brown or discolored: and she ascribes this very thing not to her own industry, but to the grace and mercy going before and sent to her. For how would she believe without a preacher? but how would they preach unless they were sent? (Rom. 10:14, 15.) She recalls that the children of her mother fought against her, not as angry, but as not ungrateful. Whence also it follows: 'They made me keeper of the vineyards.' Which word, if it is spiritually examined, I think will seem to have in it nothing of complaint or rancor, but rather to savor of something favorable. But to touch on that, first indeed, before we dare to lay our hand to it (for the place is holy), that Spirit who searches the deep things of God is to be reconciled to us with the wonted prayers, and thus to be consulted; or certainly. The Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, the Spouse of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.

30.1: They made me keeper of the vineyards (Song 1:5). Who? Those very attackers of yours whom you just now mentioned? Hear and understand, if she does not confess that she was promoted by those very ones from whom she also suffered. Nor is it a wonder, however, since the cause of fighting may have been the intention of correcting. For who does not know that many have been many times assaulted in a friendly and useful way? How many do we daily experience advancing to better things by the pious attacks of prelates, and being carried on to higher things? Let us then rather show, if we can, in what manner it was fought against the Church by the children of her mother, both with a hostile mind and with useful loss. For that is the more pleasant, that they who intend to harm profit even against their will. But the former interpretation holds both senses: since there have not been wanting those who emulated her, some well, some ill, fighting with diverse intention; but both profited. In so much, finally, does she glory that she has profited from the things she suffered from the emulous, that for one vineyard which they seemed to have taken away from her, she rejoices that she is set over many. 'This,' she says, 'they who say, 'Empty, empty it, even to the foundation in it' (Ps. 137:7), have done for me by fighting against me and against my vineyard, that I might exchange one for many.' For this is what she infers, 'My vineyard I have not kept': as though joining the cause whence this came to her, that she is set as keeper not now in one, but in many [vineyards]. And the letter indeed is so.
30.2: But if we follow it simply, content with that alone which it seems to sound on that surface, we shall think that we read in the holy Scripture about those corporeal and earthly vineyards which we daily see receiving from the dew of heaven and from the fatness of the earth, whence they pour forth wine, in which is luxury: and so we shall seem to have brought nothing, I do not say worthy of the Lord's bride, but even fitting for any one of the rest, out of so holy and divine Scripture. For what concord is there between brides and the keeping of vineyards? But even if it is thought to be fitting, whence shall we teach that the Church was once appointed to an office of this kind? Is God concerned about vineyards? But if by the spiritual sense we interpret the vineyards as the churches, that is, the faithful peoples, according to the sense of the prophet saying, 'The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel' (Isa. 5:7), perhaps it will begin to become clear to us how it is by no means unworthy of the bride to be made keeper of the vineyards.
30.3: I think that no small prerogative, moreover, will appear even in this very thing, if one is at pains to attend diligently how much it has everywhere through the world extended its bounds into vineyards of this kind, from that day on which it was attacked and driven out from Jerusalem by the children of its mother, together with that first new planting of its own; I mean the multitude of believers, of whom it is read that they were of one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32). And this is the very one which she now confesses she by no means kept, but not to her own folly. For neither was she so torn away from it in the persecution, as not to be planted elsewhere, and to be entrusted to other farmers, who may render its fruits in their seasons. By no means did she perish, but she migrated; she even grew and was enlarged, as one whom the Lord blessed. Finally, lift up your eyes, and see if its shadow has not covered the mountains, and its young plants the cedars of God; if it has not extended its shoots even to the sea, and its branches to the river (Ps. 80:11, 12). Nor is it a wonder, for it is God's building, it is God's husbandry (1 Cor. 3:9). He himself makes it fruitful, he himself propagates it, he himself prunes and purges it, that it may bring forth more fruit. For when would he desert with his care or work that which his right hand planted? It is plainly not to be held in neglect, in which the apostles are the branches, the Lord the vine, and his Father the husbandman (John 15:1, 2, 5). Planted in faith, it sends its roots in charity, dug about with the pruning-hook of discipline, manured with the tears of the penitent, watered with the words of preachers: and so truly abounding in wine in which is gladness, but not luxury; in wine of all sweetness, of no lustfulness. This wine certainly gladdens the heart of man; this, it is certain, the angels also drink with gladness. Finally, they rejoice in the conversion and repentance of sinners, thirsting for the salvation of men. The tears of the penitent are their wine, that in them there be the odor of life, the savor of grace, the taste of pardon, the pleasantness of reconciliation, the soundness of returning innocence, the sweetness of a calm conscience.
30.4: From that one vineyard, then, which the storm of savage persecution seemed to have destroyed, how many have bloomed again, propagated over the whole earth? And in all these the bride is set as keeper, that she may not be grieved that she did not keep the first vineyard. Be comforted, daughter of Zion: if blindness has in part happened in Israel, what do you lose? Admire the mystery, and do not lament the loss: enlarge your bosom, and gather the fullness of the gentiles. Say to the cities of Judah: 'It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you have rejected it, and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the gentiles' (Acts 13:46). To Moses, indeed, it was offered by God, if he would dismiss the prevaricating people and expose it to divine vengeance, that he himself could be made a great nation: but he refused (Exod. 32:9-13). Why? Because of the excessive love, surely, by which he was strongly bound to that people; and because he sought not the things that are his own, but God's honor, and not what would be useful to himself, but to many. And he indeed [acted] so.
30.5: But I think by a more secret counsel that this office was divinely reserved for the bride on account of its greatness, that she herself rather, and not Moses, would be sent to the great nation. For the friend of the bridegroom ought not to have snatched from the bride her blessing; and therefore it was not Moses, but the new bride, to whom it is said: 'Go into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature' (Mark 16:15); she, I say, was wholly sent to the great nation. For into what greater [nation] could she be sent than into the universality of the world? And the universality readily yielded to her bearing peace, offering grace. But not as the grace, so also the law. With how unlike a face do the sweetness of the one and the austerity of the other present themselves to every conscience! Who, surely, can look with equal regard upon the one condemning and the other consoling, the one demanding back and the other forgiving, the one striking and the other embracing? By no equal wish, certainly, will the shadow and the light, the wrath and the peace, the judgment and the mercy, the figure and the truth, the rod and the inheritance, the bridle and the kiss be accepted. Heavy, finally, were the hands of Moses, Aaron and Hur being witnesses (Exod. 17:12); heavy the yoke of the Law, the apostles themselves being witnesses, who cry out that it is unbearable for themselves and for the fathers (Acts 15:10); a heavy yoke, and a vile reward: for the earth is in the promise. For such a thing Moses was not sent to the great nation. But you, mother Church, having the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come, easily obtain, by your twofold grace, to be received by all, both on account of your sweet yoke and on account of your sublime kingdom. Driven out of the city, you are received by the universality, while what you promise so attracts, that what you impose does not terrify. Why do you still lament the loss of one vineyard, which has been compensated to you at so great interest? For this, that you were forsaken and hated, and there was none that passed through you: 'I will set you,' he says, 'for the pride of the ages, a joy to generation and generation; and you shall suck the milk of the gentiles, and shall be nursed with the breasts of kings: and you shall know that I am the Lord saving you, and your redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob' (Isa. 60:15, 16). In such a way, then, does the bride say that she has been made keeper of the vineyards, and that she has not kept her vineyard.
30.6: On the occasion of this passage I am wont to rebuke myself, that I have undertaken the care of souls, who would not suffice to keep my own; interpreting the vineyards as souls. But if you also approve this interpretation of ours, see then consequently whether we also rightly say that faith is the vine, virtues the branches, the grape the work, devotion the wine. Since neither is the branch anything without the vine, nor virtue without faith. For without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11:6); perhaps it will be necessary even to displease. Finally, everything that is not of faith is sin (Rom. 14:23). This, then, those who made me keeper of the vineyards ought to have considered, whether, that is, I had kept my own. But in how great a time did it lie uncultivated and desert, reduced to a wilderness! The wine had wholly failed from it, the branches of the virtues having dried up by reason of the barrenness of faith. Faith was there, but dead. For how could it not be dead without works? And that indeed in the secular life. But, converted to the Lord, I began, I confess, to keep it somewhat better; yet not as I ought. And who, indeed, is fit for this? Not even the holy Prophet, who says: 'Unless the Lord keeps the city, he watches in vain who keeps it' (Ps. 127:1). With how many snares even then, I remember, I lay open to that one who shoots at the innocent in secret! How much, O my vineyard, was stolen from us by stealthy machinations at that very time when we began to attend more vigilantly to the care and keeping of ourselves? How many and what clusters of pious works did either anger choke, or vainglory carry off, or empty glory defile? How much did we suffer from the allure of the gullet, how much from the spirit of sloth, how much from faint-heartedness of spirit and from a storm? Such was I: and nevertheless they still made me keeper of the vineyards, not considering what I would do or had done about my own, nor hearing the master rebuking and saying: 'If a man knows not how to preside over his own house, how will he have the diligence of the Church of God?' (1 Tim. 3:5.)
30.7: I marvel at the boldness of very many, whom we see gathering from their own vineyards nothing but thorns and thistles, still not fearing to thrust themselves into the Lord's vineyards. They are thieves and robbers, not keepers, nor cultivators. Let that [be said] to them. Woe, however, to me even now from the danger of my vineyard! rather the more now, when, intent on many [things], I am compelled to be less diligent, less careful about the one. Nor is it allowed to set a hedge around it, nor to dig a winepress in it. Alas! its wall is destroyed, and all who pass by the way gather its grapes! (Ps. 80:13.) It lies open, exposed to sadness, and passable to anger and impatience. Certain busy little foxes of the pressing necessities demolish it; anxieties, suspicions, cares burst in on every side; the crowds of the discordant, the annoyances of causes are wanting rarely an hour. There is no faculty of forbidding, no power of declining, but not even space for praying. With what shower of tears shall I suffice to water the barrenness of my soul? (Ps. 35:12.) I meant to say 'of my vineyard,' but from the psalm it so fell out on account of the usage, and the sense is the same; nor am I displeased with the error which reminds one of the likeness, because the discourse is not about a vineyard, but about the soul. Let the soul, then, be thought of when the vineyard is read; since under its appearance and name its barrenness is deplored. With what tears, then, shall I water the barrenness of my vineyard? All its branches have withered from want; they lie without fruit, because they have no moisture; and, good Jesus, how many bundles of twigs from them does the burning of my contrite heart consume in your daily sacrifice, you being witness! May a troubled spirit be, I beseech you, a sacrifice to you; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps. 51:19).
30.8: And I indeed, for my want of perfection, draw this present chapter to myself. But every one will be perfect who will be able otherwise to say: 'I have not kept my vineyard'; with that sense, namely, in which the Savior speaks in the Gospel: 'He who has lost his soul for my sake will find it' (Matt. 10:39). He is plainly fit and worthy to be made keeper of the vineyards, whom the care of his own vineyard does not impede or retard from the diligence and solicitude for those committed [to him]; while he seeks not the things that are his own, nor what is useful to himself, but what [is useful] to many. On this account, indeed, that care was entrusted to Peter in so many vineyards, which were of the circumcision, because the man was ready both to go to prison and to death (Luke 22:33), so far was he from being detained by the love of his own vineyard, that is, of his own soul, from intent upon the care of those entrusted [to him]. Rightly also to Paul among the gentiles so huge a forest of vineyards was entrusted, because he too was found by no means solicitous in the keeping of his own vineyard; so that he was ready not only to be bound, but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 21:13). Finally: 'None of these things,' he says, 'do I fear, nor do I make my soul dearer to me than myself' (Acts 20:24). The best appraiser of things, who judges that nothing of his own is to be preferred to himself.
30.9: How many have preferred a paltry and most vile sum of money to their own salvation! Paul [preferred] not even his soul. 'I do not,' he says, 'make it dearer than myself.' Then do you make a difference between yourself and your soul? You, indeed, prudently are more to yourself than anything of yours. But how is not your soul yourself? I think that because Paul already then walked in the spirit, and with the mind consented to the law of God that it is good (Rom. 7:16), therefore he judged that this very mind of his, as the chief and highest something of himself, was worthy to be signified by the name of himself rather than of any of his things; but the rest, which consists in a nature of the lower sort, and consequently inheres in the inferior and more vile essence, which is the body; not only in the office of quickening and giving sense, but also in the desire of fostering and nourishing it: this, I say, the spiritual man, judging the sensual and carnal [part] unworthy of the appellation of self, thought should rather be counted among his things, than that he himself should be personally expressed through it. 'When I say, I,' he says, 'understand the more excellent thing that is in me, in which I also stand by the grace of God, that is, the mind and reason.' 'When I speak of my soul, take this lower thing, which you see is adapted to quickening the flesh, and is even joined to it in concupiscence.' 'I acknowledge that I was that, but that I am now no longer, because I do not yet walk according to the flesh, but according to the spirit' (Rom. 8:4). 'I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me' (Gal. 2:20). 'According to the mind, it is I; according to the flesh, it is not.' 'For what if the soul even now lusts carnally?' 'It is no longer I that work it, but sin that dwells in me' (Rom. 7:17). 'And therefore I would call not myself indeed, but yet mine, that which savors carnally in me, and that is nothing other than the soul itself.' 'For in truth the carnal affection of the soul is a portion of it, and the life which it administers to the body.' 'This, then, his soul, Paul despised in comparison with himself, ready for the Lord not only to be bound, but even to die in Jerusalem, and so to lose his own soul according to the counsel of the Lord.'
30.10: You also, if you abandon your own will, if you perfectly renounce the pleasures of the body, if you crucify your flesh with its vices and concupiscences, but also mortify your members which are upon the earth: you will prove yourself an imitator of Paul, who do not make your soul dearer than yourself; you will prove yourself also a disciple of Christ, even by losing it healthfully. And indeed you lose it more prudently that you may keep it, than keep it that you may lose it. For he who will have wished to save his soul, will lose it (Matt. 16:25). What do you say here, you observers of foods, neglecters of morals? Hippocrates and his followers teach to save souls in this world; Christ and his disciples [teach] to lose [them]. Whom of the two do you choose as master to follow? But he makes himself manifest who disputes thus: this hurts the eyes, this the head, and that the chest or the stomach. Truly each one brings forth in the midst what he has learned from his master. Have you read these distinctions in the Gospel, or in the prophets, or in the letters of the apostles? Flesh and blood, for certain, has revealed this wisdom to you, not the Spirit of the Father; for this is the wisdom of the flesh. But hear what the physicians of ours think of it. 'The wisdom of the flesh,' they say, 'is death'; likewise: 'The wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God' (Rom. 8:6, 7). Ought I to have set before you the opinion of Hippocrates or Galen, or at least [one] from the school of Epicurus? I am a disciple of Christ; I speak to the disciples of Christ: if I shall bring in a foreign dogma, I myself have sinned. Epicurus and Hippocrates — the one prefers the pleasure of the body, the other its good condition; my Master preaches contempt of both. The life of the soul in the body, which the one with the greatest study seeks from whence to sustain it, the other from whence also to delight it, and teaches to seek — the Savior admonishes even to lose.
30.11: For what else sounded to you from the school of Christ, when it was just before cried out: 'He who loves his soul will lose it'? (John 12:25.) 'Will lose it,' he said, whether by laying it down as a martyr, or by afflicting it as a penitent. Although it is a kind of martyrdom to mortify the deeds of the flesh by the spirit; that one, of course, by which the members are cut with iron, milder indeed in horror, but more troublesome by its length. Do you see that by this sentence of my Master the wisdom of the flesh is condemned, through which, certainly, one either flows away into the luxury of pleasure, or even the good health of the body itself is desired more than it ought? Finally, that true wisdom does not flow out into pleasures, you have surely heard from the Wise Man, that it is not even to be found in the land of those that live pleasantly (Job 28:13). But he who finds it says: 'Above health and all beauty I have loved wisdom' (Wis. 7:10). If above health and beauty, how much more above pleasure and baseness? What, then, does it profit to abstain from pleasures, and to spend daily care in investigating the diversities of temperaments, and inquiring into the varieties of foods? 'Legumes,' he says, 'are windy, cheese weighs on the stomach, milk hurts the head, the chest does not bear the drink of water, cabbages nourish melancholy, leeks kindle choler, fish from a pool or from muddy water do not at all suit my temperament.' What a thing is this, that in whole rivers, fields, gardens, or cellars one can scarcely find anything you may eat!
30.12: Think, I pray, that you are a monk, not a physician; nor is one to judge of temperament, but of profession. Spare, I beseech you, first indeed your own quiet; spare then the labor of those who serve; spare the burden of the house; spare the conscience. I say the conscience, not yours, but another's; his, to wit, who, sitting near, and eating what is set before him, murmurs at your singular fasting. For it is an offense to him either your odious superstition, or the hardness which perhaps he thinks [to be] of him who has to provide for you. He is offended, I say, in your singularity, the brother judging you superstitious, as one seeking superfluous things; or certainly accusing me as hard, who do not search out what is necessary for your food. In vain do some flatter themselves with the example of Paul, exhorting the disciple not to drink water, but to use a little wine for the stomach and his frequent infirmities (1 Tim. 5:23). They ought to attend, first indeed, that the Apostle by no means recommends a thing of this kind to himself, but neither does the disciple equally require it for himself. Then that it is not intimated to a monk, but to a bishop, whose life was most necessary to the Church still tender and newly arising. This was Timothy. Give me another Timothy; and I will feed him, if you will, even with gold, and give him balsam to drink. But you dispense to yourself, having pity on yourself. Your own dispensation of yourself is, I confess, suspect to me; and I fear lest you be deluded under the cover and name of discretion by the prudence of the flesh. I would at least have you warned of this, that if the authority of the Apostle so pleases you about drinking wine, you do not omit the 'little' which he added. And enough of this. But let us return to the bride, and learn from her usefully not to keep one's own vineyards, especially we who seem to be appointed keepers in the vineyards of the Spouse of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.

31.1: Tell me, whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you lie at midday (Song 1:6). To studious minds the Word, the bridegroom, frequently appears, and not under one appearance. Why so? Surely because he is not yet seen as he is. Of course, that vision stands, because the form which is then seen stands; for it is: nor does it undergo any change from that which it is, was, or will be. Take away, then, 'Was' and 'Will Be'; whence now transmutation or the shadow of change? But whatever, coming from that which was 'Was,' does not cease to tend toward that which is 'Will Be,' has a passing, indeed, through 'Is,' but by no means remains. For how does it exist, which never remains in the same state? Only that, therefore, truly exists, which is neither cut off from 'Was,' nor erased from 'Will Be'; but only and inexpugnable there remains to it 'Is,' and it remains what it is. Nor indeed does 'Was' take away from it its being from eternity; nor 'Will Be' its being unto eternity: and through this it claims for itself true being, that is, increatable, interminable, invariable. When, therefore, he himself who so is, rather who is not so or so, is seen as he is, that vision stands, as I said, because no change interrupts it. And then that one denarius of the Gospel is rendered to all who so see (Matt. 20:9), in the one appearance which is offered. For as that which appears is invariable in itself, so it is present invariable to the beholders; and those to whom it appears will to see nothing more desirable, can [see] nothing more delightful. When, then, will that avidity be loathed, or that sweetness withdraw, or truth defraud, or eternity fail? But if into eternity the abundance of seeing is extended equally with the will, how is it not full happiness? For nothing, indeed, is wanting to those already always seeing, nor is anything overabundant to those always willing.
31.2: But such a vision is not of the present life, but is reserved for the last things, for those at least who can say: 'We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is' (1 John 3:2). And now indeed he appears to whom he wills; but as he wills, not as he is. No wise man, no saint, no prophet can or could see him, as he is, in this mortal body; but he will be able in the immortal [body], whoever shall be judged worthy. Thus he is seen also here, but as he himself appears, and not as he is. For neither have you ever seen even this great luminary (I mean that sun which you see daily) as it is, but only as it illuminates, for example, the air, the mountain, the wall. Which neither indeed could you in any way [see], if not some part of the light of your own body, by its inborn serenity and clearness, were like to the heavenly light. Finally, no other member of the body is capable of light, on account, surely, of its great dissimilitude. But neither does the eye itself, when it is troubled, come near the light, plainly on account of the lost likeness. He, therefore, who is troubled, by no means sees the serene sun on account of dissimilitude; he who is serene sees it somewhat on account of some similitude. Surely if it thrived with perfectly equal purity, it would see him altogether with an unobstructed glance, as he is, on account of the complete similitude. So also the sun of justice, that one who enlightens every man coming into this world, being enlightened, one can see in this world as he enlightens, as one already in some way like him; as he is, one cannot at all, as one not yet perfectly like him. Therefore he says: 'Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded' (Ps. 34:5). So indeed, but if we are enlightened as much as is sufficient, that, beholding with unveiled face the glory of God, we may be transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18).
31.3: We must then approach him, not burst in, lest an irreverent searcher of majesty be overwhelmed by the glory (Prov. 25:27). Nor indeed is one to approach by places, but by brightnesses; and those not corporeal, but spiritual, as by the Spirit of the Lord. From the Lord's [Spirit] plainly, and not from ours, although in ours. He, therefore, who is clearer, he is nearer; but to be clearest is to have arrived. Moreover, for those already present, to see [him] as he is is nothing other than to be as he is, and not to be confounded by any dissimilitude. But that then, as I said. In the meantime, however, this so great variety of forms, and the multitude of appearances in created things, what are they but certain rays of the Deity, showing indeed that he truly is from whom they are, yet by no means defining what he is? And so you see about him, but not him. But when, of him whom you do not see, you see the rest, you know without doubt that he exists whom you ought to seek, that grace may not defraud the seeker, nor ignorance excuse the negligent. But this kind of seeing is common. For it is at hand, according to the Apostle, to every one using reason, to behold the invisible things of God, being understood through the things that are made (Rom. 1:20).
31.4: There is, without doubt, another mode, by which formerly that frequent and ambitious familiarity of the divine presence was kindly granted to the Fathers, although to them too not as he is, but as he deigned [to be seen]. Nor in one way to all, but, as the Apostle says, at sundry times and in divers manners (Heb. 1:1); since he himself in himself is one, he himself saying to Israel, 'The Lord your God is one God' (Deut. 6:4). And this manifestation, indeed not common; but still it was made from without, manifested, to wit, through images appearing outwardly, or voices sounding. But there is a divine inspection, differing from these by so much as it is more inward, when God deigns himself to visit the soul seeking him, which yet has devoted itself wholly to the seeking with all desire and love. And this is the sign of an advent of this kind of his, as we are taught by one who has experienced it: 'Fire shall go before him, and shall burn up his enemies round about' (Ps. 97:3). For it is needful that the ardor of holy desire go before his face toward every soul to whom he himself is to come, that it may consume all the rust of vices, and so prepare a place for the Lord. And then the soul knows that the Lord is near, when it has felt itself kindled by that fire, and has said with the prophet: 'From on high he has sent fire into my bones, and has taught me' (Lam. 1:13); and that, 'My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall blaze out' (Ps. 39:3).
31.5: To such a soul, sighing frequently, indeed praying without ceasing, and afflicting itself out of desire, when at length that desired one, who is so sought, mercifully meets [it], I think it becomes her, from her own experience, to say with holy Jeremiah: 'You are good, O Lord, to those who hope in you, to the soul that seeks you' (Lam. 3:25). But also his angel, who is one of the companions of the bridegroom, deputed for this very thing, minister indeed and arbiter of the secret mutual salutation; he, I say, the angel, how he leaps for joy, how he rejoices with her and delights together, and, turned to the Lord, says: 'I give you thanks, O Lord of majesty, because you have granted her the desire of her heart, and have not defrauded her of the will of her lips!' He is the one who, in every place, a certain diligent attendant of the soul, does not cease to solicit her, and to admonish her with continual suggestions, saying: 'Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart'; and again, 'Wait on the Lord, and keep his way' (Ps. 37:4, 34); likewise, 'If he makes delay, wait for him, because coming he will come, and will not tarry' (Hab. 2:3). But to the Lord: 'As the hart,' he says, 'desires the fountains of waters, so does this soul desire you, O God' (Ps. 42:2). It desired you in the night; but your spirit also, in her inmost parts, has watched early to you in the morning (Isa. 26:9). And again: 'All the day long he has stretched out his hands to you (Ps. 88:10); send her away, because she cries after you (Matt. 15:23): turn a little, and be entreated for her (Ps. 90:13).' Look down from heaven, and see, and visit the desolate one. A faithful bridesman, who, conscious of the mutual love, but not envious, seeks not his own, but the Lord's grace: he runs in the midst between the Beloved and the beloved, offering the vows, carrying back the gifts. He rouses this one, he appeases that one. Sometimes also, though rarely, he presents them alike to each other, whether by taking this one, or bringing that one: since he is of the household and known in the palace, nor fears a repulse, and daily sees the face of the Father.
31.6: But see that you do not think that we, in this commingling of the Word and the soul, sense anything corporeal or imaginary. We say that which the Apostle says, that he who cleaves to God is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17). The ecstasy of a pure mind into God, or the pious descent of God into the soul, we express with our words, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, as best we can. Thus this union is made in the spirit, because God is a spirit (John 4:24), and he covets the beauty of that soul which perhaps he has observed walking in the spirit, and not fulfilling the care of the flesh in desire, especially if he has seen her burning with love of himself. So affected and so loved, she will by no means be wholly content either with that manifestation of the bridegroom which was made to many through the things that are made, or that which was made to few through visions and dreams, unless, by a special prerogative, she receive him, heaven-sent, slipping into her inmost affections and the very marrow of her heart, and have at hand him whom she desires not figured, but infused; not appearing, but affecting; and, without doubt, the more delightful as he is within, not without. For he is the Word, not sounding, but penetrating; not talkative, but effectual; not clamorous to the ears, but caressing the affections. He is a face not formed, but forming; not glancing upon the eyes of the body, but gladdening the face of the heart: pleasing, to wit, by the gift of love, not by color.
31.7: I would not yet, however, say that he appears as he is, although in this manner he does not exhibit something wholly other than what he is. For neither even so will he always be present, although to the most devout minds, nor uniformly to all. For it is needful that the taste of the divine presence be varied according to the various desires of the soul, and that the infused savor of the supernal sweetness delight the palate of the mind that seeks divers things in divers ways. Finally, you have observed in this amatory song how often he has changed countenance, and in how great a multitude of his sweetness he has deigned to be transformed before his beloved; and how now, indeed, like a modest bridegroom, he seeks the secret embraces of the holy soul, and delights in kisses; now, on the other hand, he appears to show himself a physician in oil and ointments, plainly on account of tender and infirm souls of this sort still needing fomentations and medicines: whence also they are designated by the delicate name of little maidens. If anyone mutters, he will hear that they who are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill (Matt. 9:12). Now again, associating himself like some traveler with the bride and the little maidens journeying together, he relieves the whole company from the labor of the way by his most pleasant conversations, so that, on his departing, they say: 'Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus, while he spoke to us on the way?' (Luke 24:32.) An eloquent companion, who, in the sweetness of his discourses and manners, as in a certain fragrance of breathing ointments, makes all run after him: whence also they say, 'We will run in the odor of your ointments' (Song 1:3). Likewise at times meeting [her], as a very rich father of a family, who abounds in bread in his house; rather as a magnificent and powerful king, who seems to lift up the faint-heartedness of the poor bride, to provoke her desire, showing her all the desirable things of his glory, the riches of the winepresses and storehouses, the abundance of gardens and fields, and at last even introducing her into the very secrets of the bedchamber. Surely the heart of her husband confides in her, and there is nothing among all that he judges to be hidden from her, whom he redeemed poor, proved faithful, embraces [as] amiable. And so he does not cease, whether in this or that inward manner, to appear continually to the sight of those who seek him, that the word may be fulfilled which he spoke: 'Behold, I am with you even to the consummation of the world' (Matt. 28:20).
31.8: And in all these [things] he is sweet and meek, and of much mercy. For in kisses indeed he shows himself affectionate and bland; but in oil and in pigments and ointments clement and flowing with the bowels of piety and compassion: moreover, on the way cheerful, affable, full of grace and consolation; but in the showing of riches and possessions he shows himself munificent, and a liberal rewarder with royal liberality. Thus through the whole texture of this song you will find the Word shadowed by similitudes of this sort. Whence I think that is signified by the prophet, where he says: 'The Spirit before our face, Christ the Lord; in his shadow we shall live among the gentiles' (Lam. 4:20): that, to wit, we now see through a glass and in an enigma, and not yet face to face. But that indeed [is the case] while we live among the gentiles: for among the angels otherwise; when already, with wholly undivided felicity, we too shall see him with them, as he is, that is, in the form of God, and not in shadow. For as we say that among the ancients the shadow and the figure existed, but that to us, through the grace of Christ present in the flesh, the truth itself shines out by itself; so we too, in respect of the future age, live meanwhile in a certain shadow of the truth — he will not deny [it], unless he who does not acquiesce in the Apostle saying: 'We know in part, and we prophesy in part' (1 Cor. 13:9); and that, 'I do not think that I have comprehended' (Phil. 3:13). For how is there not a distinction between him who walks by faith, and him [who walks] by sight? Therefore the just lives by faith (Hab. 2:4), the blessed exults in sight: and therefore a holy man lives meanwhile in the shadow of Christ, a holy angel glories in the splendor of the countenance of glory.
31.9: And the shadow of faith is good, which tempers the light to the bleary eye, and prepares the eye for the light; for it is written: 'Purifying their hearts by faith' (Acts 15:9). Faith, therefore, does not extinguish the light, but preserves it. Whatever, indeed, is that which the angel sees, this the shadow of faith keeps for me, laid up in a faithful bosom, to be revealed in time. Is it not expedient to hold even wrapped up that which you cannot take naked? Finally, even the Mother of the Lord lived in the shadow of faith, to whom it was said: 'And blessed [are you] who have believed' (Luke 1:45). She also had a shadow from the body of Christ, who heard: 'And the power of the Most High shall overshadow you' (Luke 1:35). For it is no vile shadow, which is formed of the power of the Most High. And truthfully, power in the flesh of Christ, which overshadowed the Virgin, that what was impossible to a mortal woman might, nevertheless, by the interposition of the quickening veil of the body, bear the presence of the majesty, and sustain the inaccessible light. Power plainly, in which all contrary strength has been vanquished; and power and shadow putting to flight demons, protecting men; or certainly a quickening power, a refreshing shadow.
31.10: We live, therefore, in the shadow of Christ, who walk by faith, and are fed with his flesh that we may live. For the flesh of Christ is truly food (John 6:56). And see, lest on that account even now he be described in this place as appearing, as in a pastoral guise, where the bride seems to address him as one of the shepherds, saying: 'Tell me where you feed, where you lie at midday.' The good Shepherd, who gives his life for his sheep (John 10:11): his life for them, his flesh to them; that in ransom, this in food. A wonderful thing! he himself is the shepherd, he himself the pasture, he himself the redemption. But the sermon proceeds at length, because the place is ample, and contains great things, and will not be unfolded in few [words]; and by this necessity it seems to me that it is now to be broken off rather than finished. But it is needful that, since the matter is hanging, the memory be vigilant; that where there shall be a pause, there it may soon be resumed and treated, as the Lord shall give, Jesus Christ, the Spouse of the Church, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.

32.1: Tell me where you feed, where you lie at midday (Song 1:6). Here we are; hence we proceed. But before that vision and address begins to be treated, I think it should be briefly recapitulated concerning the other visions which have gone before, how they may be spiritually fitted to us according to the desires and merits of each one, that, having grasped those — if yet that has been given — the easier understanding may shine forth in the discussion of this one too. But that is most difficult. For although those words, by which the visions themselves or similitudes are described, seem to sound bodies and corporeal things; yet it is spiritual things that are ministered to us in these, and through this it behooves us to seek also in the spirit the causes and reasons of them. And who is fit to investigate and comprehend so many affections and progressions of the soul, by which this so multiform grace concerning the presence of the bridegroom is dispensed? Yet if we enter into ourselves, and the Holy Spirit deigns to show us in his light what he does not disdain to work in us assiduously by his operation, I think that by no means shall we remain altogether without understanding in these. For I trust that we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit which is of God, that we may know the things which are given to us of God (1 Cor. 2:12).
32.2: If, then, it is good for any of us to cleave to God with the holy Prophet (Ps. 73:28), and, to speak more plainly, if there is in us any one such man of desire, that he longs to be dissolved and to be with Christ, longs, moreover, vehemently, thirsts ardently, meditates assiduously; he will surely receive the word at the time of visitation no otherwise than in the form of a bridegroom, at the hour, namely, when he shall have felt himself bound within by certain arms of wisdom, and the sweetness of holy love infused into him from thence. Inasmuch as the desire of his heart will be granted to him, although still a sojourner in the body, yet in part, and that for a time, and a short time. For when, sought with watchings, and prayers, and much labor and shower of tears, he has come, suddenly, while he is thought to be held, he slips away; and again, meeting the one weeping and pursuing, he suffers himself to be laid hold of, but by no means to be kept, while suddenly he again flies, as it were, out of the hands. Even if the devout soul has insisted on prayers and tears, he will return again, and will not defraud her of the will of her lips; but soon he will again disappear, and will not be seen, unless sought again with whole desire. So, therefore, even in this body there can be frequent joy from the presence of the bridegroom, but not abundance; because although the visitation gladdens, yet the vicissitude molests. And this the beloved must needs suffer so long, until, once the burden of the corporeal mass being laid down, she herself also, lifted on the wings of her desires, flies away, freely taking her course through the fields of contemplation, and, with the mind unencumbered, following the Beloved whithersoever he has gone.
32.3: Nor yet will he be thus present even in passing to every soul, unless to that one only whom huge devotion, and vehement desire, and most sweet affection prove a bride, and worthy, that to her the Word, about to approach with the grace of visiting, may put on beauty, assuming the form of a bridegroom. For he who is not yet found so affected, but rather pricked by the recollection of his own deeds, speaking in the bitterness of his soul says to God: 'Do not condemn me' (Job 10:2); or perhaps even now is dangerously tempted, being drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence: this one seeks not a bridegroom, but a physician; and through this he will receive, not kisses indeed, nor embraces, but only remedies for his wounds, in oil, to wit, and in ointments. Do we not often think thus, and so experience it while praying, we who are daily still tempted by our present excesses, and bitten by the past? From how much bitterness have you often delivered me, good Jesus, coming [to me]! How often, after anxious tears, unspeakable groans and sobs, have you anointed my wounded conscience with the unction of your mercy, and drenched it with the oil of gladness! How often has prayer, taking up me who was almost despairing, made me exulting, and presuming on pardon! Behold, those who are similarly affected know this, that the Lord Jesus is truly a physician, who heals the contrite of heart, and binds up their bruises (Ps. 147:3). Let those who have not experienced it believe thence in him himself saying: 'The Spirit of the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the meek, that I might heal the contrite of heart' (Isa. 61:1; Luke 4:18, 21). If they still doubt, let them approach indeed and prove [it], and so learn in themselves what it is: 'I will have mercy, and not sacrifice' (Matt. 9:13). But let us see the rest.
32.4: There are those who, wearied in spiritual studies, and turned into lukewarmness, and placed in a certain failure of spirit, walk the sad ways of the Lord, approach whatever is enjoined with a dry and weary heart, murmur frequently; they complain of the long days, the long nights too, speaking with holy Job: 'If I sleep, I shall say: When shall I arise? and again I shall wait for the evening' (Job 7:4). When, then, it happens to suffer anything of this sort, if the merciful Lord draws near to us on the way by which we walk, and begins to speak of heaven who is from heaven, and also to sing to us something favorable of the songs of Zion, to tell also of the city of God, of the peace of the city, of the eternity of peace, of the state of eternity: I tell you, the joyful narration will be, as it were, a vehicle for the slumbering and sluggish soul, so that it drives all loathing from the mind of the hearer, and from the body its fatigue. Does he seem to you to suffer or ask anything else, who says: 'My soul has slumbered through weariness; strengthen me in your words'? And will he not, when he has obtained it, cry out: 'How I have loved your law, O Lord! it is my meditation all the day'? (Ps. 119:97, 28.) For there are certain words of the Word, the bridegroom, to us, our meditations concerning him and his glory, elegance, power, majesty. Not only this, but also when we turn over his testimonies with a greedy mind, and the judgments of his mouth, and meditate on his law day and night; let us know for certain that the bridegroom is present, and addresses us, that we be not wearied with labors, delighted by his discourses.
32.5: You, then, when you feel something of this sort revolving in your mind, do not think it your own thought, but recognize him speaking, who says by the prophet: 'I who speak justice' (Isa. 63:1). For our mind's thoughts are most like to the discourses of the Truth speaking within us; nor is it easy for anyone to discern what his own heart brings forth within him, or what he hears, unless he who prudently attends to the Lord speaking in the Gospel, that 'from the heart come forth evil thoughts' (Matt. 15:19); and that: 'Why do you think evil in your hearts?' (Matt. 9:4.) And: 'He who speaks a lie, speaks from his own' (John 8:44). But the Apostle: 'Not that,' he says, 'we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves (understand: good); but our sufficiency is from God' (2 Cor. 3:5). When, therefore, we turn over evil things in our heart, it is our own thought; if good things, it is the speech of God. Our heart speaks the former; it hears the latter. 'I will hear,' he says, 'what the Lord God will speak in me, because he will speak peace to his people' (Ps. 85:8). Thus peace, piety, justice God speaks in us; nor do we think such things of ourselves, but hear them in ourselves. But murders, adulteries, thefts, blasphemies, and such like, come forth from the heart (Matt. 15:19): nor do we hear them, but speak them. Finally, the fool has said in his heart: 'There is no God' (Ps. 14:1). And for this the impious provoked God, because he said in his heart: 'He will not require [it]' (Ps. 10:13). But there is besides that which is felt indeed in the heart, yet is not the word of the heart. For neither does it go forth from the heart, as our thought [does]; nor is it that which we said is made to the heart, the word, namely, of the Word, since it is evil. But it is injected by the contrary powers, as injections are made through evil angels; as, for example, was that which is read that the devil sent into the heart, that Judas of Simon Iscariot should betray the Lord (John 13:2).
32.6: But who is so watchful and diligent an observer of his own internal motions, whether made in himself, or also from himself, that he can clearly, for each unlawful sense of his heart, discern between the disease of the mind and the bite of the serpent? I think this possible to none of mortals, unless he who, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, has received that special gift which the Apostle, among the other charisms which he enumerates, names the discerning of spirits (1 Cor. 12:10). For however much anyone, according to Solomon, keeps his heart with all watchfulness (Prov. 4:23), and observes all things that move within him with most vigilant attention; even if he has had in these a long exercise and frequent experience, he will not yet be able, purely, to discern and distinguish in himself the innate evil from the evil that was sown. For who understands his offenses? Nor does it much concern us to know whence the evil is within us, provided we know that it is within: rather we must watch and pray, from wherever it be, that we do not consent. Finally, the prophet prays against both evils, saying: 'From my hidden [faults] cleanse me, O Lord, and from those of others spare your servant' (Ps. 19:12, 13). And I — I cannot deliver to you what I have not received. But I have not received, I confess, whence to assign a certain notion between the birth of the heart and the seedplot of the enemy. For both are evil, both from evil; both are in the heart, but not both of the heart. All this is certain to me in myself, although it is uncertain what I should ascribe to the heart, what to the enemy. And that indeed, as I said, without danger.
32.7: But surely there is where one errs dangerously, nay, damnably, and there the sure rule is rightly fixed for us, that we do not give to ourselves what is God's in us, thinking the visitation of the Word to be our own thought. Therefore, as far as good is from evil, so far are these two from each other: since neither is evil from the Word, nor will good go forth from the heart, except what it has perhaps before conceived from the Word; because a good tree cannot make evil fruits, nor an evil tree good fruits (Matt. 7:18). But I believe enough has been said as to what is God's, what ours, in our heart; nor superfluously, I think, but that the enemies of grace may know that without grace the human heart does not suffice even to think good, but that its sufficiency is from God; that God's voice, the good which is thought, is not the offspring of the heart. You, then, if you hear his voice, know now whence it comes, or whither it goes; knowing that it goes forth from God, and goes to the heart. But see how the word which goes forth from the mouth of God does not return to him void, but prospers and does all things to which he sent it, that you too may be able to say, that 'the grace of God in me was not void' (1 Cor. 15:10). Blessed is the mind, to which the Word, an inseparable companion, everywhere offers himself affable, [and which], unceasingly delighted by the sweetness of his eloquence, may vindicate itself at every hour from the annoyances of the flesh and its vices, redeeming the time from the evil days (Eph. 5:16). It will not be wearied, it will not be molested; since, as the Scripture says: 'Whatever befalls him will not sadden the just man' (Prov. 12:21).
32.8: Now indeed I think the appearance of the great Father of the family, or of the royal majesty, appears to those who, approaching to the deep heart, made more magnanimous from the greater liberty of the spirit and the purity of conscience, are wont to dare greater things, restless wholly and curious to penetrate the more secret things, and to seize the more sublime, and to attempt the more perfect, not only of the senses, but of the virtues. For these, for the greatness of their faith, are found worthy to be brought into all fullness; nor is there altogether, in all the storehouses of wisdom, anything from which the Lord, the God of the sciences, should judge the lovers of truth, who are not conscious of vanity, to be kept back. Such was Moses, who dared to say to God: 'If I have found grace in your eyes, show me yourself' (Exod. 33:13, 18). Such was Philip, who demanded that the Father be shown to himself and his fellow-disciples (John 14:8): such also Thomas, who, unless he touched with his own hand the wound and the pierced side, refused to believe (John 20:25). A little faith, but one which, in a wonderful manner, descends from greatness of spirit. Such also was David, who likewise said to God: 'My heart has said to you: My face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I will seek' (Ps. 27:8). Such, therefore, dare great things, because they are great: and what they dare they obtain, according to the word of the promise to them, which is of this sort: 'Whatever place your foot shall have trodden, shall be yours' (Deut. 11:24). For great faith merits great things; and as far as you shall have stretched the foot of your confidence upon the goods of the Lord, so far shall you possess.
32.9: Finally, God speaks to Moses mouth to mouth; and he merits to see the Lord openly, not through enigmas and figures, whereas he says he appears to the other prophets only in a vision, and speaks through a dream (Num. 12:6-8). To Philip also, according to the petition of his heart, the Father was shown in the Son, in that, without doubt, he forthwith heard: 'Philip, he who sees me, sees also the Father'; and: 'Because I am in the Father, and the Father in me' (John 14:9, 10). But also to Thomas, according to the desire of his heart, he offered himself to be handled (John 20:27), and he defrauded him not of the will of his lips. What of David? does he not also signify that he is not wholly defrauded of his vow, where he says that he will not give sleep to his eyes, nor slumber to his eyelids, until he find a place for the Lord? (Ps. 132:4, 5.) Therefore, to great spirits of this sort the great Bridegroom will come forward, and will be magnificent in doing with them, sending forth his light and his truth, and leading them and bringing them into his holy mountain, and into his tabernacles, so that he who is of this sort may say: 'Because he who is mighty has done great things to me' (Luke 1:49). His eyes shall see the King in his beauty (Isa. 33:17); [him] going before them to the beautiful places of the desert, to the flowers of roses and the lilies of the valleys, to the pleasant places of gardens, the watered [places] of fountains, to the delights of cellars and the odors of spices, at last to the very secrets of the bedchamber.
32.10: These are the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden with the bridegroom, these the pastures of life prepared for the refreshment of holy souls. Blessed is the man who has filled his desire from them. Let him be admonished of this only, that he be unwilling to have alone those things which can suffice for many. For on this account perhaps, after all these things, the bridegroom is described as appearing like a shepherd, that thereby the attainer of so great gifts may be admonished to feed the flock of the simpler ones, who, namely, are as unable to seize these things by themselves as sheep dare not go out into the pastures without a shepherd. Finally, the bride, prudently attending to this very thing, asks that it be shown her where he himself feeds and lies under the noonday heat, ready (as is given to be understood from this) to be fed and to feed with him, and under him. For she judges it not safe to drive the flock far from the supreme Shepherd, plainly on account of the incursions of wolves, especially of those who come to us in the clothing of sheep: and therefore she is anxious to feed alike with him in the same pastures, and to lie in his shadows. And she assigns the cause: 'Lest,' she says, 'I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.' These are they who wish to be seen as friends of the bridegroom, and are not: and while their care is to feed their own flocks, not his; yet, lying in wait on this side and on that, they say: 'Behold, here is Christ; behold, there he is' (Mark 13:21), in order, namely, to seduce many, and lead them away from the flocks of Christ, and unite them to their own. This [much] for the text of the letter. But now expect, under another beginning of the discourse, the spiritual sense which lies hidden in it, whatever it shall be, which the Spouse of the Church, while you pray, will deign to impart to me from it by his mercy, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.

33.1: Tell me, whom my soul loves, where you feed, where you lie down at midday (Song 1:6). And another: 'Tell me,' he says, 'why you judge me thus' (Job 10:2). In which place he does not indeed plead against the sentence, but searches out the cause, seeking to be instructed by the scourges, not to be delivered. Likewise another prays, saying: 'Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths' (Ps. 25:4). Which ways or paths he means, he makes manifest elsewhere: 'He led me,' he says, 'upon the paths of justice' (Ps. 23:3). Therefore the soul curious of God never ceases to inquire these three things: justice, and judgment, and the place of the habitation of the glory of the bridegroom: as it were the way in which it walks, the caution with which it walks, and the dwelling to which it walks. Concerning which dwelling you have thus in the prophet: 'One thing I have asked of the Lord,' he says, 'this will I seek, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life' (Ps. 27:4); and again: 'Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house, and the place of the habitation of your glory' (Ps. 26:8). Moreover concerning the other two: 'Justice and judgment,' he says, 'are the preparation of your throne' (Ps. 89:15). Rightly does the devout mind require these three things, namely, the seat of God, and the preparation of the seat. And beautifully do all these things concur together for the bride's prerogative, unto the consummation of the virtues, that by the form of justice she may be beautiful, by the knowledge of judgments cautious, by the desire of the presence or glory of the bridegroom chaste. Such in truth it befits the bride of the Lord to be, beautiful, learned, and chaste. Therefore the petition which I placed last is of this place. For she asks of him whom her soul loves that it be told to her where he feeds, and where he lies down at midday.
33.2: And first observe how elegantly she distinguishes the love of the spirit from the affection of the flesh, while, wishing to express her beloved rather by the very affection than by name, she says not simply: 'Whom I love'; but: 'O,' she says, 'whom my soul loves,' designating a spiritual love. Then diligently attend to what so delights her in the place of pasture. But let not that escape you concerning the midday hour, and that that place is chiefly examined in which he who feeds lies down at the same time: which is an indication of great security. For I think that on this account 'he lies down' was added, because in that place there is by no means need to stand and watch over the keeping of the flock, when the flock, even with the shepherd lying and resting under the shades, nevertheless freely runs about in the pastures. Happy the region in which the sheep enter and go forth at will, and there is none who frightens. Who will grant me to see you, and myself likewise to feed in the mountains together with those ninety-nine which are read to have been left there, when their shepherd graciously came down to the one which had wandered? (Matt. 18:12.) Securely, without doubt, he who did not at all hesitate to withdraw far away lies near, knowing that he would leave them in safety. Rightly does the bride sigh for that [place], rightly does she gape after the place of pasture together and of peace: but of quiet, but of security, but of exultation, but of admiration, but of wonder. For even me — wretched one, alas! acting from afar and saluting from afar — behold, the very recollection of it provokes to tears, plainly according to the affection and voice of those saying: 'Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, while we remembered you, Sion' (Ps. 137:1). It pleases [me] also to cry out, together with the bride and with the Prophet: 'Praise your God, Sion; because he has strengthened the bars of your gates, he has blessed your children in you.' 'Who has placed your borders peace, and fills you with the fat of the wheat' (Ps. 147:12-14). Who would not there vehemently desire to be fed, both on account of the peace, and on account of the fatness, and on account of the satiety? Nothing there is feared, nothing is loathed, nothing fails. The secure habitation is paradise, the sweet pasture is the Word, the abundance great exceedingly is eternity.
33.3: I too have the Word, but in the flesh; and truth is set before me, but in a sacrament. The angel is fed fat from the fat of the wheat, and is satisfied with the bare grain; but it behooves me in the meantime to be content with a certain husk of the sacrament, the bran of the flesh, the chaff of the letter, the veil of faith. And these are such things as, tasted, bring death, if they do not receive some seasoning, however little, from the firstfruits of the spirit. Truly death is in the pot for me, unless it be sweetened with the prophet's meal (2 Kgs. 4:40-41). Finally, without the spirit both the sacrament is taken to judgment, and the flesh profits nothing, and the letter kills, and faith is dead. But it is the spirit that gives life, that I may live in them. But however great an abundance of the spirit may fatten these things, not with entirely equal delight is the husk of the sacrament and the fat of the wheat, faith and vision, memory and presence, eternity and time, the face and the mirror, the image of God and the form of a servant taken. Surely in all these faith is rich for me, understanding poor. Truly, indeed, is the taste equal to understanding and to faith, since this one is in merit, that one in reward? Do you see, then, that there is as much distance between the pastures as also between the places; and that, as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so those dwelling in them abound in better goods?
33.4: Let us hasten, therefore, O sons, let us hasten to the safer place, to the sweeter pasture, to the more abundant and more fertile field. Let us hasten that we may dwell without fear, abound without failure, feast without loathing. For you, O Lord of hosts, who with tranquillity judge all things, also with security feed all things equally there. You yourself are the same, both Lord of armies and shepherd of sheep. Therefore you both feed and lie down at the same time, but not here. Finally, you stood when from heaven you looked down upon one of your little sheep — I speak of Stephen — being surrounded by wolves upon the earth (Acts 7:55). And therefore, I pray, tell me where you feed, where you lie down at midday; that is, all day: for that midday is the whole day, and it itself knows no evening. And therefore that day is better in your courts above thousands (Ps. 84:11), because it knows no setting. But it perhaps had a morning, when first, namely, the sanctified day shone upon us, through the bowels, to be sure, of the mercy of our God, in which the Orient from on high visited us (Luke 1:78). Truly then we received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple (Ps. 48:10), when in the midst of the shadow of death the morning light rose for us, and in the morning we saw the glory of the Lord. How many kings and prophets wished to see, and did not see? Why? unless because it was night, and that awaited morning had not yet come, to which mercy had been promised? Whence also someone prayed, saying: 'Make your mercy heard to me in the morning, because I have hoped in you' (Ps. 143:8).
33.5: For there was a certain dawn of this day, from the time when the sun of justice was announced to the earth through the archangel Gabriel, and the Virgin conceived God in the womb by the Holy Spirit, and the Virgin brought him forth, and thereafter, as long as he was seen on earth, and conversed with men. For to such a degree did the light appear small, through that whole time, and as truly the light of the dawn, that almost the whole world did not know that it was meanwhile day among men. Finally, if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8). And indeed to those few disciples themselves it was said: 'Yet a little light is in you' (John 12:35), because it was the dawn and the beginning, or rather the indication of the day, while the Sun as yet hid his rays, and did not at all scatter them over the earth. Paul also said that the night has gone before, but the day has drawn near (Rom. 13:12), signifying that there was then still so little light, that he preferred to say that the day had approached rather than come. But when did he say this? Truly when the Sun, turning back from the lower regions, had already lifted himself up to the heights of heaven. How much more when the likeness of the flesh of sin, like a dense cloud, covered the dawn, according to all the passions, to be sure, of our body, so that neither bitter death nor the shameful cross was wanting? how much more, I say, was the light then exceedingly small and thin, and such as seemed to proceed from the presence of the dawn rather than of the Sun?
33.6: It was therefore the dawn, and itself dark enough, that whole conversation, namely, of Christ upon the earth, until, setting and rising again, he drove away the dawn with the brighter light of his solar presence, and, morning being made, the night was swallowed up in victory. Finally you have: 'And very early in the morning, on the first day of the week, they come to the tomb, the sun being now risen' (Mark 16:2). Was it not morning, when the Sun rose? But he brought a new beauty from the resurrection, and a light more serene than usual, because although we had known him according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him (2 Cor. 5:16). It is written in the Prophet: 'He has put on beauty, he has put on strength, and has girded himself' (Ps. 93:1), because he shook off the infirmities of the flesh as certain clouds, putting on the robe of glory. Surely from that time on the Sun was lifted up, and, gradually at length diffusing his rays over the earth, began little by little to appear brighter everywhere, and to be felt hotter. But however much it may grow hot and grow strong, and multiply and extend his rays through the whole course of this our mortality — for he will be with us even to the consummation of the age (Matt. 28:20) — yet he will not reach the midday light, nor will he be seen now in that fullness of himself in which he is to be seen afterward, by those only, at least, whom he himself will deign [to bless] with this vision. O truly midday, fullness of fervor and of light, station of the sun, extermination of the shadows, drying up of the marshes, repulsion of the stench! O perpetual solstice, when the day will no longer decline! o midday light, o vernal temperateness, o summer comeliness, o autumnal abundance; and, lest I seem to have omitted something, o rest and wintry holiday! Or certainly, if you rather approve this, only winter then departed and withdrew. 'This place of such great clarity and peace and fullness,' she says, 'tell me, that as Jacob, still abiding in the body, saw the Lord face to face, and his soul was made safe (Gen. 32:30); or certainly as Moses saw him, not through figures and riddles, or through dreams, as other prophets, but in a manner plainly preeminent and untried by the rest, known to himself and to God (Num. 12:6-8); or as Isaiah, the eyes of his heart being revealed, saw him upon the lofty and elevated throne (Isa. 6:1); or even as Paul, rapt into paradise, heard unspeakable words (2 Cor. 12:4), and saw his Lord Jesus Christ with his own eyes; so I also may merit to contemplate you, feeding more abundantly, resting more securely, in your light and in your beauty, through an excess of mind.'
33.7: For you feed here also, but not in satiety; nor is it permitted to lie down, but one must stand and watch on account of the nightly fears. Alas! neither clear light, nor full refreshment, nor a safe dwelling: and therefore tell me where you feed, where you lie down at midday. You call me blessed when I hunger and thirst for justice (Matt. 5:6). What is this to the happiness of those who are filled with the good things of your house (Ps. 65:5), who feast and exult in the sight of God, and delight in gladness? (Ps. 68:4.) But even if I suffer something for justice' sake, you nevertheless pronounce me blessed (Matt. 5:9). And certainly to be fed where you fear to suffer has pleasantness, but not security. Moreover, to be fed and to suffer at the same time, is it not a troublesome pleasantness? All things here turn out for me short of the perfect, many things contrary to my wish, and nothing safe. When will you fill me with gladness with your countenance? (Ps. 16:11.) 'Your face, O Lord, I will seek' (Ps. 27:8). Your face is the midday. Tell me where you feed, where you lie down at midday. I know well enough where you feed without lying down; tell me where you feed and lie down. I am not ignorant of where you are wont to feed at other times; but I would wish to know where you feed at midday. For in the time, indeed, of my mortality, and in the place of my pilgrimage, I have surely been wont, under your keeping, to feed, and to feed in the law, and the prophets, and the psalms concerning you; and likewise in the evangelical pastures, and among the apostles I have also rested; frequently also from the deeds of the saints, and their words, and their writings, I have begged for myself food, and things pertaining to me, as I could; more frequently, however — because that was more at hand — I have eaten the bread of sorrow, and drunk the wine of compunction; and my tears have been made my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily: 'Where is your God?' (Ps. 42:4.) Save that from your table; for you have prepared in my sight a table against those who trouble me (Ps. 23:5): from that same [table], I say, by the benefit of your mercy, I receive that in which I in whatever way breathe again, as often as my soul is sad, and as often as it troubles me. These pastures I have known and frequented, you having been followed as shepherd; but tell me, I pray, also those which I do not know.
33.8: There are indeed also other shepherds, who say that they are your companions, and are not, having their own flocks, and their own borders filled with the pasture of death, in which they feed neither with you, nor through you, whose borders, to be sure, I have not entered, nor drawn near to them. These are they who say: 'Behold, here is Christ, behold, he is there' (Mark 13:21), promising the richer pastures of wisdom and knowledge, and belief is given to them, and many flow together to them, and they make them sons of Gehenna twice as much as themselves. Why is this, unless because there is not there the midday and the clear light, so that the truth is plainly known; and falsity is readily received for it on account of its verisimilitude, which is not easily discerned in the dark from the true, especially because stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant? (Prov. 9:17.) And therefore I pray that you would tell me where you feed, where you lie down at midday, that is, in the manifest [light], lest, being deceived, I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions, even as they themselves are wanderers, stable in no certainty of the truth, always learning, and never coming to the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim. 3:7). The bride [says] these things on account of the various and vain dogmas of the philosophers and heretics.
33.9: But to me it seems not only on account of these things, but even on account of the deceits of the invisible powers, such as are the seducing spirits, sitting in ambush, and preparing their arrows in the quiver, that they may shoot in the dark at the upright of heart: on account of these, I say, and chiefly, does that midday seem to me to be desired even for us, that in the clear light we may detect the cunning of the devil, and most easily discern that angel of Satan, who transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14), from our angel. For not otherwise are we sufficient to keep ourselves from the attack and the midday demon (Ps. 91:6), unless [we do so] equally in the midday light. Which demon, indeed, I judge for that reason to be called midday, because there are some of the number of the malignant who, although by the merit of their dark and obstinate will they are night, and perpetual night, yet know how to feign the day for deceiving, and not only the day, but even the midday, even as their prince, not content to be equal to God, also opposes, and is lifted up above everything that is said, or that is worshipped as God (2 Thess. 2:4). And so, unless there shines from on high into the heart of him whom perhaps some midday demon of this sort has received for tempting, the true midday, which would convict and expose the false, it will not be able to be guarded against at all, but it will tempt and supplant without doubt under the appearance of good, persuading, namely, evil instead of good to the incautious and improvident. And then the midday, that is, the greater clarity, appears, tempting, when it presents, as it were, the image of a greater good.
33.10: How often, for example, has it suggested to anticipate the vigils, that it might mock the sleeping one at the solemnities of the brethren? How often [has it suggested] to lengthen the fasts, that it might render him the more useless to the divine offices, the weaker he was? How often, envying those well advancing in the monasteries, has it persuaded [them] to seek the desert under the pretext, as it were, of a greater purity; and the wretches at length knew how true is the word which they had read in vain: 'Woe to the one who is alone, because if he falls, he has none to lift him up'? (Eccles. 4:10.) How often has it incited to the work of the hands more than was needful; and, broken in strength, has rendered [him] unfit for the other regular exercises? To how many has it persuaded no small bodily exercise — which, according to the Apostle, profits for a little (1 Tim. 4:8) — and defrauded them of piety? Finally, you yourselves have experienced how certain ones — I say it to the shame of those who before could not be restrained, so were they carried in a vehement spirit to all things — afterward came to such great sloth, that, according to that word of the Apostle, having begun in the spirit, they are now consummated in the flesh (Gal. 3:3): how shamefully they made a covenant with their bodies, to which they had before declared a cruel war. You may see, O shame! that they importunately seek superfluous things, who before most obstinately refused necessary things.
