And yet, if any perchance endure unconquered in their own obstinacy, abstaining more indiscreetly, and disturbing by their notable singularity those with whom they ought to dwell of one manner in the house — truly I hardly know whether they think they retain piety, since men of this sort seem to me to have cast it off even farther. For they who, wise in their own eyes, have decreed within themselves to acquiesce neither in counsel nor in precept — let them see what they answer, not to me, but to him saying: 'Because to resist is as the sin of divination, and to refuse to acquiesce is as the crime of idolatry.' But he had premised that obedience is better than sacrifice, and to hearken rather than to offer the fat of rams (1 Sam. 15:22-23), that is, the abstinence of the obstinate. Whence the Lord through the Prophet: 'Shall I eat,' he says, 'the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats'? (Ps. 50:13) signifying that the fasts of the proud or the unclean would by no means be acceptable to him.
33.11: But truly I fear, lest, condemning the superstitious, we seem to loosen the reins to the gluttonous; and they hear to their own peril that which is said to these for their remedy. Wherefore hear, both parties, that there are four kinds of temptations, and that they themselves are so described to us in the prophetic discourse. 'With his shield,' he says, 'his truth will surround you; you shall not fear the nightly terror, the arrow flying in the day, the business walking about in darkness, the attack and the midday demon' (Ps. 91:5-6). Nevertheless, attend, you others also, to that which I hope will profit all. That we all feel and have felt in ourselves, we who are converted to the Lord, which holy Scripture says: 'Son, coming to the service of God, stand in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation' (Sir. 2:1). And so, the beginnings of our conversion, according to, indeed, the account of common experience, the first fear besets, which the horror of a straiter life, and the austerity of unused discipline, immediately brings upon those entering. And that fear is called nightly, either because night in the Scriptures is wont to designate adversities, or because that for the sake of which we undertake to suffer adversities is not yet revealed. For if that day shone, in whose light we would see equally both the labors and the rewards, there would be no fear at all of any labors before the desire of the rewards; since it would appear in the clear light that the sufferings of this time are not worthy [to be compared] with the future glory which will be revealed in us (Rom. 8:18). But now, since they are hidden from our eyes, and it is night in the meantime in this respect, we are assuredly tempted by the nightly fear, and for the good things which we do not see, we dread to bear the adversities which are present. One must therefore watch and pray in the first place, for those entering, against this first temptation, lest, being suddenly preoccupied by faint-heartedness of spirit and by a storm, they start back from a good work begun — which God forbid!
33.12: But, this temptation being overcome, let us nevertheless arm ourselves also against the praises of men, which chiefly take their matter from a praiseworthy life. Otherwise we shall lie open to the wound of the arrow flying in the day, which is vainglory. For fame flies; and therefore [it shoots] in the day, because [it springs] from the works of light. If this is blown away as an empty breeze, it remains that something more solid be brought forward from the riches and honors of the world, if perhaps he who does not care for praises should covet dignities. And see if this order of tempting was not kept in our Lord, to whom, after the precipice suggested for the sake of mere vanity, all the kingdoms of the world were shown and offered (Matt. 4:6, 8). You, therefore, by the example of the Lord, refuse these also. Otherwise it is necessary that you be circumvented by the business walking about in darkness, which is hypocrisy. For that [business] descends from ambition, and its dwelling is in darkness: inasmuch as it hides what it is, and feigns what it is not. But it traffics at all times, keeping the form of piety for hiding itself, but claiming its power, and buying honors.
33.13: The last temptation is the midday demon, which is wont to lie in wait chiefly for the perfect, who, namely, like men of virtue, have overcome all things: pleasures, favors, honors. For what now remains to him who tempts, in which he could fight openly against men of this sort? He comes, therefore, hidden, who does not dare [to come] manifest; and him whom he has sufficiently experienced to abhor every open evil, he strives to supplant with a false good. But they who can say with the Apostle: 'For we are not ignorant of his devices' (2 Cor. 2:11), the more they profit, the more anxious they are to beware of that snare. Hence it is that Mary is troubled at the angelic salutation (Luke 1:29), suspecting deceit, if I am not mistaken; and Joshua does not receive the friend angel before he has learned that he is a friend. Finally, he asks whether he is his own, or of the adversaries (Josh. 5:13-15), as one who has experienced the wiles of the midday demon. The apostles also, once while they labored in rowing, the wind being contrary and tossing the little ship, seeing the Lord walking upon the sea, and thinking him to be a phantom, so that they cried out for fear — did they not put forward an open suspicion of the midday demon? And remember the Scripture saying that in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea. Let this temptation, then, be feared in the fourth, that is, at last in the supreme place; and the more one sees himself to stand on the summit, let him understand that he must beware so much the more vigilantly of the attack and the midday demon. Moreover, to the disciples the true midday manifested itself in that which they heard: 'It is I; do not fear' (Matt. 14:25-27); and the suspicion of the false was driven away from them. Would that also to us, as often as disguised falsity strives to creep in, the true midday, rising from on high, would send forth his light and his truth to expose it, and would divide the light from the darkness, that we be not marked by the prophet as those who put light for darkness, and darkness for light (Isa. 5:20).
33.14: Still, unless the length of the discourse be wearisome, I will try to assign these four temptations, in their order, to the very body of Christ, which is the Church. And behold, I run through them as briefly as I can. See the primitive Church, whether it was not first pervaded too sharply by the nightly fear. For it was night, when everyone who killed the saints thought that he was offering a service to God. But, this temptation having been overcome and the storm calmed, it became renowned, and, according to the promise made to it, in a short time raised up to the glory of the ages. And the enemy, grieving that he had been frustrated, turned himself cunningly from the nightly fear to the arrow flying in the day, and wounded in it certain ones of the Church. And vain men rose up, greedy of glory, and wished to make a name for themselves: and, going out of the Church, they long afflicted that same mother of theirs with diverse and perverse dogmas. But this pest too was driven away by the wisdom of the saints, as also the first was by the patience of the martyrs.
33.15: Behold, these times are free, indeed, by God's mercy, from that twofold malice; but plainly foul with the business walking about in darkness. Woe to this generation, of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy! if however it ought to be called hypocrisy, which can no longer hide itself by reason of its abundance, and does not seek to do so by reason of its impudence. A putrid corruption creeps today through the whole body of the Church; and the wider it spreads, the more desperate; and the more dangerous, the more inward. For if an open heretical enemy rose up, he would be sent outside and would wither; if a violent enemy, he would perhaps hide himself from him. But now whom will it cast out, or from whom will it hide itself? All are friends, and all are enemies; all necessary, and all adversaries; all domestics, and none peaceful; all neighbors, and all seek the things that are their own. They are ministers of Christ, and they serve Antichrist. Honored, they walk proudly of the Lord's goods, who do not pay honor to the Lord. Thence is that harlot-like splendor which you daily see, the stage-player dress, the royal array. Thence gold in bridles, in saddles and spurs; and spurs shine more than altars. Thence splendid tables, both with foods and with cups; thence feastings and drunkennesses; thence the harp, and the lyre, and the flute; thence overflowing winepresses, and full storehouses, belching out from this to that. Thence perfume vessels, thence stuffed purses. For such things they wish to be, and are, the provosts of churches, deans, archdeacons, bishops, archbishops. For these are not granted to merit, but to that business which walks about in darkness.
33.16: It was foretold long ago, and now the time of fulfillment has come: 'Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter' (Isa. 38:17). Bitter before in the death of the martyrs, more bitter afterward in the conflict of the heretics, most bitter now in the manners of the household. It can neither drive them out, nor flee them; so much have they grown strong, and have been multiplied beyond number. Internal and incurable is the wound of the Church; and therefore in peace its bitterness is most bitter. But in what peace? And there is peace, and there is no peace. Peace from the pagans, and peace from the heretics; but not, to be sure, from the sons. The voice of one lamenting in this time: 'I have nourished and raised up sons, but they themselves have despised me' (Isa. 1:2). They have despised and stained me by a base life, by base gain, by base traffic, by the business, finally, that walks about in darkness. It remains that the midday demon now arise from the midst, to seduce those, if any remain in Christ, who still abide in their simplicity. For it has swallowed up the rivers of the wise, and the torrents of the powerful, and has confidence that the Jordan should flow into its mouth (Job 40:18), that is, the simple and humble who are in the Church. For he himself is the Antichrist, who will feign himself not only the day, but even the midday, and will be lifted up above everything that is said, or that is worshipped as God: whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the spirit of his mouth, and will destroy with the brightness of his coming (2 Thess. 2:4, 8), as being the true and eternal Midday, the spouse and advocate of the Church, who is God blessed above all things forever. Amen.

34.1: If you know not yourself, O fairest among women, go forth, and depart after the flocks of your companions, and feed your kids beside the tents of the shepherds (Song 1:7). Of old the holy Moses, because he presumed much upon the grace and intimacy which he had found with God, aspired to a certain great vision, so that he would say to God: If I have found grace in your eyes, show me yourself. But he received in place of it a vision far inferior, from which nevertheless he might at length attain to that which he wished (Exod. 33:13-23). The sons of Zebedee also, walking in the simplicity of their heart, dared something great themselves; but they were nonetheless reduced to the step by which one had to ascend (Matt. 20:21-23). So too now the bride, since she seems to ask a great thing, is indeed checked by a rather severe answer, but clearly a useful and faithful one. For one striving toward higher things must think humbly of himself, lest, while he is raised above himself, he fall away from himself, unless he has been firmly established in himself by true humility. And because the greatest things are by no means obtained except by the merit of humility, therefore he who is to be advanced is humbled by correction, and by humility merits. You therefore, when you see yourself humbled, hold that as a sign, altogether for the good, as an argument of approaching grace. For just as the heart is exalted before ruin (Prov. 16:18), so likewise before exaltation it is humbled; surely you read both, namely that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), and did he not finally take care first to humble his servant Job in many and strict questionings, and so to prepare the way for the blessing (Job 38ff), when after his notable triumph he judged that his so great and so proven patience was to be rewarded with a bountiful blessing?
34.2: But it is too little that when God humbles us by himself we then willingly accept it, unless when he does this also through another, we be of like mind. Wherefore receive a marvelous example of this thing from holy David. Once he was also cursed by a servant; but he did not even feel the heaped-up injury, because he foresaw the grace. 'What is there to me and to you,' he says, 'sons of Zeruiah?' (2 Sam. 16:10). O truly a man after God's own heart, who thought that he should be angry rather with one avenging than with one reproaching! Whence also with a secure conscience he spoke: If I have rendered evil to those rendering evil to me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies (Ps. 7:4). He therefore forbade that the reviling curser be prohibited, counting curses as gain. And he adds: The Lord sent him to curse David (2 Sam. 16:10). Truly according to God's own heart, who was bearing the sentence from the heart of God. The cursing tongue raged, and he attended to what God was doing in secret. The voice of the curser was in his ears, and his mind bent itself toward blessing. Is God [really] in the mouth of the blasphemer? God forbid! But he used him to humble David. Nor did it escape the Prophet; for he to whom God had manifested the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom (Ps. 51:8) therefore says: It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I may learn your justifications (Ps. 119:71).
34.3: Do you see that humility justifies us? Humility, I said; and not: humbling. How many are humbled who are not humble? Some are humbled with rancor, others patiently, others even willingly. The first are guilty, the following guiltless, the last just. Although even innocence is a portion of justice, yet its consummation is in the humble; but he who can say: It is good for me that you have humbled me, that one is truly humble. He who tolerates unwillingly cannot say this; even less he who murmurs. We promise grace to neither of these because he is humbled: although indeed these two differ far from one another, and the one indeed in his patience possesses his soul, the other perishes in his murmur. But in truth although the one [deserves] wrath, neither however merits grace; because God gives grace not to the humbled but to the humble. Now he is humble who converts humiliation into humility, and he is the one who says to God: It is good for me that you have humbled me. To no one at all is what he bears patiently good, but plainly troublesome. But we know that God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7). Whence also when we fast we are commanded to anoint our head with oil, and to wash our face (Matt. 6:17), that our good work may namely be seasoned with a certain spiritual joy, and our whole burnt offering become fat. For only a glad and free humility merits the grace which it offers. For humility which shall have been forced or extorted, such as indeed it is in that patient man who possesses his soul; this, I say, humility, although it obtains life by reason of patience, yet by reason of sadness will not have grace. For that saying of Scripture does not befit him who is such: Let the humble glory in his exaltation (James 1:9); because he is not humbled of his own accord, nor willingly.
34.4: But do you wish to see the humble man rightly glorying, and truly worthy of glory? Gladly, he says, will I glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me (2 Cor. 12:9). He does not say that he bears his infirmities patiently; but even to glory, and gladly to glory in them, proving that it is even good for him that he is humbled; nor that it suffices altogether to possess his soul as one humbled patiently, unless he also receive grace as one humbled willingly. Hear indeed from this the general rule: Every one who humbles himself, he says, shall be exalted (Luke 14:11). He signifies indeed that not every humility is to be exalted, but that only which comes of the will, not of sadness, nor of necessity. For neither, on the contrary, will every one who is exalted be humbled; but only he who exalts himself shall be humbled, namely by reason of a voluntary vanity. So therefore not he who is humbled, but he who humbles himself of his own accord, shall be exalted; certainly by reason of the merit of the will. For grant that the material of humility is ministered by another, for example, reproaches, losses, punishments; yet not therefore will he be rightly said to be humbled by another rather than by himself, who shall have decreed to undergo all those things with a silent and glad conscience for the sake of God.
34.5: But where are we advancing to? Patiently, as I perceive, you bear the excess in the word concerning humility and patience; but let us return to the place from which we have digressed. For that fell to us by occasion of the answer by which the bridegroom judged that the bride presuming great things was to be checked, and not to her folly; but that surely from it occasion of a more approved and greater humility might be given, by which she might be rendered worthier of greater things, and more capable of those very things which she asked. Nevertheless because we are still at the doors of the present chapter, let us begin the discussion of it, if you please, at the beginning of another sermon, especially lest the words of the bridegroom be either rehearsed with weariness, or be heard. May he avert that from his servants, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all God blessed forever. Amen.

35.1: If you do not know yourself, he says, go forth (Song 1:7). A hard and harsh rebuke it is, that he says: go forth. For servants are wont to hear this word from masters who are very angry and indignant, or handmaids from their mistresses, when they have grievously offended them: Depart hence, depart from me, go forth from my sight and from this house. With this word, then, hard and bitter enough, and all too reproachful, does the bridegroom now use against his beloved, under a condition, however, if she has failed to know herself. For nothing more powerful or more effectual for the terrifying said he could direct against her, than to threaten that she should go forth. Which you too can observe, if you attend well to whence and whither she is bidden to go forth. For whence, do you think, and whither, except from the spirit to the flesh, from the goods of the soul to worldly desires, from the inward rest of the mind to the clamor of the world and the disquiet of outward cares? In all of which there is nothing but labor and sorrow, and affliction of spirit. For what soul, having once learned and received from the Lord to enter into herself, and to sigh in her inmost parts for the presence of God 鈥?for God is a spirit, and those who seek him must walk in the spirit and not in the flesh, so as to live according to the flesh 鈥?such a soul, I say, I do not know whether she would deem the very gehenna itself, were it to be experienced for a time, more horrible and more grievous, than, after having once tasted the sweetness of this spiritual study, to go forth again to the enticements, or rather to the annoyances, of the flesh, and to repeat the insatiable curiosity of the senses, the Ecclesiastes saying: The eye is not filled with seeing, nor the ear with hearing (Eccl. 1:8). For hear a man who has experienced what we speak: You are good, he says, O Lord, to those who hope in you, to the soul that seeks you (Lam. 3:25). If any one should try to turn that holy soul away from this good, I think she would have taken it no otherwise than if she saw herself cast down from paradise, and from the very entrance of glory. Hear yet another also like to this: My heart has said to you, he says, my face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I will seek (Ps. 27:8). Whence he also said: But for me it is good to cleave to God (Ps. 73:28); and likewise, speaking to his own soul, he says: Turn, O my soul, into your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you (Ps. 116:7). I say, therefore, to you: there is nothing which any one who has once received this benefit fears so much as that, being forsaken by grace, he should have need to go forth again to the consolations of the flesh 鈥?nay, its desolations 鈥?and again to endure the tumults of the carnal senses.
35.2: Terrible, therefore, and all too fearful is the threatening: Go forth, and feed your kids. That is: know yourself unworthy of that your familiar and sweet contemplation of things heavenly, intelligible, divine. Wherefore go forth from my sanctuary, your heart, where you were wont sweetly to drink in the secret and sacred senses of truth and wisdom; and rather, as one of the worldly, entangle yourself in feeding and delighting the senses of your flesh. For by kids (which signify sin, and are to be set on the left hand in the judgment) he means the wandering and wanton senses of the body, through which sin, like death through the windows, entered into the soul. To which also that which follows in the Scripture well agrees: Beside the tents of the shepherds. For kids are not fed above, like lambs, but beside the tents of the shepherds. For shepherds, who are true shepherds, although they have tents of the earth and on the earth 鈥?namely, their bodies 鈥?in the days in which they now serve as soldiers, are nevertheless wont to feed the Lord's flocks not from the earth, but from heavenly pastures: for they preach to them not their own will, but the will of the Lord. But kids, which are the senses of the body, do not seek heavenly things; but beside the tents of the shepherds, namely among all the sensible goods of this world, which is the region of bodies, they take whence they may not so much satisfy as irritate their desires.
35.3: A shameful change of pursuits! that she to whom it had before been her study to feed her wandering and exiled soul with sacred meditations, as with heavenly goods, to search out the good pleasure of God and the mysteries of his will, to penetrate the heavens with devotion, and to go round in her mind the mansions above, to greet the fathers and the apostles and the choirs of prophets, to admire the triumphs of the martyrs, and to marvel at the most beautiful orders of the angels, should now, with all these set aside, enslave herself to the shameful servitude of the body, to obey the flesh, to satisfy the belly and the palate, and to beg over the whole earth, whence, out of that figure of this world which passes away, she may in some measure console her ever hungry curiosity. Let my eyes bring down streams of water over such a soul, which, when it was nourished in saffron, at length embraces dung (Lam. 4:5). For, according to the saying of the blessed man, he who had not children fed the barren, and did no good to the widow (Job 24:21). And see, that not simply: go forth; but, go forth, he says, and go after the flocks of your companions, and feed your kids. In which, as it seems to me, he admonishes us of some great thing. What is that? Alas! that the excellent creature, having long ago been made from the flock, and now miserably rushing to the worse, is not at least permitted to remain among the flocks, but is bidden to go after. How, you ask? How you read: Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he is compared to the senseless beasts, and is made like to them (Ps. 49:13). Behold how, from the flock, the excellent creature was made. I think the beasts would say, if it were lawful to speak: Behold, Adam has been made as one of us (Gen. 3:22). When he was in honor, he says. In what honor, you ask? He dwelt in paradise, and his conversation was in the place of delight. He felt nothing of annoyance, nothing of want, hedged about with fragrant fruits, propped up with flowers, crowned with glory and honor, and set over the works of the hands of the Maker; but more by the mark of the divine likeness he excelled; and his lot and fellowship was with the people of angels, and with all the host of the heavenly army.
35.4: But he changed this glory of God into the likeness of a calf that eats hay. Hence it is that the bread of angels was made hay set in a manger, set before us as before beasts of burden. For the Word was made flesh (John 1:14), and, according to the prophet: All flesh is hay. But that hay was by no means dried up, nor did the flower fall from it, because the Spirit of the Lord rested upon it. For on this account the end of all flesh once came, because the spirit of life had departed. At length he says: My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh (Gen. 6:3). Understand that in this place by the name of flesh a vice is signified, not nature: for it is not nature that expels the spirit, but vice. Therefore, on account of vice, all flesh is hay, and all its glory like the flower of hay. The hay is dried up, he says, and the flower fell; but not that flower which came up from the rod and root of Jesse, because the Spirit of the Lord rested upon him (Isa. 11:1-2); nor that hay which the Word was made, for what follows in the prophet: But the word of the Lord abides forever (Isa. 40:6-8). For if the Word is hay, and the Word abides forever, the hay also must needs abide forever. Otherwise how does it give eternal life, if it does not itself abide forever? For he says: If any one eat of this bread, he shall live forever. And what bread he means, he opens when he adds: And the bread which I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world (John 6:52). How, then, is that not eternal, by which one lives eternally?
35.5: But recall now with me the voice of the Son speaking to the Father in the psalm: You will not give, he says, your Holy One to see corruption (Ps. 16:10). No doubt but that he speaks of the body, which lay lifeless in the sepulcher. For this holy thing the angel too who announced to the Virgin said, saying: And that which shall be born of you shall be called holy, the Son of God (Luke 1:35). In what way, then, could that holy hay see corruption, which, sprung from the incorrupt womb in the perpetual greenness of vernant pastures, could fix upon itself even the eager gazes of the angels, to be delighted insatiably? Let the hay surely lose its greenness, if Mary has lost her virginity. Therefore the food of man changed itself into the fodder of a beast, man having been changed into a beast. Alas, a sad and tearful change! that man, the inhabitant of paradise, lord of the earth, citizen of heaven, intimate of the Lord of hosts, brother of the blessed spirits, and coheir of the heavenly powers, should by a sudden conversion have found himself, because of his infirmity, lying in a stable, and, because of his beastlike likeness, needing hay, and, because of his untamed savageness, tied to the manger, as it is written: With bit and bridle bind fast their jaws, who do not draw near to you (Ps. 32:9). Yet acknowledge, O ox, your owner; and you, O ass, the manger of your lord; that the prophets of God may be found faithful, who foretold these wonders of God. Know, O beast, him whom as a man you did not know; adore in the stable him whom you fled from in paradise; honor the manger whose command you despised; eat the hay, whom as bread, even angelic bread, you loathed.
35.6: But what, you ask, is the cause of so great a casting down? Truly, that man, when he was in honor, did not understand. What did he not understand? He does not say: let us say. Placed in honor, he did not understand that he was clay, delighted with the pinnacle of honor; and straightway he experienced in himself what a man of the sons of captivity, after so long a time, both prudently observed and truly uttered, saying: He who thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself (Gal. 6:3). Woe to the wretch, that there was not one who even then would say to him: Why do you exalt yourself, dust and ashes? (Sir. 10:9.) Hence the excellent creature was mingled with the flock, hence the likeness of God was changed into a beastly likeness, hence fellowship with the beasts was entered into in place of the companionship of angels. Do you see how this ignorance is to be fled by us, from which so many thousands of evils have come upon our whole race? For he says that on this account man is compared to the senseless beasts, because he did not understand. Ignorance, therefore, is to be avoided in every way, lest perhaps, if we are found still without understanding even after the vexation, evils much more numerous and more grievous than the former find us, and it be said of us: We have cured Babylon, and she is not healed (Jer. 51:9). Rightly indeed, because not even the vexation gave understanding to the hearing.
35.7: And see whether perhaps even on this account the bridegroom, when he would deter the beloved from ignorance with so great a thunder of reproach, did not for that reason say: Go forth with the flocks; or: Go forth to the flocks; but: Go forth, he says, after the flocks of your companions. Why this? Surely that he might thereby show the second ignorance to be more to be feared and more to be ashamed of than the former, because that one made man equal to the beasts, this one also [made him] after them. For men, indeed, on account of their ignorance being ignored 鈥?that is, reprobated 鈥?have to stand at that terrible judgment, and to be delivered to the perpetual fire, but not also the beasts. Nor is there doubt that it will be worse for those who shall be so, than for those who shall not be at all. It had been better for him, he says, if that man had not been born (Mark 14:21). Not, of course, if he had not been born at all, but if he had not been born a man; but, for example, a beast, or some other creature: which, since it would have no judgment, would not come to judgment, and through this neither to punishment. Let the rational soul know, then, which blushes for the former ignorance, that the beasts have as companions, in enjoying, namely, the goods of the earth; but that it will not likewise have them as sharers in enduring the torments of gehenna; and that at length even from the very flocks of its companion beasts it is to be thrust out with disgrace; and that it will not even go with them any longer, but plainly after, when, while they feel nothing evil, it itself shall be exposed to all evils: from which it shall not be delivered forever, if indeed it shall have added to this a second ignorance. Man, therefore, goes forth, and goes alone after the flocks of his companions, when he alone is thrust back into the lower hell. Does it not seem to you that he holds the later place, who, with hands and feet bound, is cast into the outer darkness? And the last state of that man shall indeed be worse than the former, when he who was before made equal to the beasts is now even put after them.
35.8: I think that even in the present life, if you observe well, you will judge that a man goes behind the beasts. Or does it not indeed seem to you that a man who flourishes in reason, and does not live by reason, is in a certain manner more beastly than the very beasts? For a beast, indeed, if it does not govern itself by reason, has an excuse from nature, by which this office was utterly denied to it; but man does not, to whom it was given as a special prerogative by her. Rightly, therefore, is man judged to go forth for this very reason, and to go after the gregarious animals, because, the only animal of this sort, by a degenerate way of life transgressing the laws of nature, being possessed of reason, he imitates in manners and affections those lacking reason. Man is therefore convicted of going after the flocks, now indeed by the depravation of nature, but afterward also by the extremity of punishment.
35.9: Behold, so shall man be cursed who shall have been found to have the ignorance of God. Shall I say of God, or of himself? Both without doubt: each ignorance is damnable, either one suffices for perdition. Do you wish to know that it is so? But concerning God you by no means doubt, if only it is established for you that there is no other eternal life, than to know the Father, the true God, and him whom he sent, Jesus Christ (John 17:3). Hear, then, the bridegroom plainly and openly condemning in the soul even the ignorance of the soul. For what does he say? Not of course: if you ignore God, but: If you do not know yourself, he says, and so forth; it is clear, therefore, that he who is ignorant shall be ignored (1 Cor. 14:38), whether it happen that he be ignorant of himself or of God. Concerning which twofold ignorance there will be for us 鈥?if God sets his hand to it 鈥?a most useful discussion. Not now, however; lest, wearied, and the customary prayer not sent before, either I pursue a necessary matter less diligently, or you hear less attentively things which are to be undertaken with great desire. For if bodily food, when, without appetite and satiated, you take it, not only does not profit, but even harms very much; much more the bread of the soul, taken with loathing, will bring not the nourishment of knowledge, but rather the torment of conscience. May the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is over all, God blessed forever, avert this from us. Amen.

36.1: Behold me, bound to my promise; behold me, bound to your desires; behold me also, bound to God by the debt of my service. By a threefold reason, as you see, I am urged to speak; by the truth of my engagement, by brotherly charity, by the fear of the Lord. If I am silent, my mouth will condemn me. What, then, if I speak? Truly I fear the same judgment, lest, namely, speaking and yet not doing, my mouth condemn me in like manner. Help me with your prayers, that I may always be able both to speak the things that are fitting and to fulfill in deed the things I speak. You are not ignorant that a sermon on ignorance is today set before us, or rather on ignorances; for two, if you remember, have been proposed, one of ours, and the other of God; and we have warned that both are to be avoided, because both are damnable. It remains that I make this same thing clearer, and set it forth more fully. But first I think it must be asked whether all ignorance is damnable; and to me indeed it seems not to be; for not all ignorance condemns, but that there are many and numberless things which it is lawful not to know without diminution of salvation. For example, if you are ignorant of the craft of the smith, or of the carpenter, or of the mason, and whatever arts there are of this sort, which are exercised by men for the uses of this present life, does it in any way hinder salvation? Even without all those arts which are called liberal (although they are both learned and practiced with more honorable and more useful studies), very many men have been made safe, pleasing in morals and in works: how many the Apostle enumerates in the Epistle to the Hebrews, made beloved, not in the knowledge of letters, but in a pure conscience and a faith not feigned (Heb. 11). They all pleased God in their life, by the merits of life, not of knowledge. Peter, and Andrew, and the sons of Zebedee, and all the other fellow-disciples, were not taken from the school of rhetoricians or of philosophers; and nevertheless the Savior through them worked salvation in the midst of the earth. Not in the wisdom which would have been in them more than in all living things (Eccl. 1:16) (as a certain holy one confessed of himself), but in their faith and gentleness he made them safe, even holy, even teachers. Finally, they made known to the world the ways of life, and not in the sublimity of speech, or in the learned words of human wisdom, but as it pleased God by the foolishness of their preaching to save those who believe, because the world in its wisdom did not know him (1 Cor. 2:1; 1:17, 21).
36.2: Perhaps I may seem excessive in the reproach of knowledge, and, as it were, to reprove the learned, and to forbid the study of letters. God forbid! I am not unaware how much its learned men have profited and do profit the Church, whether for refuting those who are against us, or for instructing the simple. Finally, I have read: Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you, that you may not discharge for me the priesthood (Hos. 4:6); I have read: They who have been learned will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and they who instruct many unto justice, like stars in perpetuities everlasting (Dan. 12:3). But I also know where I have read: Knowledge puffs up (1 Cor. 8:1); and again: He who increases knowledge increases also sorrow (Sir. 1:18). You see that there is a difference of knowledges, when one is puffing up, the other grieving. But I would wish you to know which of these seems more useful or more necessary to salvation, that which swells or that which grieves. But I do not doubt that you prefer the grieving to the swelling, because the health which the swelling feigns, the grief demands. But he who demands approaches salvation; because he who asks receives (Luke 11:10). Finally, he who heals the contrite of heart abhors the puffed up, Wisdom saying that God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). And the Apostle was saying: But I say, through the grace which has been given to me, to all who are among you, not to be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety (Rom. 12:3). He does not forbid being wise, but being wise beyond what is fitting. But what is it to be wise unto sobriety? To observe most watchfully what it is fitting to know more, or first. For the time is short. But every knowledge, in itself, is good, provided that it be supported by truth; but you, who, on account of the brevity of time, hasten to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, take care rather and more to know those things which you have perceived to be nearer to salvation. Do not the physicians of bodies determine to choose a portion of medicine in the taking of foods, what first, what later, and in what manner each thing ought to be taken? For, although it is agreed that the foods which God created are good, you nevertheless, if you do not observe measure and order in taking them, plainly render them not good for yourself. Therefore what I say of foods, think this also of knowledges.
36.3: But I better send you to the Master. For this opinion is not ours, but his; nay rather also ours, since it is of the Truth. He who thinks himself to know something, says he, does not yet know how it behooves him to know (1 Cor. 8:2). You see that he does not approve one who knows many things, if he has not known the manner of knowing. You see, I say, how he places the fruit and the usefulness of knowledge in the manner of knowing? What, then, does he call the manner of knowing? What, unless that you know in what order, with what zeal, and to what end each thing ought to be known? In what order: that that be first which is riper for salvation; with what zeal: that that be more ardently pursued which is more vehemently for love; to what end: that it be not for vain glory, or curiosity, or anything like it, but only for the edification of yourself or of your neighbor. For there are those who wish to know to this end only, that they may know; and it is shameful curiosity. And there are those who wish to know, that they themselves may be known; and it is shameful vanity. These indeed will not escape the sneering satirist, singing to him who is of such a sort: Your knowledge is nothing, unless another knows that you know this (Persius, Satire 1, v. 27). And there are likewise those who wish to know in order to sell their knowledge; for example, for money, for honors; and it is shameful gain. But there are also those who wish to know, in order to edify; and it is charity. And likewise those who wish to know, in order to be edified; and it is prudence.
36.4: Of all these, only the last two are not found in the abuse of knowledge, inasmuch as they wish to understand to this end, that they may do well. Finally: A good understanding to all who do it (Ps. 111:10). Let all the rest hear: To him who knows good and does not do it, it is sin to him (James 4:17); as if by a likeness he were saying: To him who takes food and does not digest it, it is harmful to him. For undigested food, and that which does not have a good digestion, generates bad humors, and corrupts the body, and does not nourish. So too, much knowledge taken into the stomach of the soul, which is the memory, if it has not been digested by the fire of charity, and thus transfused and digested through certain members of the soul, namely the morals and the acts, so that it itself, of the good things it has known, life and morals bearing witness, becomes good; will not that knowledge be reputed unto sin, as food turned into evil and harmful humors? Or is not a bad humor sin; are not bad humors evil morals? But will not he who is of such a sort, knowing, namely, good and not doing it, endure swellings and torments in his conscience? Or will he not have in himself the answer of death and damnation as many times as the word which God spoke has come to mind, that the servant knowing the will of his Lord, and not doing the worthy things, will be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47)? And see lest perhaps the prophet would lament in the person of such a soul, saying: I grieve for my belly, I grieve for my belly (Jer. 4:19). Except that the very repetition seems to hint at a twofold sense, so that besides this which we have said we may also seek another. For I think that the Prophet could have said this in his own person, that, namely, full of knowledge, and burning with charity, and altogether wishing to pour it out, he would not find one who would care to hear; and so his knowledge was to himself, as it were, a burden, which he could not communicate. The pious doctor of the Church accordingly laments both those who despise to know how one ought to live, and those who, knowing, nevertheless live badly. And this, for the reason that the Prophet repeats the same word.
36.5: Do you now perceive how truly the Apostle felt that knowledge puffs up? I wish, therefore, that the soul first of all know itself, which the reason both of usefulness and of order demands. And indeed of order, because what we are is first for us; but of usefulness, because such knowledge does not puff up, but humbles; and it is a certain preparation for edifying. For unless upon the stable foundation of humility, a spiritual building can in no way stand. Moreover, for humbling itself the soul can find nothing more lively or more fitting than if it finds itself in truth: only let it not dissemble, let there be no guile in its spirit, let it set itself before its own face, and not be drawn away to turn itself from itself. Thus beholding itself in the clear light of truth, will it not find itself in the region of dissimilitude; and, the wretched soul sighing, which now will not be able to hide that it is truly wretched, will it not with the Prophet cry to the Lord: In your truth you have humbled me (Ps. 119:75)? For how will it not be truly humbled in this true knowledge of itself, when it has perceived itself weighed down with sins, burdened with the mass of this mortal body, entangled with earthly cares, infected with the dregs of carnal desires, blind, bent, weak, involved in many errors, exposed to a thousand perils, trembling with a thousand fears, anxious with a thousand difficulties, liable to a thousand suspicions, afflicted with a thousand necessities, prone to vices, powerless for virtues? Whence, to this one, now the haughtiness of the eyes, whence to lift up the head? Will it not rather be turned in its affliction, while it is pierced with the thorn (Ps. 32:4)? It will turn, I say, to tears, it will turn to lamentations and groans, it will turn to the Lord, and in humility it will cry: Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you (Ps. 41:5). Moreover, turned to the Lord it will receive consolation, because he is the Father of mercies, and the God of all consolation.
36.6: As long as I look upon myself, my eye abides in bitterness. But if I look up and lift my eyes to the help of the divine mercy, the joyful vision of God will soon temper the bitter vision of myself, to whom I also say: My soul is troubled within myself, therefore I will be mindful of you (Ps. 42:7). Nor is it a slight vision of God to experience him as kind and to be entreated, as indeed he is benign and merciful, and excellent above malice (Joel 2:13), inasmuch as his nature is goodness, and to whom it is proper always to have mercy and to spare. By such experience, therefore, and in such order does God become healthfully known, when man has first known himself placed in necessity, and will cry to the Lord, and he will hear him, and will say: I will deliver you, and you will glorify me (Ps. 50:15). And in this manner the knowledge of yourself will be a step to the knowledge of God; and from his image, which is renewed in you, he himself will be seen, while you, indeed, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord with confidence, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18).
36.7: But now at length observe how each knowledge is necessary to you for salvation, so that you cannot lack either one with salvation. For, if you are ignorant of yourself, you will not have the fear of God in you, nor humility. But whether you presume concerning salvation without the fear of God and without humility, you will see. You have done well, by grunting, to signify that you by no means think so, nay rather that you are not so foolish, lest we linger on that which is plain. But attend to the rest. Or should we rather pause on account of the sleepy ones? I thought to fulfill in one sermon what I promised concerning the twofold ignorance; and I would have done so, unless it had seemed longer to the fastidious. For I behold some yawning, some also dozing. Nor is it a wonder: the vigils of the preceding night (for they were very long) excuse them. But what shall I say to those who slept then, and now nevertheless sleep? But I do not now proceed further to harrow up their bashfulness: it is enough to have touched upon it. I think that hereafter they will watch better, about to fear the cautery of our observance. In this hope we indulge them this time; and what reason demanded should be continued, out of charity toward them, although the disputation is left hanging, we share out, making an end where there was no end. But they themselves, for the indulgence shown them, let them glorify with us the Spouse of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all, God blessed forever. Amen.

37.1: I think we have no need now to urge you to watch, since that reproving sermon is certainly watchful, being still fresh, which, delivered by us charitably yesterday, has well awakened some. Therefore you hold in memory what I hold your assent to, that no one is saved without knowledge of himself, from which, of course, that mother of salvation, humility, arises, and the fear of the Lord, which, just as it is the beginning of wisdom, so also it is of salvation. No one, I say, is saved without that knowledge, who nevertheless has the age and the faculty of knowing. I say this on account of little children, and on account of the foolish, whose account is other. What, if you are ignorant of God? can there be hope of salvation with ignorance of God? Not even that. For you cannot either love one whom you do not know, or have one whom you have not loved. Know therefore yourself, that you may fear God; know him, that you may in like manner appease him. In the one you are initiated into wisdom, in the other you are perfected, because the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Ps. 111:10), and the fullness of the law is charity (Rom. 13:10). Both ignorances, then, are to be shunned by you, even as without the fear and love of God salvation cannot be. Other things are indifferent, having neither salvation, if they are known, nor damnation, if they are unknown.
37.2: I do not, however, say that the knowledge of letters is to be despised or neglected, which adorns the soul, and instructs it, and makes it able to instruct even others. But those two it behooves and profits to go before, in which the higher reason declared that the sum of salvation is constituted. And see whether he did not behold, and did not teach this order, who said: Sow for yourselves unto justice, reap the hope of life; and then at length, he says, enlighten for yourself the light of knowledge (Hos. 10:12). He placed knowledge last, as a picture, which cannot have standing upon emptiness, and therefore those two he set before and subjected to it, as if he were laying some solid thing under the picture. I shall already attend to knowledge in security, if I have first received security of life through the benefit of hope. You, then, have sown for yourself unto justice, if from the true knowledge of yourself you have awakened to fear God, humbled yourself, poured forth tears, poured out alms, and devoted yourself to the other works of piety, if you have afflicted the body with fastings and watchings, if you have wearied the breast with beatings, and the heavens with cries. For this is to sow unto justice. Seeds are good works, good strivings; seeds are the tears. They went, he says, and wept, casting their seeds. But what? will they weep forever? God forbid! But they will come with exultation, bearing their sheaves (Ps. 126:6). Justly with exultation, when they bring back the sheaves of glory. To that, you say, in the resurrection on the last day, and it is a very long expectation. Do not be broken in spirit, do not fail through faintness of spirit; you have meanwhile, of the first fruits of the Spirit, that which you may for the present reap in exultation. Sow, he says, for yourself unto justice, reap the hope of life. He does not send you only to the last day, when the thing will already be in reality, and not in hope; but he speaks of the present. Truly great joy, and much and exceedingly great exultation, when life comes.
37.3: But shall the hope of so great joy be without joy? 'Rejoicing in hope,' says the Apostle (Rom. 12:12). And David said that he would not have rejoiced, but had rejoiced, because he hoped that he would go into the house of the Lord (Ps. 122:1). He did not yet hold life, but he had indeed reaped the hope of life; and in himself he experienced the truth of Scripture testifying that not only the reward, but the very expectation itself of the righteous is joy. This the presumed pardon of offenses brings forth in the soul of him who has sown for himself unto justice, if indeed the efficacy of grace received for living more holily henceforth attests the pardon itself. Every one of you who feels these things to be transacted within himself knows what the Spirit says, whose voice and working never at all disagree among themselves. Therefore, then, he understands the things that are said, because the things he hears without he feels within. For he who speaks in us works in you, one and the same Spirit, dividing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11), to some indeed to speak, but to others to do what is good.
37.4: Whoever, then, of you, after those bitter and tearful beginnings of his conversion, rejoices that he has breathed again into hope and, lifted up by the wings of grace into a certain calm of heavenly consolation, has flown forth, he indeed already reaps, receiving the temporary fruit of his tears; and he has seen God, and has heard the voice saying: Give her of the fruit of her hands (Prov. 31:31). For how has he not seen God, who has tasted and seen that the Lord is sweet? How sweet and pleasant did he feel you, Lord Jesus, to whom by you not only are sins forgiven, but also the gift of holiness is granted; and not only that, but there is added besides, to the full measure of good things, the promise of eternal life! Happy he who has already reaped so much, having in the meantime indeed his fruit unto sanctification, but the end, eternal life! Justly did he who wept at having found himself rejoice at having seen the Lord, at the gaze, indeed, of whose mercy he has already lifted up so many sheaves: remission, sanctification, the hope of life. O how true is the saying which is read in the Prophet: They who sow in tears shall reap in exultation (Ps. 126:5). Where both kinds of knowledge are briefly comprehended, sowing indeed that of ourselves in tears; but that of God, reaping in joy.
37.5: This twofold knowledge, then, going before in us, that knowledge which may have grown over and above by no means puffs up, since it can bring nothing of earthly advantage or honor which is not surely inferior to conceived hope, and to the joy of hope now rooted more deeply in the soul. But hope does not confound, because the charity of God is diffused in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is given to us (Rom. 5:5). Therefore it does not confound, because this one infuses certainty. For through this the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit, that we are sons of God (Rom. 8:16). What, then, could come to us from our knowledge, however great, that would not be less than this glory, by which we are numbered among the sons of God? I have said too little: the world itself and all its fullness cannot even be regarded in comparison with it, even if it should wholly pass to each one of us in possession. But if ignorance of God holds us, how do we hope in him whom we do not know? if ignorance of ourselves, how shall we be humble, thinking ourselves to be something, when we are nothing? But we know that neither for the proud nor for the despairing is there a part or a fellowship in the lot of the saints.
37.6: Behold now with me, with how great care and solicitude we ought to repel these two ignorances from us, of which the one brings forth the beginning of every sin, the other its consummation; even as, of the two opposing kinds of knowledge, the one begets the beginning of wisdom, the other its perfection; the former the fear of the Lord, the latter charity. But that concerning the kinds of knowledge has been shown above. Now see concerning the ignorances. For just as the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Sir. 1:16), so the beginning of every sin is pride (Sir. 10:15); and as the love of God claims for itself the perfection of wisdom, so despair claims for itself the whole consummation of malice. And just as from the knowledge of yourself the fear of God comes into you, and likewise from the knowledge of God the love of God; so, on the contrary, from ignorance of yourself comes pride, and from ignorance of God comes despair. Now ignorance of yourself brings forth pride in you in this way, when your thought, deceived and deceiving, falsely tells you that you are better than you are. For this is indeed pride, this the beginning of every sin, when you are greater in your own eyes than before God, than in truth. And therefore of him who first sinned this great sin (I speak of the devil), it was said of him that he did not stand in the truth, but is a liar from the beginning (John 8:44); because what was in his thought was not in the truth. What if he disagreed from the truth in this, so as to think himself less and lower than truth held him to be? His ignorance would undoubtedly excuse him, and he would by no means be counted proud, nor would his iniquity be found so much unto hatred, as his humility perhaps unto grace. For if we clearly knew in what state God holds each one of us, we should indeed neither withdraw above nor below, acquiescing to the truth in all things. But now, because he has placed this counsel in darkness as its hiding place, and the word is hidden from us, so that no one knows whether he is worthy of love or of hatred (Eccl. 9:1); more justly and more safely indeed, according to the counsel of Truth himself, do we choose for ourselves the last place, from which afterward we may be led up higher with honor, than we presume one loftier, from which we must presently give way with shame (Luke 14:9-10).
37.7: There is, then, no danger in how much you ever humble yourself, in how much you ever count yourself less than you are, that is, than truth holds you. But it is a great evil, and a dreadful danger, if you exalt yourself ever so little beyond the true, if you prefer yourself in your thought even to one whom truth perhaps judges equal to you, or even superior. For just as if you pass through a door whose lintel, to speak intelligibly, is too low, it does no harm however much you bow yourself down; but it does harm if you raise yourself up even by the space of a transverse finger more than the measure of the door allows, so that you strike and, with your head injured, are dashed; so in the soul no amount whatever of humiliation is at all to be feared, but even the least rashly presumed raising up is dreadful and to be greatly dreaded. Wherefore do not, O man, compare yourself to your betters, do not to your inferiors, do not to anyone, do not to a single one. For what do you know, O man, whether that one, whom you perhaps repute the vilest and most wretched of all, whose most wicked and singularly foulest life you abhor, and therefore think him to be despised not only before yourself, who perhaps already trust that you live soberly, and justly, and piously, but even before all other wicked men as the most wicked of all: what do you know, I say, whether he is to become better than both you and them by the change of the right hand of the Most High, indeed in himself in the future, but in God already is? And therefore he did not will us to choose a middle place, not even the penultimate, not even the last among the last, but, he says, recline in the lowest place, that you may sit, indeed, the very last of all, and that you may not presume to prefer yourself, I do not say, to anyone, but even to compare yourself. Behold how great an evil comes from ignorance of ourselves, namely the sin of the devil, and the beginning of every sin, pride. What ignorance of God also brings forth, we shall see elsewhere. For now the brevity of the hour does not permit it, since today we have convened late. Therefore let it suffice that each one has now been admonished, lest he ignore himself, not only by our sermon, but also by the condescension itself of the Bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ our Lord, who is above all things God, blessed forever. Amen.
